paragraphs: This paper asks how to select a small amount of data that still permits a good reconstruction of a larger surface. It frames learning an input-output mapping as surface reconstruction, where the retained observations must preserve enough structure for an approximate reconstruction. Images are one example of the piecewise smooth surfaces considered.

The authors connect this selection problem to both information compression by removing data and learning how to teach. A useful teacher chooses examples according to what a model can reconstruct from them. Their key step is a statistical selection process guided by the model, with the system able to predict the approximated surface produced by the selected observations.

For piecewise smooth surfaces, the authors use mean field techniques to obtain a deterministic network and demonstrate image-data compression. The contribution makes example selection depend on the reconstruction it enables. This gives the retained data a clear purpose: each selection is evaluated through the surface that can be learned from the reduced information.
summary.tldr: A model-guided selection process compresses surface data by choosing sparse examples that support an approximate reconstruction.

title: Learning How to Teach or Selecting Minimal Surface Data

abstract: We demonstrate in this paper how certain forms of rule-based knowledge can be used to prestructure a neural network of nor(cid:173) malized basis functions and give a probabilistic interpretation of the network architecture. We describe several ways to assure that rule-based knowledge is preserved during training and present a method for complexity reduction that tries to minimize the num(cid:173) ber of rules and the number of conjuncts. After training the refined rules are extracted and analyzed.
originalAbstract: We demonstrate in this paper how certain forms of rule-based knowledge can be used to prestructure a neural network of nor(cid:173) malized basis functions and give a probabilistic interpretation of the network architecture. We describe several ways to assure that rule-based knowledge is preserved during training and present a method for complexity reduction that tries to minimize the num(cid:173) ber of rules and the number of conjuncts. After training the refined rules are extracted and analyzed.

paragraphs: The paper describes how existing rules can shape a neural network before training begins. Certain forms of rule-based knowledge determine the initial structure of a network built from normalized basis functions. The authors also give the architecture a probabilistic interpretation, connecting the network's organization to a meaningful interpretation of its computations.

Training must account for the knowledge used to construct the network. The authors describe several ways to preserve that rule-based knowledge as learning proceeds. This makes preservation an explicit part of the method: the initial rules influence both the architecture and the constraints on how it is refined.

The approach also includes complexity reduction, seeking fewer rules and fewer conjuncts, the individual conditions joined within a rule. After training, refined rules are extracted and analyzed. The overall contribution is a workflow that moves from rules into a trainable neural representation and back into inspectable rules, while addressing both knowledge preservation and the simplicity of the resulting description.
summary.tldr: Rule knowledge structures a neural network, guides knowledge-preserving training, and is recovered as simplified refined rules.

title: Network Structuring and Training Using Rule-based Knowledge

abstract: This paper shows that neural networks which use continuous acti(cid:173) vation functions have VC dimension at least as large as the square of the number of weights w. This result settles a long-standing open question, namely whether the well-known O( w log w) bound, known for hard-threshold nets, also held for more general sigmoidal nets. Implications for the number of samples needed for valid gen(cid:173) eralization are discussed.
originalAbstract: This paper shows that neural networks which use continuous acti(cid:173) vation functions have VC dimension at least as large as the square of the number of weights w. This result settles a long-standing open question, namely whether the well-known O( w log w) bound, known for hard-threshold nets, also held for more general sigmoidal nets. Implications for the number of samples needed for valid gen(cid:173) eralization are discussed.

paragraphs: This paper studies the expressive capacity of neural networks through VC dimension. This measure concerns how flexibly a model class can assign labels to examples and is relevant to reasoning about generalization. The question is how that capacity grows with the number of network weights and how activation functions affect the answer.

The authors establish a quadratic lower bound in the number of weights for networks using continuous activation functions. In other words, the capacity considered can grow at least as fast as the square of the weight count. This resolves whether the established O(w log w) bound for hard-threshold networks also extends to more general sigmoidal networks.

The result shows that the hard-threshold bound cannot simply be carried over to the more general setting. Counting weights alone therefore needs to be interpreted alongside the kind of activation used. The paper discusses consequences for the number of samples needed to support valid generalization. Its contribution is a theoretical capacity distinction with implications for sample requirements, rather than an empirical comparison of training procedures.
summary.tldr: A quadratic VC-dimension lower bound shows that the capacity bound for hard-threshold networks does not extend to general sigmoidal networks.

title: Neural Networks with Quadratic VC Dimension

abstract: We present a connectionist method for representing images that explicitly addresses their hierarchical nature. It blends data from neuroscience about whole-object viewpoint sensitive cells in inferotemporal cortex8 and attentional basis-field modulation in V4 3 with ideas about hierarchical descriptions based on microfeatures.5 ,11 The resulting model makes critical use of bottom-up and top-down pathways for analysis and synthesis.6 We illustrate the model with a simple example of representing information about faces.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a connectionist representation of images that explicitly captures their hierarchical organization. Its focus is the relationship between parts and wholes: image information should be represented at multiple connected levels. The model combines hierarchical descriptions based on small features with observations about visual processing in the brain.

Two neuroscience ingredients inform the design. One concerns cells in inferotemporal cortex whose responses to whole objects depend on viewpoint. The other concerns attentional basis-field modulation in V4. The authors bring these ideas together with microfeature-based descriptions to construct a representation that connects detailed image information with more complete object descriptions.

Both bottom-up and top-down pathways are essential to the resulting model, supporting analysis and synthesis. Information can therefore participate in interpreting a whole from its parts and in relating a whole representation back to lower-level detail. A simple face example illustrates the representation. The contribution is an explicit architecture for these hierarchical relationships, showing how multiple levels and both directions of processing can coexist in a neural image model.
summary.tldr: A neural image model links parts and wholes through hierarchical representations and essential bottom-up and top-down pathways.

title: Neural Models for Part-Whole Hierarchies

abstract: If globally high dimensional data has locally only low dimensional distribu(cid:173) tions, it is advantageous to perform a local dimensionality reduction before further processing the data. In this paper we examine several techniques for local dimensionality reduction in the context of locally weighted linear re(cid:173) gression. As possible candidates, we derive local versions of factor analysis regression, principle component regression, principle component regression on joint distributions, and partial least squares regression. After outlining the statistical bases of these methods, we perform Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate their robustness with respect to violations of their statistical as(cid:173) sumptions. One surprising outcome is that locally weighted partial least squares regression offers the best average results, thus outperforming even factor analysis, the theoretically most appealing of our candidate techniques.

paragraphs: Data can require many coordinates overall while occupying only a few important directions within a small neighborhood. This paper studies how to exploit that local simplicity before fitting a prediction model. The setting is locally weighted linear regression, where nearby observations receive greater influence on the prediction being made.

The authors derive local forms of several dimensionality-reduction methods: factor analysis regression, principal component regression, principal component regression on joint distributions, and partial least squares regression. Each offers a different statistical route to reducing the variables used in local prediction. Comparing them within the same regression setting makes it possible to ask which assumptions are useful in practice.

Monte Carlo simulations test robustness when the methods' statistical assumptions are violated. Locally weighted partial least squares produces the best average results, outperforming factor analysis despite the latter's theoretical appeal. The finding emphasizes that an attractive statistical model is not enough to determine practical performance. For the examined local regression problems, resilience to assumption violations matters when choosing a reduced representation.
summary.tldr: Locally weighted partial least squares performs best on average in simulations comparing local dimensionality-reduction methods.

title: Local Dimensionality Reduction

abstract: A model of motion detection is presented. The model contains three stages. The first stage is unoriented and is selective for con(cid:173) trast polarities. The next two stages work in parallel. A phase insensitive stage pools across different contrast polarities through a spatiotemporal filter and thus can detect first and second order motion. A phase sensitive stage keeps contrast polarities separate, each of which is filtered through a spatiotemporal filter, and thus only first order motion can be detected. Differential phase sensitiv(cid:173) ity can therefore account for the detection of first and second order motion. Phase insensitive detectors correspond to cortical complex cells, and phase sensitive detectors to simple cells.

A phase sensitive stage keeps contrast polarities separate, each of which is filtered through a spatiotemporal filter, and thus only first order motion can be detected. Differential phase sensitiv(cid:173) ity can therefore account for the detection of first and second order motion. paragraphs: The paper proposes a motion-detection model that explains different motion sensitivities through the handling of contrast polarity. Its first stage responds selectively to different polarities without selecting an orientation. The subsequent processing splits into two parallel pathways, creating different capabilities from the same initial representation of the visual input.

One pathway pools across contrast polarities through a filter operating over space and time. This pathway is insensitive to phase and can detect both first-order and second-order motion. The other keeps the polarities separate and applies spatial and temporal filtering to each. This phase-sensitive pathway detects only first-order motion in the proposed model.

The authors associate phase-insensitive detectors with cortical complex cells and phase-sensitive detectors with simple cells. The explanatory point is that the distinction between the two motion responses can arise from a concrete processing choice: combining polarity channels or preserving their separation. A common initial stage and two differently organized pathways therefore account for the model's different motion-detection abilities.
summary.tldr: Two parallel pathways explain motion-detection differences by either pooling contrast polarities or keeping them separate.

title: Detection of First and Second Order Motion

abstract: The learning of many visual perceptual tasks has been shown to be specific to practiced stimuli, while new stimuli require re-Iearning from scratch. Here we demonstrate generalization using a novel paradigm in motion discrimination where learning has been previ(cid:173) ously shown to be specific. We trained subjects to discriminate the directions of moving dots, and verified the previous results that learning does not transfer from the trained direction to a new one. However, by tracking the subjects' performance across time in the new direction, we found that their rate of learning doubled. Therefore, learning generalized in a task previously considered too difficult for generalization. We also replicated, in the second ex(cid:173) periment, transfer following training with "easy" stimuli. The specificity of perceptual learning and the dichotomy between learning of "easy" vs. "difficult" tasks were hypothesized to involve different learning processes, operating at different visual cortical areas. Here we show how to interpret these results in terms of signal detection theory. With the assumption of limited computational resources, we obtain the observed phenomena - direct transfer and change of learning rate - for increasing levels of task 'difficulty. It appears that human generalization concurs with the expected behavior of a generic discrimination system.

paragraphs: Visual learning can appear highly specific: practice improves performance on a trained stimulus without immediately helping on a new one. This paper revisits that conclusion using moving-dot direction discrimination. It asks whether transfer might be visible in how quickly people learn a new direction, even when their initial performance shows no benefit.

The experiments reproduce the absence of immediate transfer between directions. However, tracking performance over time reveals that the learning rate for the new direction doubles. A second experiment also reproduces transfer after training with easy stimuli. These observations distinguish two benefits of prior practice: starting a new task better and improving at it faster.

The authors interpret both patterns through signal detection theory with limited computational resources. Their account produces direct transfer and changes in learning rate as task difficulty increases. This provides a common explanation for results previously associated with different learning processes or visual areas, and shows why measuring only immediate performance can overlook a meaningful form of generalization.
summary.tldr: Visual practice can generalize by doubling learning speed on a new motion direction even when immediate performance does not improve.

title: Mechanisms of Generalization in Perceptual Learning

paragraphs: The paper analyzes calcium oscillations inside an insulin-secreting hamster cell under pharmacological stimulation. Intracellular calcium helps regulate cellular processes, and its signals can form complex patterns across both space and time. The authors use independent component analysis to investigate whether measured mixtures contain distinguishable independent temporal signals.

A fast fixed-point ICA algorithm performs blind source separation on five differently mixed input signals from the cell. The analysis identifies two significant independent components. One has an average oscillation period of 68 seconds. The other contains high-frequency activity with a broad power spectrum and considerable spectral density. These findings distinguish components with different temporal characteristics within the measured calcium dynamics.

The authors report agreement with a separate study of high-frequency calcium oscillations. The decomposition provides evidence about the structure of the recorded signals, but their biological function remains unresolved. The paper explicitly calls for further theoretical and experimental work to determine the functional impact of these independent signals on intracellular signaling. Its contribution is signal separation and characterization, with that functional question left open.
summary.tldr: ICA separates five calcium recordings into two significant components with distinct temporal behavior, while their functional roles remain unresolved.

title: Independent Component Analysis of Intracellular Calcium Spike Data

abstract: We describe a method to learn to make sequential stopping decisions, such as those made along a processing pipeline. We envision a scenario in which a series of decisions must be made as to whether to continue to process. Further processing costs time and resources, but may add value. Our goal is to create, based on historic data, a series of decision rules (one at each stage in the pipeline) that decide, based on information gathered up to that point, whether to continue processing the part. We demonstrate how our framework encompasses problems from manufacturing to vision processing. We derive a quadratic (in the number of decisions) bound on testing performance and provide empirical results on object detection.

paragraphs: This paper studies decisions about whether to continue processing an item through a sequence of stages. Continuing consumes time and resources but may also produce additional value. The learning problem is to decide when that extra processing is worthwhile, using only the information available at the current stage.

The proposed framework learns a separate decision rule for each stage from historical data. Together, those rules determine how far an item proceeds through the pipeline. This connects learning to the structure of a processing sequence: later decisions can use information accumulated along the way, while earlier decisions must act before that information has been gathered.

The authors show how the framework covers settings ranging from manufacturing to vision processing, and they provide empirical results for object detection. They also derive a testing-performance bound with quadratic dependence on the number of decisions. This supplies a theoretical account of how the length of the decision sequence enters the bound, alongside an application demonstrating the framework in visual processing.
summary.tldr: Chained boosting learns stage-specific rules for deciding whether the potential value of further processing justifies its cost.

title: Chained Boosting

abstract: The visual and auditory map alignment in the Superior Colliculus (SC) of barn owl is important for its accurate localization for prey behavior. Prism learning or Blindness may interfere this alignment and cause loss of the capability of accurate prey. However, juvenile barn owl could recover its sensory map alignment by shifting its auditory map. The adaptation of this map alignment is believed based on activity dependent axon developing in Inferior Colliculus (IC). A model is built to explore this mechanism. In this model, axon growing process is instructed by an inhibitory network in SC while the strength of the inhibition adjusted by Spike Timing Dependent Plasticity (STDP). We test and analyze this mechanism by application of the neural structures involved in spatial localization in a robotic system.

paragraphs: Barn owls rely on aligned visual and auditory maps to locate prey accurately. Changes to vision, including prism-induced displacement or blindness, can disrupt that alignment. Juvenile owls can recover alignment by shifting their auditory map. This paper builds a model to investigate a proposed neural mechanism behind that adaptation.

The proposed mechanism involves activity-dependent axon development in the inferior colliculus. In the model, an inhibitory network in the superior colliculus guides axon growth. The strength of that inhibition changes through spike timing dependent plasticity, linking the adjustment of inhibitory connections to the relative timing of neural activity. Together, these components describe how neural activity could guide changes in the spatial mapping of sound.

The authors implement the relevant spatial-localization structures in a robotic system to test and analyze the mechanism. The robot provides a setting for examining how the modeled structures interact during sensory alignment. The contribution is a concrete computational and robotic investigation of a biologically motivated adaptation process, while the biological mechanism itself is presented as a proposed explanation.
summary.tldr: A robotic barn owl tests a model in which plastic inhibition guides axon growth to realign auditory and visual maps.

title: Bio-inspired Real Time Sensory Map Realignment in a Robotic Barn Owl

abstract: Resting state activity is brain activation that arises in the absence of any task, and is usually measured in awake subjects during prolonged fMRI scanning sessions where the only instruction given is to close the eyes and do nothing. It has been recognized in recent years that resting state activity is implicated in a wide variety of brain function. While certain networks of brain areas have different levels of activation at rest and during a task, there is nevertheless significant similarity between activations in the two cases. This suggests that recordings of resting state activity can be used as a source of unlabeled data to augment discriminative regression techniques in a semi-supervised setting. We evaluate this setting empirically yielding three main results: (i) regression tends to be improved by the use of Laplacian regularization even when no additional unlabeled data are available, (ii) resting state data may have a similar marginal distribution to that recorded during the execution of a visual processing task reinforcing the hypothesis that these conditions have similar types of activation, and (iii) this source of information can be broadly exploited to improve the robustness of empirical inference in fMRI studies, an inherently data poor domain.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether brain recordings collected during rest can improve analyses of recordings collected during a task. Resting activity occurs without an assigned task, yet it shares substantial structure with task-related activity. The authors use this similarity to motivate treating resting recordings as unlabeled examples in a semi-supervised regression approach.

The approach uses Laplacian regularization, which encourages predictions to respect relationships among the observed data. Their empirical evaluation finds that this regularization tends to improve regression even without adding unlabeled recordings. That finding distinguishes the value of the regularization itself from the additional value that resting-state data might provide.

The results also suggest that resting recordings may have a marginal distribution similar to recordings from a visual processing task. This supports, without establishing equivalence between the conditions, the idea that resting data contain useful information for task-based analysis. The broader contribution is a way to strengthen inference in fMRI studies, where labeled observations are scarce, by drawing on structure in recordings that do not require task labels.
summary.tldr: Resting-state brain recordings can provide unlabeled information that helps make task-based fMRI regression more robust.

title: Augmenting Feature-driven fMRI Analyses: Semi-supervised learning and resting state activity

abstract: Energy disaggregation is the task of taking a whole-home energy signal and separating it into its component appliances. Studies have shown that having device-level energy information can cause users to conserve significant amounts of energy, but current electricity meters only report whole-home data. Thus, developing algorithmic methods for disaggregation presents a key technical challenge in the effort to maximize energy conservation. In this paper, we examine a large scale energy disaggregation task, and apply a novel extension of sparse coding to this problem. In particular, we develop a method, based upon structured prediction, for discriminatively training sparse coding algorithms specifically to maximize disaggregation performance. We show that this significantly improves the performance of sparse coding algorithms on the energy task and illustrate how these disaggregation results can provide useful information about energy usage.

paragraphs: Energy disaggregation separates a home's total electricity signal into contributions from individual appliances. The motivation is that device-level information can help people conserve energy, whereas conventional meters provide only a household total. The paper tackles the computational problem of recovering useful appliance information from that combined measurement.

The authors extend sparse coding and train it specifically for disaggregation. Their method uses structured prediction to make the training discriminative: the learning objective targets performance on separating the appliance contributions. The important methodological choice is to shape the representation around the task the system ultimately needs to perform.

On a large-scale energy disaggregation task, the authors report a significant improvement over the sparse coding algorithms considered. They also illustrate how the resulting appliance estimates reveal useful information about energy usage. The demonstrated result concerns better disaggregation and informative outputs; the conservation motivation comes from the cited relationship between device-level information and user behavior.
summary.tldr: Training sparse coding directly for appliance separation significantly improves its performance on a large-scale household energy disaggregation task.

title: Energy Disaggregation via Discriminative Sparse Coding

abstract: Matrix factorization in the presence of missing data is at the core of many computer vision problems such as structure from motion (SfM), non-rigid SfM and photometric stereo. We formulate the problem of matrix factorization with missing data as a low-rank semidefinite program (LRSDP) with the advantage that: $1)$ an efficient quasi-Newton implementation of the LRSDP enables us to solve large-scale factorization problems, and $2)$ additional constraints such as ortho-normality, required in orthographic SfM, can be directly incorporated in the new formulation. Our empirical evaluations suggest that, under the conditions of matrix completion theory, the proposed algorithm finds the optimal solution, and also requires fewer observations compared to the current state-of-the-art algorithms. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in solving the affine SfM problem, non-rigid SfM and photometric stereo problems.

paragraphs: Many vision problems require factoring a matrix even though some entries were never observed. They may also impose geometric requirements on the factors, such as orthonormality in orthographic structure from motion. This paper develops a formulation that handles missing observations and additional constraints within the same optimization problem.

The authors express matrix factorization as a low-rank semidefinite program and solve it using an efficient quasi-Newton implementation. The formulation supports large-scale problems while allowing constraints to be incorporated directly. That combination matters because a useful reconstruction must both fit the available measurements and respect the structure required by its application.

Empirical evaluations suggest that, under the conditions of matrix completion theory, the algorithm reaches the optimal solution and needs fewer observations than the compared state-of-the-art algorithms. This is experimental evidence under stated conditions, rather than an unconditional optimality guarantee. The paper also demonstrates effectiveness on affine and non-rigid structure from motion and photometric stereo, showing the formulation's usefulness across several vision tasks.
summary.tldr: A low-rank semidefinite formulation enables large matrix factorizations with missing data and directly incorporates application-specific constraints.

title: Large-Scale Matrix Factorization with Missing Data under Additional Constraints

abstract: We consider the estimation of an i.i.d.\ vector $\xbf \in \R^n$ from measurements $\ybf \in \R^m$ obtained by a general cascade model consisting of a known linear transform followed by a probabilistic componentwise (possibly nonlinear) measurement channel. We present a method, called adaptive generalized approximate message passing (Adaptive GAMP), that enables joint learning of the statistics of the prior and measurement channel along with estimation of the unknown vector $\xbf$. The proposed algorithm is a generalization of a recently-developed method by Vila and Schniter that uses expectation-maximization (EM) iterations where the posteriors in the E-steps are computed via approximate message passing. The techniques can be applied to a large class of learning problems including the learning of sparse priors in compressed sensing or identification of linear-nonlinear cascade models in dynamical systems and neural spiking processes. We prove that for large i.i.d.\ Gaussian transform matrices the asymptotic componentwise behavior of the adaptive GAMP algorithm is predicted by a simple set of scalar state evolution equations. This analysis shows that the adaptive GAMP method can yield asymptotically consistent parameter estimates, which implies that the algorithm achieves a reconstruction quality equivalent to the oracle algorithm that knows the correct parameter values. The adaptive GAMP methodology thus provides a systematic, general and computationally efficient method applicable to a large range of complex linear-nonlinear models with provable guarantees.

paragraphs: Adaptive generalized approximate message passing addresses recovery of an unknown vector when the statistical assumptions needed for recovery must also be learned. Measurements arise from a known linear transformation followed by a probabilistic channel acting on individual components, which may be nonlinear. The unknown vector's entries are assumed to be independent and identically distributed.

The algorithm jointly estimates the vector and learns parameters describing its prior and the measurement channel. It extends an earlier approach that combines expectation-maximization with approximate message passing. This makes the framework applicable to problems such as learning sparse priors in compressed sensing and identifying linear–nonlinear models of dynamical systems or neural spiking.

In that setting, reconstruction can match an oracle that already knows the correct parameters, giving conditional theoretical support for learning those parameters during recovery.
summary.tldr: Adaptive GAMP jointly learns unknown statistical parameters and reconstructs signals, with asymptotic guarantees for large Gaussian transformation matrices.

title: Approximate Message Passing with Consistent Parameter Estimation and Applications to Sparse Learning

abstract: We present a novel marginalized particle Gaussian process (MPGP) regression, which provides a fast, accurate online Bayesian filtering framework to model the latent function. Using a state space model established by the data construction procedure, our MPGP recursively filters out the estimation of hidden function values by a Gaussian mixture. Meanwhile, it provides a new online method for training hyperparameters with a number of weighted particles. We demonstrate the estimated performance of our MPGP on both simulated and real large data sets. The results show that our MPGP is a robust estimation algorithm with high computational efficiency, which outperforms other state-of-art sparse GP methods.

Using a state space model established by the data construction procedure, our MPGP recursively filters out the estimation of hidden function values by a Gaussian mixture. Meanwhile, it provides a new online method for training hyperparameters with a number of weighted particles. We demonstrate the estimated performance of our MPGP on both simulated and real large data sets. The results show that our MPGP is a robust estimation algorithm with high computational efficiency, which outperforms other state-of-art sparse GP methods.

paragraphs: The paper introduces marginalized particle Gaussian process regression, or MPGP, for estimating an underlying function as data arrive. Its goal is online Bayesian filtering: repeatedly updating estimates of hidden function values while representing uncertainty. This makes the updating process, rather than a single fixed fit, central to the regression method.

The approach builds a state space model from the data construction procedure. Within that model, it recursively represents estimates of hidden function values using a Gaussian mixture. It also learns hyperparameters online through a collection of weighted particles. These are two connected parts of the method: one tracks the hidden function, while the other updates the settings governing the model.

The authors evaluate MPGP on simulated data and large real datasets. They report robust estimation, high computational efficiency, and better performance than the sparse Gaussian process methods used for comparison. These findings support the proposed combination of recursive function estimation and particle-based hyperparameter learning as an effective online regression framework in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: MPGP combines Gaussian-mixture filtering with weighted-particle hyperparameter learning for efficient online Gaussian process regression.

title: A Marginalized Particle Gaussian Process Regression

abstract: Time series often have a temporal hierarchy, with information that is spread out over multiple time scales. Common recurrent neural networks, however, do not explicitly accommodate such a hierarchy, and most research on them has been focusing on training algorithms rather than on their basic architecture. In this pa- per we study the effect of a hierarchy of recurrent neural networks on processing time series. Here, each layer is a recurrent network which receives the hidden state of the previous layer as input. This architecture allows us to perform hi- erarchical processing on difficult temporal tasks, and more naturally capture the structure of time series. We show that they reach state-of-the-art performance for recurrent networks in character-level language modelling when trained with sim- ple stochastic gradient descent. We also offer an analysis of the different emergent time scales.

paragraphs: Time series can contain structure unfolding over several temporal scales. This paper investigates whether a hierarchy of recurrent networks provides a useful architecture for processing that structure. Its focus is the organization of the network itself, addressing a setting where much recurrent-network research had concentrated on training procedures.

The architecture stacks recurrent networks so that each layer receives the hidden state of the preceding layer as its input. Every layer therefore performs recurrent processing on a representation produced below it. This enables hierarchical treatment of temporal information and gives the model a way to represent structure at multiple levels while processing difficult sequence tasks.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance among recurrent networks on character-level language modeling using simple stochastic gradient descent. They also analyze the different time scales that emerge in the trained hierarchy. These findings connect architectural depth with both predictive performance and the organization of temporal representations, without requiring the reported improvement to be attributed to a more elaborate training algorithm.
summary.tldr: Stacked recurrent networks achieve strong character-level language-modeling results with simple stochastic gradient descent and exhibit different emergent time scales.

title: Training and Analysing Deep Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Stochastic And-Or grammars compactly represent both compositionality and reconfigurability and have been used to model different types of data such as images and events. We present a unified formalization of stochastic And-Or grammars that is agnostic to the type of the data being modeled, and propose an unsupervised approach to learning the structures as well as the parameters of such grammars. Starting from a trivial initial grammar, our approach iteratively induces compositions and reconfigurations in a unified manner and optimizes the posterior probability of the grammar. In our empirical evaluation, we applied our approach to learning event grammars and image grammars and achieved comparable or better performance than previous approaches.

paragraphs: Stochastic And-Or grammars represent both how parts compose larger structures and how those structures can take alternative forms. They have been used for data such as images and events. The paper develops a unified formalization that does not depend on which type of data is being modeled.

The authors also propose an unsupervised procedure for learning both a grammar's structure and its parameters. Starting from a trivial grammar, the method repeatedly introduces compositions and reconfigurations through a unified process. It optimizes the grammar's posterior probability, allowing the organization of the model itself to be learned alongside its probabilistic quantities.

Empirical evaluations apply the approach to event grammars and image grammars, obtaining performance comparable to or better than previous approaches. These results support the usefulness of one learning framework across both applications. The main contribution is the combination of a shared formalism with structural learning: the method can build richer grammatical organization from a simple starting point rather than requiring that organization to be specified in advance.
summary.tldr: A unified unsupervised method learns And-Or grammar structure and parameters, with comparable or better results on image and event grammars.

title: Unsupervised Structure Learning of Stochastic And-Or Grammars

abstract: Many fundamental image-related problems involve deconvolution operators. Real blur degradation seldom complies with an deal linear convolution model due to camera noise, saturation, image compression, to name a few. Instead of perfectly modeling outliers, which is rather challenging from a generative model perspective, we develop a deep convolutional neural network to capture the characteristics of degradation. We note directly applying existing deep neural networks does not produce reasonable results. Our solution is to establish the connection between traditional optimization-based schemes and a neural network architecture where a novel, separable structure is introduced as a reliable support for robust deconvolution against artifacts. Our network contains two submodules, both trained in a supervised manner with proper initialization. They yield decent performance on non-blind image deconvolution compared to previous generative-model based methods.

paragraphs: Image deconvolution becomes difficult when actual image degradation differs from an ideal linear blur model. Camera noise, saturation, and compression can all create such differences. This paper develops a convolutional neural network that learns characteristics of the degradation, addressing the challenge of explicitly modeling these effects within a generative approach.

The architecture is central to the proposal. The authors report that directly applying existing deep networks does not produce reasonable results. They instead connect traditional optimization-based methods to a neural network design and introduce a separable structure intended to support deconvolution that is robust to artifacts. The resulting network has two submodules, both trained with supervision and appropriate initialization.

The reported application is non-blind image deconvolution, and the authors describe performance as decent compared with earlier generative-model methods. The stated result supports the usefulness of a purpose-built architecture for this task without claiming universal superiority. Its broader methodological point is that optimization-based structure can guide a learned image-restoration system when a simple degradation model is inadequate.
summary.tldr: A supervised convolutional network with an optimization-inspired separable structure addresses non-blind image deconvolution under imperfect blur models.

title: Deep Convolutional Neural Network for Image Deconvolution

abstract: The Continuous-Time Hidden Markov Model (CT-HMM) is an attractive approach to modeling disease progression due to its ability to describe noisy observations arriving irregularly in time. However, the lack of an efficient parameter learning algorithm for CT-HMM restricts its use to very small models or requires unrealistic constraints on the state transitions. In this paper, we present the first complete characterization of efficient EM-based learning methods for CT-HMM models. We demonstrate that the learning problem consists of two challenges: the estimation of posterior state probabilities and the computation of end-state conditioned statistics. We solve the first challenge by reformulating the estimation problem in terms of an equivalent discrete time-inhomogeneous hidden Markov model. The second challenge is addressed by adapting three approaches from the continuous time Markov chain literature to the CT-HMM domain. We demonstrate the use of CT-HMMs with more than 100 states to visualize and predict disease progression using a glaucoma dataset and an Alzheimer's disease dataset.

paragraphs: Disease measurements can be noisy and collected at uneven intervals. Continuous-time hidden Markov models accommodate both features, describing progression through hidden states between observations. Their usefulness has been restricted by difficult parameter learning, which previously limited models to small state spaces or required unrealistic constraints on how states could change.

The paper organizes efficient expectation-maximization learning around two separate calculations. One estimates the probabilities of hidden states given the observations. The authors reformulate this calculation as an equivalent discrete-time hidden Markov model whose transitions vary with time. The other computes statistics conditioned on endpoint states, using three methods adapted from continuous-time Markov chain research.

This separation gives a complete characterization of efficient EM-based learning methods for these models. The authors demonstrate models with more than 100 states on glaucoma and Alzheimer's disease datasets, using them to visualize and predict progression. The demonstrations show that the learning approach supports substantially richer state descriptions while retaining a model suited to irregular, noisy observations.
summary.tldr: Efficient EM learning enables continuous-time hidden Markov disease models with more than 100 states for irregular, noisy observations.

title: Efficient Learning of Continuous-Time Hidden Markov Models for Disease Progression

abstract: The paradigm of multi-task learning is that one can achieve better generalization by learning tasks jointly and thus exploiting the similarity between the tasks rather than learning them independently of each other. While previously the relationship between tasks had to be user-defined in the form of an output kernel, recent approaches jointly learn the tasks and the output kernel. As the output kernel is a positive semidefinite matrix, the resulting optimization problems are not scalable in the number of tasks as an eigendecomposition is required in each step. Using the theory of positive semidefinite kernels we show in this paper that for a certain class of regularizers on the output kernel, the constraint of being positive semidefinite can be dropped as it is automatically satisfied for the relaxed problem. This leads to an unconstrained dual problem which can be solved efficiently. Experiments on several multi-task and multi-class data sets illustrate the efficacy of our approach in terms of computational efficiency as well as generalization performance.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning uses relationships between prediction tasks to help them learn together. An output kernel represents those relationships as a matrix. Learning this matrix alongside the tasks avoids requiring users to specify it, but enforcing its positive semidefinite structure can require an eigendecomposition at every optimization step, making many-task problems expensive.

The paper shows that, for a particular class of regularizers, explicitly imposing the positive semidefinite constraint is unnecessary. The relaxed problem automatically satisfies it. This qualification is central: the result identifies a useful class of formulations in which the structural requirement is preserved even after removing the explicit constraint.

That observation leads to an unconstrained dual optimization problem that can be solved efficiently. Experiments on several multi-task and multi-class datasets demonstrate computational efficiency and generalization performance. The practical significance is that learning task relationships need not always carry the repeated matrix-decomposition cost associated with directly enforcing the kernel constraint, provided the regularizer belongs to the class covered by the result.
summary.tldr: For a specified class of regularizers, output-kernel learning can drop an explicit matrix constraint and use an efficient unconstrained dual formulation.

title: Efficient Output Kernel Learning for Multiple Tasks

abstract: How do people learn about complex functional structure? Taking inspiration from other areas of cognitive science, we propose that this is accomplished by harnessing compositionality: complex structure is decomposed into simpler building blocks. We formalize this idea within the framework of Bayesian regression using a grammar over Gaussian process kernels. We show that participants prefer compositional over non-compositional function extrapolations, that samples from the human prior over functions are best described by a compositional model, and that people perceive compositional functions as more predictable than their non-compositional but otherwise similar counterparts. We argue that the compositional nature of intuitive functions is consistent with broad principles of human cognition.

paragraphs: When people learn a complex relationship, they may understand it by combining simpler patterns. This paper investigates that compositional explanation of intuitive function learning. Its central proposal is that complex functional structure is represented through reusable building blocks, giving people a structured way to generalize beyond the observations they have seen.

The authors formalize the proposal using Bayesian regression with a grammar over Gaussian process kernels. The grammar supplies a way to construct more complex function models from simpler components. This makes compositionality a specific modeling hypothesis that can be compared with human judgments, rather than only a verbal description of how learning might work.

The reported findings provide three forms of support. Participants prefer compositional extrapolations, samples from their prior expectations over functions are best described by a compositional model, and they judge compositional functions as more predictable than otherwise similar noncompositional ones. Together, these results support the proposed account of intuitive functions. The authors interpret that account as consistent with broader principles of cognition, rather than proving that all human function learning uses one mechanism.
summary.tldr: Human extrapolation, prior expectations, and predictability judgments support a compositional account of intuitive function learning.

title: Probing the Compositionality of Intuitive Functions

abstract: Nonlinear independent component analysis (ICA) provides an appealing framework for unsupervised feature learning, but the models proposed so far are not identifiable. Here, we first propose a new intuitive principle of unsupervised deep learning from time series which uses the nonstationary structure of the data. Our learning principle, time-contrastive learning (TCL), finds a representation which allows optimal discrimination of time segments (windows). Surprisingly, we show how TCL can be related to a nonlinear ICA model, when ICA is redefined to include temporal nonstationarities. In particular, we show that TCL combined with linear ICA estimates the nonlinear ICA model up to point-wise transformations of the sources, and this solution is unique --- thus providing the first identifiability result for nonlinear ICA which is rigorous, constructive, as well as very general.

paragraphs: Nonlinear independent component analysis aims to recover underlying sources from nonlinear observations, making it appealing for unsupervised feature learning. A central obstacle is identifiability: the earlier models discussed in the abstract do not determine a unique source explanation. This paper uses changes in a time series’ statistical structure to address that obstacle.

The proposed principle, time-contrastive learning, learns a representation that optimally distinguishes different time windows. Its learning signal comes from temporal nonstationarity. The authors then connect this discrimination task to a nonlinear ICA model redefined to include those temporal changes, giving the learned features a source-recovery interpretation.

When combined with linear ICA, time-contrastive learning estimates that nonlinear ICA model up to pointwise transformations of the sources. The solution is unique within this remaining ambiguity. The authors present this as the first rigorous, constructive, and very general identifiability result for nonlinear ICA. The qualification about source transformations is essential: the guarantee identifies the model to that equivalence, rather than recovering a completely fixed numerical representation of every source.
summary.tldr: Time-contrastive learning uses temporal nonstationarity to identify a nonlinear ICA model up to pointwise source transformations.

title: Unsupervised Feature Extraction by Time-Contrastive Learning and Nonlinear ICA

abstract: Learning a regression function using censored or interval-valued output data is an important problem in fields such as genomics and medicine. The goal is to learn a real-valued prediction function, and the training output labels indicate an interval of possible values. Whereas most existing algorithms for this task are linear models, in this paper we investigate learning nonlinear tree models. We propose to learn a tree by minimizing a margin-based discriminative objective function, and we provide a dynamic programming algorithm for computing the optimal solution in log-linear time. We show empirically that this algorithm achieves state-of-the-art speed and prediction accuracy in a benchmark of several data sets.

paragraphs: This paper studies regression when training labels specify intervals of possible outcomes rather than exact numerical values. Such data arise in settings involving censored measurements, including genomics and medicine. The learner must still produce a real-valued prediction, but its training procedure needs to work with the partial information provided by each interval.

The authors investigate nonlinear tree models for this task, where most existing approaches use linear models. They propose a margin-based discriminative objective for learning the tree and give a dynamic programming algorithm that computes the optimal solution in log-linear time. This combines a nonlinear prediction model with an optimization procedure that has a stated efficiency guarantee.

On a benchmark containing several datasets, the method achieves state-of-the-art speed and prediction accuracy empirically. The result supports trees as a practical approach to interval-valued supervision, with both computational and predictive benefits in the reported evaluation. The algorithm’s optimality concerns the optimization problem it solves; the accuracy finding comes from the benchmark experiments.
summary.tldr: Maximum Margin Interval Trees learn nonlinear regression models from interval-valued labels using an efficient dynamic programming algorithm.

title: Maximum Margin Interval Trees

abstract: We introduce a simple yet surprisingly powerful model to incorporate attention in action recognition and human object interaction tasks. Our proposed attention module can be trained with or without extra supervision, and gives a sizable boost in accuracy while keeping the network size and computational cost nearly the same. It leads to significant improvements over state of the art base architecture on three standard action recognition benchmarks across still images and videos, and establishes new state of the art on MPII dataset with 12.5% relative improvement. We also perform an extensive analysis of our attention module both empirically and analytically. In terms of the latter, we introduce a novel derivation of bottom-up and top-down attention as low-rank approximations of bilinear pooling methods (typically used for fine-grained classification). From this perspective, our attention formulation suggests a novel characterization of action recognition as a fine-grained recognition problem.

We also perform an extensive analysis of our attention module both empirically and analytically. paragraphs: Recognizing actions and human interactions with objects requires a model to emphasize relevant visual information. This paper introduces an attention module for those tasks that can be trained either with additional supervision or without it. Its practical attraction is that it improves recognition while leaving network size and computational cost nearly unchanged.

The authors evaluate the module on three standard action-recognition benchmarks covering still images and videos. They report significant improvements over a state-of-the-art base architecture. On MPII, the method establishes a new state of the art with a 12.5% relative improvement. That figure describes a relative gain, rather than an increase of 12.5 percentage points.

The paper also develops an analytical explanation of the attention mechanism. It derives bottom-up and top-down attention as low-rank approximations to bilinear pooling, a method associated with fine-grained classification. This connection suggests viewing action recognition as a fine-grained recognition problem. Together, the empirical and analytical results present attention as both a lightweight architectural improvement and a way to understand the visual distinctions involved in recognizing actions.
summary.tldr: A lightweight attention module improves action recognition and connects attention to bilinear pooling for fine-grained classification.

title: Attentional Pooling for Action Recognition

abstract: Autoregressive feedback is considered a necessity for successful unconditional text generation using stochastic sequence models. However, such feedback is known to introduce systematic biases into the training process and it obscures a principle of generation: committing to global information and forgetting local nuances. We show that a non-autoregressive deep state space model with a clear separation of global and local uncertainty can be built from only two ingredients: An independent noise source and a deterministic transition function. Recent advances on flow-based variational inference can be used to train an evidence lower-bound without resorting to annealing, auxiliary losses or similar measures. The result is a highly interpretable generative model on par with comparable auto-regressive models on the task of word generation.

However, such feedback is known to introduce systematic biases into the training process and it obscures a principle of generation: committing to global information and forgetting local nuances. We show that a non-autoregressive deep state space model with a clear separation of global and local uncertainty can be built from only two ingredients: An independent noise source and a deterministic transition function. paragraphs: Autoregressive generation feeds earlier outputs back into the process that produces later ones. This paper challenges the view that such feedback is necessary for successful unconditional generation with stochastic sequence models. The authors argue that feedback can introduce systematic training biases and obscure a useful separation between global information and local variation.

They construct a non-autoregressive deep state space model from an independent noise source and a deterministic transition function. The model explicitly separates global and local uncertainty. This organization supports the paper's view of generation as committing to broader information while allowing local nuances to be forgotten, and contributes to the model's stated interpretability.

Training uses advances in flow-based variational inference to optimize an evidence lower bound. The authors report doing so without annealing, auxiliary losses, or similar interventions. On word generation, the resulting model performs on par with comparable autoregressive models. That result supports the feasibility of their alternative construction for the evaluated task, rather than establishing that autoregressive feedback is unnecessary in every generation setting.
summary.tldr: A non-autoregressive state space model separates global and local uncertainty and matches comparable autoregressive models on word generation.

title: Deep State Space Models for Unconditional Word Generation

abstract: We propose the algorithms for online convex optimization which lead to cumulative squared constraint violations of the form $\sum\limits_{t=1}^T\big([g(x_t)]_+\big)^2=O(T^{1-\beta})$, where $\beta\in(0,1)$. Previous literature has focused on long-term constraints of the form $\sum\limits_{t=1}^Tg(x_t)$. There, strictly feasible solutions can cancel out the effects of violated constraints. In contrast, the new form heavily penalizes large constraint violations and cancellation effects cannot occur. Furthermore, useful bounds on the single step constraint violation $[g(x_t)]_+$ are derived. For convex objectives, our regret bounds generalize existing bounds, and for strongly convex objectives we give improved regret bounds. In numerical experiments, we show that our algorithm closely follows the constraint boundary leading to low cumulative violation.

In contrast, the new form heavily penalizes large constraint violations and cancellation effects cannot occur. Furthermore, useful bounds on the single step constraint violation $[g(x_t)]_+$ are derived. For convex objectives, our regret bounds generalize existing bounds, and for strongly convex objectives we give improved regret bounds. In numerical experiments, we show that our algorithm closely follows the constraint boundary leading to low cumulative violation.

paragraphs: Online optimization makes decisions repeatedly while balancing objective performance against constraints. Earlier long-term constraint formulations add signed constraint values across time. Under that accounting, a decision comfortably inside the feasible region can offset a violation elsewhere, potentially hiding how much actual violation occurred during the sequence.

This paper instead sums squared positive violations. Feasible decisions contribute no negative credit, and squaring gives large violations greater weight. The proposed algorithms bound this cumulative quantity by O(T to the power 1 − β), with β between zero and one. Because this grows more slowly than the number of rounds T, the average squared positive violation decreases with the horizon.

The authors also derive bounds for constraint violation at an individual step. Their regret bounds generalize existing results for convex objectives and improve results for strongly convex objectives. Numerical experiments show the algorithm tracking the constraint boundary closely and accumulating little violation. Together, these results address objective performance while using a constraint measure that cannot erase violations through cancellation.
summary.tldr: The proposed online algorithms control squared positive constraint violations, preventing feasible decisions from canceling earlier violations.

title: Online convex optimization for cumulative constraints

abstract: There is growing interest in combining model-free and model-based approaches in reinforcement learning with the goal of achieving the high performance of model-free algorithms with low sample complexity. This is difficult because an imperfect dynamics model can degrade the performance of the learning algorithm, and in sufficiently complex environments, the dynamics model will always be imperfect. As a result, a key challenge is to combine model-based approaches with model-free learning in such a way that errors in the model do not degrade performance. We propose stochastic ensemble value expansion (STEVE), a novel model-based technique that addresses this issue. By dynamically interpolating between model rollouts of various horizon lengths, STEVE ensures that the model is only utilized when doing so does not introduce significant errors. Our approach outperforms model-free baselines on challenging continuous control benchmarks with an order-of-magnitude increase in sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Combining model-based and model-free reinforcement learning promises strong performance with fewer interactions with the environment. The difficulty is that a learned dynamics model is imperfect, especially in complex environments. Predictions generated by that model can introduce errors into learning, potentially undermining the benefit of using simulated experience.

Stochastic ensemble value expansion, or STEVE, addresses this by dynamically interpolating between model rollouts of different lengths. A rollout uses the model to predict a sequence of future steps. Combining different horizons allows the procedure to adjust how extensively it relies on model predictions, using the model only when doing so does not introduce significant errors.

The authors evaluate STEVE on challenging continuous-control benchmarks and report outperforming model-free baselines with an order-of-magnitude improvement in sample efficiency. The findings support adaptive use of model predictions as a way to gain more learning from limited environment interaction. The central contribution is controlling the extent of model use so that prediction errors do not erase its efficiency benefits.
summary.tldr: STEVE adaptively combines model rollouts of different lengths to improve sample efficiency while controlling model-induced errors.

title: Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning with Stochastic Ensemble Value Expansion

abstract: In this paper, we use a linear program to empirically decompose fitted neural networks into ensembles of low-bias sub-networks. We show that these sub-networks are relatively uncorrelated which leads to an internal regularization process, very much like a random forest, which can explain why a neural network is surprisingly resistant to overfitting. We then demonstrate this in practice by applying large neural networks, with hundreds of parameters per training observation, to a collection of 116 real-world data sets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. This collection of data sets contains a much smaller number of training examples than the types of image classification tasks generally studied in the deep learning literature, as well as non-trivial label noise. We show that even in this setting deep neural nets are capable of achieving superior classification accuracy without overfitting.

paragraphs: A neural network can have far more parameters than training examples and still predict well on new data. This paper investigates that behavior in small datasets, where overfitting is an especially relevant concern. It combines an empirical analysis of fitted networks with classification experiments on a broad collection of real-world datasets.

Using a linear program, the authors decompose trained networks into ensembles of subnetworks with low bias. They find that these subnetworks are relatively uncorrelated. Their proposed explanation is that this internal diversity creates a regularizing effect similar to a random forest, helping explain why a large network can resist overfitting.

The experimental study covers 116 datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, including nontrivial label noise and substantially fewer examples than typical deep-learning image tasks. Networks with hundreds of parameters per training observation achieve superior classification accuracy without overfitting in the reported study. The evidence supports the possibility of effective large-network learning on small data, alongside an empirical explanation for that behavior.
summary.tldr: Experiments suggest that relatively uncorrelated subnetworks provide internal regularization, helping large neural networks generalize on small, noisy datasets.

title: Modern Neural Networks Generalize on Small Data Sets

abstract: We propose a novel randomized incremental gradient algorithm, namely, VAriance-Reduced Accelerated Gradient (Varag), for finite-sum optimization. Equipped with a unified step-size policy that adjusts itself to the value of the conditional number, Varag exhibits the unified optimal rates of convergence for solving smooth convex finite-sum problems directly regardless of their strong convexity. Moreover, Varag is the first accelerated randomized incremental gradient method that benefits from the strong convexity of the data-fidelity term to achieve the optimal linear convergence. It also establishes an optimal linear rate of convergence for solving a wide class of problems only satisfying a certain error bound condition rather than strong convexity. Varag can also be extended to solve stochastic finite-sum problems.

paragraphs: Many optimization problems express their objective as a sum of component losses. The paper introduces Varag, a randomized incremental gradient method for these finite-sum problems. It combines variance reduction with acceleration and uses a unified step-size policy that adapts to the problem's condition number, which describes its numerical conditioning.

The central result is a common algorithmic approach with optimal convergence rates for smooth convex finite-sum objectives, whether or not they are strongly convex. Strong convexity provides additional curvature that can support faster progress. Varag can exploit strong convexity in the data-fidelity term specifically to achieve optimal linear convergence, meaning that optimization error decreases at a geometric rate.

The guarantees also extend to a broad class of objectives satisfying a particular error-bound condition instead of strong convexity. This matters because the faster rate is available under that alternative condition as well. The authors additionally describe an extension to stochastic finite-sum problems, broadening the settings addressed by the method.
summary.tldr: Varag unifies accelerated finite-sum optimization across convex settings and achieves optimal linear convergence under strong convexity or a suitable error-bound condition.

title: A unified variance-reduced accelerated gradient method for convex optimization

abstract: The study of object representations in computer vision has primarily focused on developing representations that are useful for image classification, object detection, or semantic segmentation as downstream tasks. In this work we aim to learn object representations that are useful for control and reinforcement learning (RL). To this end, we introduce Transporter, a neural network architecture for discovering concise geometric object representations in terms of keypoints or image-space coordinates. Our method learns from raw video frames in a fully unsupervised manner, by transporting learnt image features between video frames using a keypoint bottleneck. The discovered keypoints track objects and object parts across long time-horizons more accurately than recent similar methods. Furthermore, consistent long-term tracking enables two notable results in control domains -- (1) using the keypoint co-ordinates and corresponding image features as inputs enables highly sample-efficient reinforcement learning; (2) learning to explore by controlling keypoint locations drastically reduces the search space, enabling deep exploration (leading to states unreachable through random action exploration) without any extrinsic rewards.

paragraphs: The paper develops visual object representations for control and reinforcement learning. Its model, Transporter, represents objects through a small set of keypoints expressed as image coordinates. This gives the learner a concise geometric description, with the intended usefulness measured through tracking and action-oriented tasks.

Transporter learns from raw video frames without supervision. It moves learned image features between frames through a keypoint bottleneck, making the keypoints central to how the network relates observations over time. The discovered points track objects and object parts over long periods more accurately than the recent similar methods considered in the paper.

The resulting temporal consistency supports two control findings. Feeding keypoint coordinates and associated image features into reinforcement learning enables high sample efficiency. Learning to explore by controlling keypoint positions also sharply reduces the search space, reaching states that random-action exploration did not reach, without extrinsic rewards. These results connect an unsupervised geometric representation to both efficient learning and deeper exploration in the studied control domains.
summary.tldr: Transporter learns object keypoints from unlabeled video that support accurate tracking, sample-efficient reinforcement learning, and exploration without extrinsic rewards.

title: Unsupervised Learning of Object Keypoints for Perception and Control

abstract: The usage of deep generative models for image compression has led to impressive performance gains over classical codecs while neural video compression is still in its infancy. Here, we propose an end-to-end, deep generative modeling approach to compress temporal sequences with a focus on video. Our approach builds upon variational autoencoder (VAE) models for sequential data and combines them with recent work on neural image compression. The approach jointly learns to transform the original sequence into a lower-dimensional representation as well as to discretize and entropy code this representation according to predictions of the sequential VAE. Rate-distortion evaluations on small videos from public data sets with varying complexity and diversity show that our model yields competitive results when trained on generic video content. Extreme compression performance is achieved when training the model on specialized content.

paragraphs: Video compression must represent a sequence compactly while preserving useful visual detail. This paper proposes an end-to-end learned approach built around a generative model for sequential data. It combines sequential variational autoencoders with techniques from neural image compression to address the temporal structure of video.

The system jointly learns several parts of the compression process. It transforms the original sequence into a lower-dimensional representation, discretizes that representation, and entropy codes it using predictions from the sequential model. Learning these components together connects the representation being stored with the model used to encode it efficiently.

Evaluations examine the trade-off between compressed size and reconstruction distortion on small videos from public datasets with different levels of complexity and diversity. Training on generic video content produces competitive results, while training on specialized content achieves extreme compression. The findings distinguish a broadly trained compressor from one adapted to particular content: the strongest compression claim is tied to that specialized training setting.
summary.tldr: A sequential generative model jointly learns video representation and coding, with competitive generic performance and extreme compression on specialized content.

title: Deep Generative Video Compression

abstract: We propose an empirical measure of the approximate accuracy of feature importance estimates in deep neural networks. Our results across several large-scale image classification datasets show that many popular interpretability methods produce estimates of feature importance that are not better than a random designation of feature importance. Only certain ensemble based approaches---VarGrad and SmoothGrad-Squared---outperform such a random assignment of importance. The manner of ensembling remains critical, we show that some approaches do no better then the underlying method but carry a far higher computational burden.
originalAbstract: We propose an empirical measure of the approximate accuracy of feature importance estimates in deep neural networks. Our results across several large-scale image classification datasets show that many popular interpretability methods produce estimates of feature importance that are not better than a random designation of feature importance. Only certain ensemble based approaches---VarGrad and SmoothGrad-Squared---outperform such a random assignment of importance. The manner of ensembling remains critical, we show that some approaches do no better then the underlying method but carry a far higher computational burden.

paragraphs: Feature importance methods assign importance to parts of an input to explain a neural network’s prediction. This paper asks how accurately those assignments identify important features. It introduces an empirical measure of approximate accuracy, providing a way to assess explanations rather than simply inspecting whether they appear persuasive.

Across several large image classification datasets, the authors find that many popular interpretability methods perform no better under this measure than assigning importance randomly. In the reported comparisons, only the ensemble methods VarGrad and SmoothGrad-Squared outperform that random reference. These findings concern the tested methods and the proposed evaluation measure; they do not establish that every use of feature importance is ineffective.

The paper also shows that combining multiple estimates does not automatically produce a better explanation. Some ensemble approaches add substantial computation without improving on their underlying method. The practical contribution is therefore both an evaluation tool and evidence that the particular way estimates are combined matters when judging explanation quality and computational cost.
summary.tldr: An empirical benchmark finds that many tested feature importance methods perform no better than random assignments, while certain ensemble methods improve.

title: A Benchmark for Interpretability Methods in Deep Neural Networks

abstract: We investigate stochastic combinatorial multi-armed bandit with semi-bandit feedback (CMAB). In CMAB, the question of the existence of an efficient policy with an optimal asymptotic regret (up to a factor poly-logarithmic with the action size) is still open for many families of distributions, including mutually independent outcomes, and more generally the multivariate \emph{sub-Gaussian} family. We propose to answer the above question for these two families by analyzing variants of the Combinatorial Thompson Sampling policy (CTS). For mutually independent outcomes in $[0,1]$, we propose a tight analysis of CTS using Beta priors. We then look at the more general setting of multivariate sub-Gaussian outcomes and propose a tight analysis of CTS using Gaussian priors. This last result gives us an alternative to the Efficient Sampling for Combinatorial Bandit policy (ESCB), which, although optimal, is not computationally efficient.

We propose to answer the above question for these two families by analyzing variants of the Combinatorial Thompson Sampling policy (CTS). For mutually independent outcomes in $[0,1]$, we propose a tight analysis of CTS using Beta priors.
