paragraphs: In a combinatorial semi-bandit problem, a learner selects structured actions and receives feedback about their selected components. The challenge is to learn which actions are valuable while limiting regret from exploration. This paper asks whether computationally efficient policies can also achieve asymptotically optimal regret, up to a factor polylogarithmic in action size.

The authors analyze two variants of Combinatorial Thompson Sampling for different outcome families. For mutually independent outcomes bounded between zero and one, they provide a tight analysis using Beta priors. For the more general family of multivariate sub-Gaussian outcomes, they provide a tight analysis using Gaussian priors. The separate constructions match the analysis to the assumptions about observations.

These results address the efficiency question for both families covered by the paper. In the multivariate sub-Gaussian setting, the Gaussian-prior result supplies an alternative to Efficient Sampling for Combinatorial Bandit, which has optimal regret but lacks computational efficiency. The contribution links the statistical quality of exploration with the practical requirement that action-selection policies remain efficient to compute.
summary.tldr: Tight analyses establish statistical efficiency for combinatorial Thompson Sampling under independent bounded and multivariate sub-Gaussian outcomes.

title: Statistical Efficiency of Thompson Sampling for Combinatorial Semi-Bandits

abstract: Several problems in machine learning, statistics, and other fields rely on computing eigenvectors. For large scale problems, the computation of these eigenvectors is typically performed via iterative schemes such as subspace iteration or Krylov methods. While there is classical and comprehensive analysis for subspace convergence guarantees with respect to the spectral norm, in many modern applications other notions of subspace distance are more appropriate. Recent theoretical work has focused on perturbations of subspaces measured in the ℓ2→∞ norm, but does not consider the actual computation of eigenvectors. Here we address the convergence of subspace iteration when distances are measured in the ℓ2→∞ norm and provide deterministic bounds. We complement our analysis with a practical stopping criterion and demonstrate its applicability via numerical experiments. Our results show that one can get comparable performance on downstream tasks while requiring fewer iterations, thereby saving substantial computational time.

paragraphs: Many machine learning and statistical procedures depend on eigenvectors, which large problems usually compute through repeated numerical updates. Classical convergence analysis measures the error of an estimated subspace using the spectral norm. The paper asks how convergence behaves under a different measure that better reflects errors across individual entries or rows.

The authors analyze subspace iteration using the ℓ2→∞ norm and derive deterministic convergence bounds. This addresses a gap between recent work on how perturbations affect subspaces and the practical process of actually computing them. Studying the iteration itself makes the analysis relevant to deciding how much numerical work an application needs.

The paper also develops a practical stopping criterion and evaluates it numerically. The reported results show that downstream tasks can achieve comparable performance with fewer iterations, reducing computational time. The significance is that the stopping decision can be informed by a notion of error suited to the application, rather than relying solely on the classical spectral-norm analysis.
summary.tldr: Entrywise convergence bounds yield a stopping criterion that can reduce eigenvector iterations while preserving comparable downstream performance.

title: Entrywise convergence of iterative methods for eigenproblems

abstract: The presence of missing values makes supervised learning much more challenging. Indeed, previous work has shown that even when the response is a linear function of the complete data, the optimal predictor is a complex function of the observed entries and the missingness indicator. As a result, the computational or sample complexities of consistent approaches depend on the number of missing patterns, which can be exponential in the number of dimensions. In this work, we derive the analytical form of the optimal predictor under a linearity assumption and various missing data mechanisms including Missing at Random (MAR) and self-masking (Missing Not At Random). Based on a Neumann-series approximation of the optimal predictor, we propose a new principled architecture, named NeuMiss networks. Their originality and strength come from the use of a new type of non-linearity: the multiplication by the missingness indicator. We provide an upper bound on the Bayes risk of NeuMiss networks, and show that they have good predictive accuracy with both a number of parameters and a computational complexity independent of the number of missing data patterns. As a result they scale well to problems with many features, and remain statistically efficient for medium-sized samples. Moreover, we show that, contrary to procedures using EM or imputation, they are robust to the missing data mechanism, including difficult MNAR settings such as self-masking.

paragraphs: Missing inputs can make prediction complicated even when the response depends linearly on complete data. The optimal predictor must account for both the observed values and which entries are absent. Methods whose cost depends on the number of missingness patterns can face an exponential increase as the number of features grows.

The authors derive the optimal predictor under a linearity assumption and several missing-data mechanisms, including Missing at Random and self-masking Missing Not At Random. They approximate this predictor using a Neumann series and translate that approximation into the NeuMiss architecture. The authors also show robustness across missing-data mechanisms, including difficult self-masking settings, compared with procedures based on expectation-maximization or imputation. These claims concern the mechanisms studied, alongside the stated linearity assumption behind the derivation.
summary.tldr: NeuMiss incorporates missingness directly into a theoretically motivated network whose computational cost does not depend on the number of missing-data patterns.

title: NeuMiss networks: differentiable programming for supervised learning with missing values.

abstract: This paper develops a Pontryagin Differentiable Programming (PDP) methodology, which establishes a unified framework to solve a broad class of learning and control tasks. The PDP distinguishes from existing methods by two novel techniques: first, we differentiate through Pontryagin's Maximum Principle, and this allows to obtain the analytical derivative of a trajectory with respect to tunable parameters within an optimal control system, enabling end-to-end learning of dynamics, policies, or/and control objective functions; and second, we propose an auxiliary control system in the backward pass of the PDP framework, and the output of this auxiliary control system is the analytical derivative of the original system's trajectory with respect to the parameters, which can be iteratively solved using standard control tools. We investigate three learning modes of the PDP: inverse reinforcement learning, system identification, and control/planning. We demonstrate the capability of the PDP in each learning mode on different high-dimensional systems, including multi-link robot arm, 6-DoF maneuvering quadrotor, and 6-DoF rocket powered landing.
originalAbstract: This paper develops a Pontryagin Differentiable Programming (PDP) methodology, which establishes a unified framework to solve a broad class of learning and control tasks. The PDP distinguishes from existing methods by two novel techniques: first, we differentiate through Pontryagin's Maximum Principle, and this allows to obtain the analytical derivative of a trajectory with respect to tunable parameters within an optimal control system, enabling end-to-end learning of dynamics, policies, or/and control objective functions; and second, we propose an auxiliary control system in the backward pass of the PDP framework, and the output of this auxiliary control system is the analytical derivative of the original system's trajectory with respect to the parameters, which can be iteratively solved using standard control tools. We demonstrate the capability of the PDP in each learning mode on different high-dimensional systems, including multi-link robot arm, 6-DoF maneuvering quadrotor, and 6-DoF rocket powered landing.

paragraphs: Pontryagin Differentiable Programming connects learning with optimal control by calculating how a system's trajectory changes when tunable parameters change. Those parameters can belong to the system dynamics, its policy, or its control objective. This provides a common route to end-to-end learning across several kinds of control problems.

The framework differentiates through Pontryagin's Maximum Principle to obtain analytical trajectory derivatives. It also constructs an auxiliary control system for the backward pass. The output of that auxiliary system is the derivative of the original trajectory with respect to the parameters, and standard control tools can solve it iteratively. This turns the derivative calculation itself into a control problem that existing methods can address.

The authors investigate inverse reinforcement learning, system identification, and control or planning within this framework. Demonstrations include a multi-link robot arm, a six-degree-of-freedom quadrotor, and a six-degree-of-freedom rocket landing system. These examples demonstrate the framework's capabilities across different learning modes and high-dimensional systems, supporting its role as a shared methodology for learning and control.
summary.tldr: Pontryagin Differentiable Programming computes trajectory derivatives through optimal control conditions to support end-to-end learning of dynamics, policies, and objectives.

title: Pontryagin Differentiable Programming: An End-to-End Learning and Control Framework

abstract: Lossy gradient compression has become a practical tool to overcome the communication bottleneck in centrally coordinated distributed training of machine learning models. However, algorithms for decentralized training with compressed communication over arbitrary connected networks have been more complicated, requiring additional memory and hyperparameters. We introduce a simple algorithm that directly compresses the model differences between neighboring workers using low-rank linear compressors. We prove that our method does not require any additional hyperparameters, converges faster than prior methods, and is asymptotically independent of both the network and the compression. Inspired the PowerSGD algorithm for centralized deep learning, we execute power iteration steps on model differences to maximize the information transferred per bit. Out of the box, these compressors perform on par with state-of-the-art tuned compression algorithms in a series of deep learning benchmarks.
originalAbstract: Lossy gradient compression has become a practical tool to overcome the communication bottleneck in centrally coordinated distributed training of machine learning models. However, algorithms for decentralized training with compressed communication over arbitrary connected networks have been more complicated, requiring additional memory and hyperparameters. We introduce a simple algorithm that directly compresses the model differences between neighboring workers using low-rank linear compressors. We prove that our method does not require any additional hyperparameters, converges faster than prior methods, and is asymptotically independent of both the network and the compression. Inspired the PowerSGD algorithm for centralized deep learning, we execute power iteration steps on model differences to maximize the information transferred per bit. Out of the box, these compressors perform on par with state-of-the-art tuned compression algorithms in a series of deep learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Distributed training can be slowed by communication between workers. Compression reduces the information sent, but decentralized methods must coordinate workers through a connected network without a central coordinator. Previous compressed approaches in this setting have required more complicated algorithms, extra memory, and additional hyperparameters.

This paper introduces an algorithm that directly compresses differences between neighboring workers' models using low-rank linear compressors. Inspired by PowerSGD, it applies power iteration to those differences to concentrate communication on informative components. The goal is to transfer more useful model information per bit while keeping the decentralized training procedure simple to use.

The authors prove faster convergence than prior methods without introducing additional hyperparameters. They also establish an asymptotic convergence behavior independent of the network and compression, a statement about the eventual regime rather than every stage of training. In deep learning benchmarks, the proposed compressors perform comparably to leading tuned compression algorithms without requiring that tuning. The findings combine a simpler algorithmic interface with theoretical and empirical support for effective communication compression.
summary.tldr: Compressing neighboring workers' model differences with low-rank methods simplifies decentralized training and matches tuned compression methods in the reported benchmarks.

title: Practical Low-Rank Communication Compression in Decentralized Deep Learning

abstract: Motivated by decentralized approaches to machine learning, we propose a collaborative Bayesian learning algorithm taking the form of decentralized Langevin dynamics in a non-convex setting. Our analysis show that the initial KL-divergence between the Markov Chain and the target posterior distribution is exponentially decreasing while the error contributions to the overall KL-divergence from the additive noise is decreasing in polynomial time. We further show that the polynomial-term experiences speed-up with number of agents and provide sufficient conditions on the time-varying step-sizes to guarantee convergence to the desired distribution. The performance of the proposed algorithm is evaluated on a wide variety of machine learning tasks. The empirical results show that the performance of individual agents with locally available data is on par with the centralized setting with considerable improvement in the convergence rate.
originalAbstract: Motivated by decentralized approaches to machine learning, we propose a collaborative Bayesian learning algorithm taking the form of decentralized Langevin dynamics in a non-convex setting. Our analysis show that the initial KL-divergence between the Markov Chain and the target posterior distribution is exponentially decreasing while the error contributions to the overall KL-divergence from the additive noise is decreasing in polynomial time. We further show that the polynomial-term experiences speed-up with number of agents and provide sufficient conditions on the time-varying step-sizes to guarantee convergence to the desired distribution. The performance of the proposed algorithm is evaluated on a wide variety of machine learning tasks. The empirical results show that the performance of individual agents with locally available data is on par with the centralized setting with considerable improvement in the convergence rate.

paragraphs: Bayesian learning seeks a posterior distribution over model parameters rather than only a single fitted solution. This paper develops a collaborative algorithm in which multiple agents perform that learning through decentralized Langevin dynamics. The analysis addresses a non-convex setting and asks how the resulting Markov chain approaches the desired posterior.

The authors measure distributional error using KL divergence and distinguish contributions with different rates of decay. The contribution from the initial discrepancy decreases exponentially, while contributions associated with additive noise decrease polynomially. They further show that the polynomial term improves with the number of agents. These separate terms explain why the overall convergence behavior cannot be described by one exponential rate.

The theory supplies sufficient conditions on changing step sizes that guarantee convergence to the target distribution. Across the evaluated machine learning tasks, individual agents using locally available data achieve performance comparable to a centralized setup, with substantially improved convergence rates. Together, the analysis and experiments support decentralized collaboration as a way to perform Bayesian learning while distributing access to training data.
summary.tldr: Decentralized Langevin dynamics enables collaborative Bayesian learning, with convergence guarantees under step-size conditions and empirical performance comparable to centralized learning.

title: Decentralized Langevin Dynamics for Bayesian Learning

abstract: Symmetry transformations induce invariances and are a crucial building block of modern machine learning algorithms. In many complex domains, such as the chemical space, invariances can be observed, yet the corresponding symmetry transformation cannot be formulated analytically. We propose to learn the symmetry transformation with a model consisting of two latent subspaces, where the first subspace captures the target and the second subspace the remaining invariant information. Our approach is based on the deep information bottleneck in combination with a continuous mutual information regulariser. Unlike previous methods, we focus on the challenging task of minimising mutual information in continuous domains. To this end, we base the calculation of mutual information on correlation matrices in combination with a bijective variable transformation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our model outperforms state-of-the-art methods on artificial and molecular datasets.

In complex domains such as chemical space, researchers may observe an invariance without being able to write down the transformation responsible for it. This paper approaches the problem inversely: it learns the symmetry transformation from the available information.

The model divides its latent representation into two subspaces. One captures the target, while the other captures the remaining invariant information. Training combines a deep information bottleneck with a regularizer based on continuous mutual information. Minimizing this information quantity is central to the approach because it addresses the relationship between the information stored in the representation’s different parts.

Experiments on artificial and molecular datasets show better performance than state-of-the-art methods. These results support learning transformations in settings where invariances are observable but an analytical description is unavailable, with the continuous mutual-information treatment serving as a key technical contribution.
summary.tldr: The method learns symmetry transformations through two latent subspaces and continuous mutual-information regularization, outperforming compared methods on artificial and molecular datasets.

title: Inverse Learning of Symmetries

abstract: In real-world classification tasks, each class often comprises multiple finer-grained "subclasses." As the subclass labels are frequently unavailable, models trained using only the coarser-grained class labels often exhibit highly variable performance across different subclasses. This phenomenon, known as hidden stratification, has important consequences for models deployed in safety-critical applications such as medicine. We propose GEORGE, a method to both measure and mitigate hidden stratification even when subclass labels are unknown. We first observe that unlabeled subclasses are often separable in the feature space of deep neural networks, and exploit this fact to estimate subclass labels for the training data via clustering techniques. We then use these approximate subclass labels as a form of noisy supervision in a distributionally robust optimization objective. We theoretically characterize the performance of GEORGE in terms of the worst-case generalization error across any subclass. We empirically validate GEORGE on a mix of real-world and benchmark image classification datasets, and show that our approach boosts worst-case subclass accuracy by up to 22 percentage points compared to standard training techniques, without requiring any prior information about the subclasses.

When only the broad labels are available, these disparities can remain hidden. The paper addresses this hidden stratification, which is especially consequential when models are used in safety-critical settings such as medicine.

GEORGE uses the observation that subclasses are often distinguishable in a deep network’s feature representation. It clusters training examples in that representation to estimate subclass membership. These estimated labels then serve as noisy supervision for distributionally robust optimization, giving training a way to address group-level weaknesses even without supplied subclass annotations.

summary.tldr: GEORGE estimates hidden subclasses through feature clustering and uses robust optimization to improve worst-case subclass accuracy without subclass annotations.

title: No Subclass Left Behind: Fine-Grained Robustness in Coarse-Grained Classification Problems

abstract: Multiple instance learning (MIL) is a powerful tool to solve the weakly supervised classification in whole slide image (WSI) based pathology diagnosis. However, the current MIL methods are usually based on independent and identical distribution hypothesis, thus neglect the correlation among different instances. To address this problem, we proposed a new framework, called correlated MIL, and provided a proof for convergence. Based on this framework, we devised a Transformer based MIL (TransMIL), which explored both morphological and spatial information. The proposed TransMIL can effectively deal with unbalanced/balanced and binary/multiple classification with great visualization and interpretability. We conducted various experiments for three different computational pathology problems and achieved better performance and faster convergence compared with state-of-the-art methods. The test AUC for the binary tumor classification can be up to 93.09% over CAMELYON16 dataset. And the AUC over the cancer subtypes classification can be up to 96.03% and 98.82% over TCGA-NSCLC dataset and TCGA-RCC dataset, respectively. Implementation is available at: https://github.com/szc19990412/TransMIL.

paragraphs: Whole-slide pathology classification can use multiple instance learning to learn from slide-level supervision. A slide contains multiple instances whose relationships may carry useful information. This paper challenges the common assumption that those instances are independent and identically distributed, arguing that it neglects correlations within the slide.

The authors propose a correlated multiple-instance-learning framework and provide a convergence proof. Their transformer-based implementation, TransMIL, incorporates both morphological and spatial information. This allows the classification process to consider what instances look like and how they relate spatially. The method is reported to handle balanced and unbalanced data, binary and multiclass tasks, and to offer useful visualization and interpretability.

These results support explicitly modeling instance correlations when learning slide-level predictions from weak supervision.
summary.tldr: TransMIL models correlations among whole-slide image instances using morphological and spatial information, improving classification and convergence in three pathology evaluations.

title: TransMIL: Transformer based Correlated Multiple Instance Learning for Whole Slide Image Classification

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) extend basic Neural Networks (NNs) by using graph structures based on the relational inductive bias (homophily assumption). While GNNs have been commonly believed to outperform NNs in real-world tasks, recent work has identified a non-trivial set of datasets where their performance compared to NNs is not satisfactory. Heterophily has been considered the main cause of this empirical observation and numerous works have been put forward to address it. In this paper, we first revisit the widely used homophily metrics and point out that their consideration of only graph-label consistency is a shortcoming. Then, we study heterophily from the perspective of post-aggregation node similarity and define new homophily metrics, which are potentially advantageous compared to existing ones. Based on this investigation, we prove that some harmful cases of heterophily can be effectively addressed by local diversification operation. Then, we propose the Adaptive Channel Mixing (ACM), a framework to adaptively exploit aggregation, diversification and identity channels to extract richer localized information in each baseline GNN layer. ACM is more powerful than the commonly used uni-channel framework for node classification tasks on heterophilic graphs. When evaluated on 10 benchmark node classification tasks, ACM-augmented baselines consistently achieve significant performance gain, exceeding state-of-the-art GNNs on most tasks without incurring significant computational burden. (Code: https://github.com/SitaoLuan/ACM-GNN)

paragraphs: Graph neural networks use relationships between nodes to improve predictions, yet graph information does not always help. Heterophily, where linked nodes have different labels, is often blamed. This paper argues that common homophily measures overlook something important by considering only agreement between graph connections and labels.

The authors instead examine node similarity after neighborhood aggregation and define new metrics from that perspective. They prove that local diversification can address some harmful forms of heterophily. Building on this analysis, their Adaptive Channel Mixing framework combines aggregation, diversification, and identity channels within each baseline GNN layer, adapting how these information sources are used.

Across ten node-classification benchmarks, adding ACM consistently yields significant performance gains. The augmented models exceed state-of-the-art GNNs on most tasks without substantial computational burden. The findings support examining what neighborhood processing does to node representations, rather than judging a graph solely by label agreement. They also show the value of giving each layer several ways to use local information.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Channel Mixing combines aggregation, diversification, and identity information to improve node classification, guided by a revised analysis of heterophily.

title: Revisiting Heterophily For Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Neural networks have shown great predictive power when applied to unstructured data such as images and natural languages. The Bayesian neural network captures the uncertainty of prediction by computing the posterior distribution of the model parameters. In this paper, we show that the Bayesian neural network with spikeand-slab prior has posterior consistency with a near minimax optimal convergence rate when the true regression function belongs to the Besov space. The spikeand-slab prior is adaptive to the smoothness of the regression function and the posterior convergence rate does not change even when the smoothness of the regression function is unknown. We also consider the shrinkage prior, which is computationally more feasible than the spike-and-slab prior, and show that it has the same posterior convergence rate as the spike-and-slab prior.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty using a posterior distribution over model parameters. This paper studies what happens to that posterior as more data become available. Its theoretical setting assumes that the true regression function belongs to a Besov space, a function class used here to describe the target’s regularity.

For a network with a spike-and-slab prior, the authors prove posterior consistency and a near-minimax optimal convergence rate. Consistency means that the posterior increasingly concentrates around the true regression function. The rate describes how quickly this happens and is close to the best worst-case rate for the relevant function class.

The result also adapts to unknown smoothness: the convergence rate does not worsen merely because the function’s smoothness is not supplied in advance. The authors then establish the same rate for a shrinkage prior, which they describe as more computationally feasible. This connects a more practical prior choice to the same asymptotic statistical guarantee within the studied setting.
summary.tldr: Bayesian neural networks with spike-and-slab or shrinkage priors achieve near-optimal posterior convergence for regression functions in Besov spaces.

title: Asymptotic Properties for Bayesian Neural Network in Besov Space

abstract: Massive datasets and high-capacity models have driven many recent advancements in computer vision and natural language understanding. This work presents a platform to enable similar success stories in Embodied AI. We propose ProcTHOR, a framework for procedural generation of Embodied AI environments. ProcTHOR enables us to sample arbitrarily large datasets of diverse, interactive, customizable, and performant virtual environments to train and evaluate embodied agents across navigation, interaction, and manipulation tasks. We demonstrate the power and potential of ProcTHOR via a sample of 10,000 generated houses and a simple neural model. Models trained using only RGB images on ProcTHOR, with no explicit mapping and no human task supervision produce state-of-the-art results across 6 embodied AI benchmarks for navigation, rearrangement, and arm manipulation, including the presently running Habitat 2022, AI2-THOR Rearrangement 2022, and RoboTHOR challenges. We also demonstrate strong 0-shot results on these benchmarks, via pre-training on ProcTHOR with no fine-tuning on the downstream benchmark, often beating previous state-of-the-art systems that access the downstream training data.

paragraphs: Embodied AI agents learn to navigate and act within environments, making the availability of varied training worlds important. ProcTHOR is a procedural generation framework for creating diverse, interactive, customizable virtual environments. It supports generating arbitrarily large datasets for training and evaluating navigation, interaction, and manipulation.

The authors demonstrate the framework using 10,000 generated houses and a simple neural model. Models trained with RGB images, without explicit mapping or human task supervision, achieve reported state-of-the-art results across six embodied AI benchmarks. These benchmarks cover navigation, rearrangement, and arm manipulation, showing the usefulness of generated environments across several kinds of action.

The paper also evaluates transfer without fine-tuning on the downstream benchmark. Pretraining on ProcTHOR produces strong zero-shot results, often exceeding earlier leading systems that used downstream training data. The findings support procedural environment generation as a route to scalable embodied learning. In particular, the transfer results suggest that experience across many generated houses can be useful beyond the environments used during pretraining.
summary.tldr: ProcTHOR generates diverse interactive houses at scale, enabling strong embodied-agent performance and zero-shot transfer across multiple benchmarks.

title: 🏘️ ProcTHOR: Large-Scale Embodied AI Using Procedural Generation

abstract: We study algorithms using randomized value functions for exploration in reinforcement learning. This type of algorithms enjoys appealing empirical performance. We show that when we use 1) a single random seed in each episode, and 2) a Bernstein-type magnitude of noise, we obtain a worst-case $\widetilde{O}\left(H\sqrt{SAT}\right)$ regret bound for episodic time-inhomogeneous Markov Decision Process where $S$ is the size of state space, $A$ is the size of action space, $H$ is the planning horizon and $T$ is the number of interactions. This bound polynomially improves all existing bounds for algorithms based on randomized value functions, and for the first time, matches the $\Omega\left(H\sqrt{SAT}\right)$ lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Our result highlights that randomized exploration can be near-optimal, which was previously achieved only by optimistic algorithms. To achieve the desired result, we develop 1) a new clipping operation to ensure both the probability of being optimistic and the probability of being pessimistic are lower bounded by a constant, and 2) a new recursive formula for the absolute value of estimation errors to analyze the regret.

Although such methods had appealing empirical performance, their theoretical regret guarantees lagged behind those of optimistic algorithms. This paper shows that a carefully designed randomized approach can achieve nearly optimal worst-case regret in episodic tabular decision processes whose dynamics may vary within an episode.

The construction combines one random seed per episode with a Bernstein-type noise magnitude. Its regret bound scales as H times the square root of SAT, up to logarithmic factors, where H is the planning horizon, S and A count states and actions, and T counts interactions. This matches the stated lower bound apart from logarithmic factors.

It also develops a recursive expression for absolute estimation errors. Together, these tools establish that randomized value-function exploration can reach the near-optimal theoretical performance previously obtained only by optimistic algorithms.
summary.tldr: Carefully calibrated randomized value functions achieve worst-case regret matching the tabular episodic lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

title: Near-Optimal Randomized Exploration for Tabular Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Partial-label learning (PLL) is a peculiar weakly-supervised learning task where the training samples are generally associated with a set of candidate labels instead of single ground truth. While a variety of label disambiguation methods have been proposed in this domain, they normally assume a class-balanced scenario that may not hold in many real-world applications. Empirically, we observe degenerated performance of the prior methods when facing the combinatorial challenge from the long-tailed distribution and partial-labeling. In this work, we first identify the major reasons that the prior work failed. We subsequently propose SoLar, a novel Optimal Transport-based framework that allows to refine the disambiguated labels towards matching the marginal class prior distribution. SoLar additionally incorporates a new and systematic mechanism for estimating the long-tailed class prior distribution under the PLL setup. Through extensive experiments, SoLar exhibits substantially superior results on standardized benchmarks compared to the previous state-of-the-art PLL methods. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/hbzju/SoLar.

paragraphs: Partial-label learning gives each training example several candidate labels instead of a single confirmed answer. The learner must determine which candidate is correct. This paper examines what happens when that ambiguity is combined with a long-tailed class distribution, where classes occur at very different frequencies. Methods developed around balanced classes can perform poorly in this combined setting.

The authors propose SoLar, an optimal-transport framework that refines the labels inferred during disambiguation. Its refinement encourages the overall label distribution to match the marginal class prior. Because that prior must be determined under ambiguous labeling, SoLar also includes a systematic mechanism for estimating the long-tailed class distribution within the partial-label setting.

Experiments on standardized benchmarks show substantially better results than the compared state-of-the-art partial-label methods. The approach matters because label disambiguation and class frequency are handled together: the method adjusts inferred labels using an estimated distribution that reflects imbalance. The reported findings support this combination for learning when examples have both uncertain labels and uneven class representation.
summary.tldr: SoLar uses optimal transport and class-prior estimation to refine ambiguous labels when classes are imbalanced.

title: SoLar: Sinkhorn Label Refinery for Imbalanced Partial-Label Learning

abstract: Driven by several successful applications such as in stochastic gradient descent or in Bayesian computation, control variates have become a major tool for Monte Carlo integration. However, standard methods do not allow the distribution of the particles to evolve during the algorithm, as is the case in sequential simulation methods. Within the standard adaptive importance sampling framework, a simple weighted least squares approach is proposed to improve the procedure with control variates. The procedure takes the form of a quadrature rule with adapted quadrature weights to reflect the information brought in by the control variates. The quadrature points and weights do not depend on the integrand, a computational advantage in case of multiple integrands. Moreover, the target density needs to be known only up to a multiplicative constant. Our main result is a non-asymptotic bound on the probabilistic error of the procedure. The bound proves that for improving the estimate's accuracy, the benefits from adaptive importance sampling and control variates can be combined. The good behavior of the method is illustrated empirically on synthetic examples and real-world data for Bayesian linear regression.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo integration estimates integrals using sampled points. Control variates improve these estimates by incorporating additional information, but standard approaches do not accommodate sampling distributions that change as an algorithm runs. This creates a mismatch with adaptive importance sampling, where the distribution producing the points evolves during computation.

The paper combines these techniques through a weighted least squares procedure. The resulting estimate is a quadrature rule: sampled points receive weights that account for the information supplied by the control variates. Both the points and their weights are independent of the particular function being integrated, which offers a computational advantage when estimating integrals for several functions.

The method also requires the target density only up to an unknown multiplicative constant. Its main theoretical result bounds the probability of estimation error at a finite stage of computation. That bound establishes that the accuracy benefits of adaptation and control variates can work together. Synthetic examples and Bayesian linear regression on real data illustrate the procedure’s empirical behavior.
summary.tldr: A weighted integration rule combines control variates with adaptive importance sampling and provides a finite-sample probabilistic error bound.

title: A Quadrature Rule combining Control Variates and Adaptive Importance Sampling

abstract: Chaotic systems are notoriously challenging to predict because of their sensitivity to perturbations and errors due to time stepping. Despite this unpredictable behavior, for many dissipative systems the statistics of the long term trajectories are governed by an invariant measure supported on a set, known as the global attractor; for many problems this set is finite dimensional, even if the state space is infinite dimensional. For Markovian systems, the statistical properties of long-term trajectories are uniquely determined by the solution operator that maps the evolution of the system over arbitrary positive time increments. In this work, we propose a machine learning framework to learn the underlying solution operator for dissipative chaotic systems, showing that the resulting learned operator accurately captures short-time trajectories and long-time statistical behavior. Using this framework, we are able to predict various statistics of the invariant measure for the turbulent Kolmogorov Flow dynamics with Reynolds numbers up to $5000$.

paragraphs: Chaotic dynamics are sensitive to small perturbations and numerical errors, making individual trajectories difficult to predict far into the future. Yet many dissipative systems have stable long-term statistical structure. Their trajectories are governed statistically by an invariant measure supported on a global attractor, which can be finite-dimensional even when the full state space is infinite-dimensional.

The paper builds on the fact that, for Markovian systems, the solution operator determines long-term trajectory statistics. This operator describes how the system evolves over a positive time interval. The authors propose learning that operator with machine learning, connecting short-term evolution and long-term statistical behavior through the same learned object.

They show that their learned operator captures both short-time trajectories and long-time statistics. In turbulent Kolmogorov Flow, the framework predicts various statistics of the invariant measure at Reynolds numbers up to 5000. The significance is that useful long-term prediction can concern statistical properties even when sustained accuracy for an individual chaotic trajectory is difficult.
summary.tldr: Learning a chaotic system's solution operator captures short-term trajectories and long-term statistics in the reported dissipative-system experiments.

title: Learning Chaotic Dynamics in Dissipative Systems

abstract: In this paper, we present the first stepsize schedule for Newton method resulting in fast global and local convergence guarantees. In particular, we a) prove an $\mathcal O \left( 1/{k^2} \right)$ global rate, which matches the state-of-the-art global rate of cubically regularized Newton method of Polyak and Nesterov (2006) and of regularized Newton method of Mishchenko (2021), and the later variant of Doikov and Nesterov (2021), b) prove a local quadratic rate, which matches the best-known local rate of second-order methods, and c) our stepsize formula is simple, explicit, and does not require solving any subproblem. Our convergence proofs hold under affine-invariant assumptions closely related to the notion of self-concordance. Finally, our method has competitive performance when compared to existing baselines which share the same fast global convergence guarantees.

In particular, we a) prove an $\mathcal O \left( 1/{k^2} \right)$ global rate, which matches the state-of-the-art global rate of cubically regularized Newton method of Polyak and Nesterov (2006) and of regularized Newton method of Mishchenko (2021), and the later variant of Doikov and Nesterov (2021), b) prove a local quadratic rate, which matches the best-known local rate of second-order methods, and c) our stepsize formula is simple, explicit, and does not require solving any subproblem. Our convergence proofs hold under affine-invariant assumptions closely related to the notion of self-concordance. Finally, our method has competitive performance when compared to existing baselines which share the same fast global convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Newton's method uses second-order information to guide optimization, but choosing how far to move is important for convergence. This paper introduces a step-size schedule that gives the method both a fast global convergence guarantee and quadratic convergence near a solution. The contribution joins these two guarantees within a damped Newton method.

The global rate is O(1/k²), where k counts iterations, matching the rates of the regularized Newton methods discussed in the abstract. Locally, the quadratic rate matches the best known rate for second-order methods. The step-size formula is explicit and does not require solving an additional subproblem, making the rule straightforward to evaluate.

These guarantees hold under affine-invariant assumptions closely related to self-concordance; they are not claims about arbitrary optimization problems. Affine invariance means the assumptions respect changes of coordinates of the relevant kind. The paper also reports competitive performance against methods with similarly fast global guarantees. Its main result is therefore a simple step-size rule backed by strong, conditional convergence theory.
summary.tldr: An explicit Newton step-size schedule achieves fast global and quadratic local convergence under affine-invariant assumptions related to self-concordance.

title: A Damped Newton Method Achieves Global $\mathcal O \left(\frac{1}{k^2}\right)$ and Local Quadratic Convergence Rate

abstract: Criminal justice is an increasingly important application domain for machine learning and algorithmic fairness, as predictive tools are becoming widely used in police, courts, and prison systems worldwide. A few relevant benchmarks have received significant attention, e.g., the COMPAS dataset, often without proper consideration of the domain context. To raise awareness of publicly available criminal justice datasets and encourage their responsible use, we conduct a survey, consider contexts, highlight potential uses, and identify gaps and limitations. We provide datasheets for 15 datasets and upload them to a public repository. We compare the datasets across several dimensions, including size, coverage of the population, and potential use, highlighting concerns. We hope that this work can provide a useful starting point for researchers looking for appropriate datasets related to criminal justice, and that the repository will continue to grow as a community effort.

The paper argues that this attention has not always been accompanied by adequate consideration of domain context. Choosing a dataset requires understanding what it covers and how that coverage relates to the intended research question.

The authors survey publicly available US criminal justice datasets and create datasheets for 15 of them. These documents are placed in a public repository. The survey compares datasets by dimensions including their size, the populations they cover, and their potential uses. It also discusses context, concerns, gaps, and limitations to support more informed selection.

The main contribution is a documented resource for researchers, rather than a new predictive model. Bringing alternatives into view can broaden the starting point for criminal justice and algorithmic fairness studies. The authors present the repository as a resource for responsible use and hope that community contributions will expand it over time.
summary.tldr: A survey and public repository document 15 criminal justice datasets to help researchers select and use them with better contextual understanding.

title: A Survey and Datasheet Repository of Publicly Available US Criminal Justice Datasets

abstract: One concern with the rise of large language models lies with their potential for significant harm, particularly from pretraining on biased, obscene, copyrighted, and private information. Emerging ethical approaches have attempted to filter pretraining material, but such approaches have been ad hoc and failed to take context into account. We offer an approach to filtering grounded in law, which has directly addressed the tradeoffs in filtering material. First, we gather and make available the Pile of Law, a ~256GB (and growing) dataset of open-source English-language legal and administrative data, covering court opinions, contracts, administrative rules, and legislative records. Pretraining on the Pile of Law may help with legal tasks that have the promise to improve access to justice. Second, we distill the legal norms that governments have developed to constrain the inclusion of toxic or private content into actionable lessons for researchers and discuss how our dataset reflects these norms. Third, we show how the Pile of Law offers researchers the opportunity to learn such filtering rules directly from the data, providing an exciting new research direction in model-based processing.

paragraphs: Filtering language-model training data involves context-sensitive decisions about harmful, private, copyrighted, and other problematic material. The paper argues that existing ethical filtering approaches have often been ad hoc and insufficiently attentive to context. It proposes drawing on law, where governments have already developed rules for managing some of these inclusion and exclusion tradeoffs.

The authors release Pile of Law, an approximately 256GB and growing collection of open-source English legal and administrative text. It includes court opinions, contracts, administrative rules, and legislative records. They also distill legal norms governing toxic or private content into lessons for researchers and explain how those norms are reflected in the dataset.

A further contribution is the proposal to learn filtering rules directly from this legal data. The dataset therefore serves both as training material and as a resource for studying context-aware filtering. Pretraining on it may also support legal tasks with potential benefits for access to justice. Those downstream benefits and learned filtering possibilities are presented as opportunities, rather than established outcomes.
summary.tldr: Pile of Law releases a large legal-text dataset and proposes using legal norms and data to guide context-sensitive training-data filtering.

title: Pile of Law: Learning Responsible Data Filtering from the Law and a 256GB Open-Source Legal Dataset

abstract: We develop Temporal Quantile Adjustment (TQA), a general method to construct efficient and valid prediction intervals (PIs) for regression on cross-sectional time series data. Such data is common in many domains, including econometrics and healthcare. A canonical example in healthcare is predicting patient outcomes using physiological time-series data, where a population of patients composes a cross-section. Reliable PI estimators in this setting must address two distinct notions of coverage: cross-sectional coverage across a cross-sectional slice, and longitudinal coverage along the temporal dimension for each time series. Recent works have explored adapting Conformal Prediction (CP) to obtain PIs in the time series context. However, none handles both notions of coverage simultaneously. CP methods typically query a pre-specified quantile from the distribution of nonconformity scores on a calibration set. TQA adjusts the quantile to query in CP at each time $t$, accounting for both cross-sectional and longitudinal coverage in a theoretically-grounded manner. The post-hoc nature of TQA facilitates its use as a general wrapper around any time series regression model. We validate TQA's performance through extensive experimentation: TQA generally obtains efficient PIs and improves longitudinal coverage while preserving cross-sectional coverage.

paragraphs: Prediction intervals for collections of time series face two distinct coverage questions. At a particular time, they should cover outcomes across the population. Across time, they should also cover outcomes for each individual series. For patient monitoring, these correspond to reliability across patients and reliability throughout one patient's trajectory.

Temporal Quantile Adjustment, or TQA, modifies conformal prediction to account for both questions. Conformal methods typically construct intervals using a fixed quantile of calibration nonconformity scores. TQA instead adjusts which quantile is queried at each time step, with a theoretically grounded treatment of cross-sectional and longitudinal coverage.

Because this adjustment happens after prediction, TQA can wrap any time-series regression model. The experiments generally find efficient intervals and improved longitudinal coverage while maintaining cross-sectional coverage. The contribution is a method for addressing the two dimensions of reliability together: good population-wide coverage at individual times does not by itself describe coverage over each series' history.
summary.tldr: TQA adjusts conformal quantiles over time to improve coverage along individual series while preserving coverage across the population.

title: Conformal Prediction with Temporal Quantile Adjustments

abstract: In recent computer vision research, the advent of the Vision Transformer (ViT) has rapidly revolutionized various architectural design efforts: ViT achieved state-of-the-art image classification performance using self-attention found in natural language processing, and MLP-Mixer achieved competitive performance using simple multi-layer perceptrons. In contrast, several studies have also suggested that carefully redesigned convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can achieve advanced performance comparable to ViT without resorting to these new ideas. Against this background, there is growing interest in what inductive bias is suitable for computer vision. Here we propose Sequencer, a novel and competitive architecture alternative to ViT that provides a new perspective on these issues. Unlike ViTs, Sequencer models long-range dependencies using LSTMs rather than self-attention layers. We also propose a two-dimensional version of Sequencer module, where an LSTM is decomposed into vertical and horizontal LSTMs to enhance performance. Despite its simplicity, several experiments demonstrate that Sequencer performs impressively well: Sequencer2D-L, with 54M parameters, realizes 84.6% top-1 accuracy on only ImageNet-1K. Not only that, we show that it has good transferability and the robust resolution adaptability on double resolution-band. solution-band. Our source code is available at https://github.com/okojoalg/sequencer.

Sequencer adds another architectural option by using long short-term memory networks, or LSTMs, to model long-range dependencies. The work contributes to the question of which built-in architectural preferences suit visual learning.

The authors also introduce a two-dimensional Sequencer module that decomposes processing into vertical and horizontal LSTMs. This adapts the recurrent approach to the two spatial directions of an image and is proposed to improve performance. It provides a specific mechanism for organizing long-range interactions within the model.

In the reported experiments, Sequencer2D-L has 54 million parameters and reaches 84.6% top-1 accuracy using only ImageNet-1K. The authors also report good transferability and robust adaptability to changes in image resolution. These findings establish Sequencer as a competitive alternative architecture in the evaluated settings and show that LSTM-based long-range modeling can work well for image classification.
summary.tldr: Sequencer uses vertical and horizontal LSTMs for image classification, reaching 84.6% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 54 million parameters.

title: Sequencer: Deep LSTM for Image Classification

abstract: Learning predictive models from observations using deep neural networks (DNNs) is a promising new approach to many real-world planning and control problems. However, common DNNs are too unstructured for effective planning, and current control methods typically rely on extensive sampling or local gradient descent. In this paper, we propose a new framework for integrated model learning and predictive control that is amenable to efficient optimization algorithms. Specifically, we start with a ReLU neural model of the system dynamics and, with minimal losses in prediction accuracy, we gradually sparsify it by removing redundant neurons. This discrete sparsification process is approximated as a continuous problem, enabling an end-to-end optimization of both the model architecture and the weight parameters. The sparsified model is subsequently used by a mixed-integer predictive controller, which represents the neuron activations as binary variables and employs efficient branch-and-bound algorithms. Our framework is applicable to a wide variety of DNNs, from simple multilayer perceptrons to complex graph neural dynamics. It can efficiently handle tasks involving complicated contact dynamics, such as object pushing, compositional object sorting, and manipulation of deformable objects. Numerical and hardware experiments show that, despite the aggressive sparsification, our framework can deliver better closed-loop performance than existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper develops a joint model-learning and control framework that makes the learned dynamics more suitable for efficient optimization.

Numerical and hardware experiments show that aggressive sparsification can coexist with better closed-loop performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The key result connects a simpler dynamics model to improved optimization during control.
summary.tldr: Sparsifying learned ReLU dynamics makes mixed-integer predictive control tractable enough to improve performance on the tested manipulation tasks.

title: Model-Based Control with Sparse Neural Dynamics

abstract: We initiate the study of $\textit{behavioral information design}$ through deep learning. In information design, a $\textit{sender}$ aims to persuade a $\textit{receiver}$ to take certain actions by strategically revealing information. We address scenarios in which the receiver might exhibit different behavior patterns other than the standard Bayesian rational assumption. We propose HAIDNet, a neural-network-based optimization framework for information design that can adapt to multiple representations of human behavior. Through extensive simulation, we show that HAIDNet can not only recover information policies that are near-optimal compared with known analytical solutions, but also can extend to designing information policies for settings that are computationally challenging (e.g., when there are multiple receivers) or for settings where there are no known solutions in general (e.g., when the receiver behavior does not follow the Bayesian rational assumption). We also conduct real-world human-subject experiments and demonstrate that our framework can capture human behavior from data and lead to more effective information policy for real-world human receivers.

paragraphs: Information design studies how a sender can influence a receiver's actions by choosing what information to reveal. Standard formulations often assume that the receiver reasons in a Bayesian-rational way. This paper considers receivers with other behavioral patterns and asks how information policies can be optimized when those patterns matter.

The proposed framework, HAIDNet, uses neural networks to optimize information design while accommodating multiple representations of human behavior. Simulations show that it can recover policies close to known analytical optima. The authors also apply it to computationally difficult situations involving multiple receivers and to behavior settings for which general analytical solutions are unavailable.

Human-subject experiments provide a further test beyond simulation. The authors report that HAIDNet can learn human behavior from data and use that information to produce more effective policies for human receivers. The significance is an approach that connects behavioral modeling with policy optimization, allowing the assumed response to information to reflect observed behavior instead of relying exclusively on the standard rationality assumption.
summary.tldr: HAIDNet learns and incorporates human behavior to optimize information-revelation policies beyond standard Bayesian-rational receiver assumptions.

title: Encoding Human Behavior in Information Design through Deep Learning

abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) aims to address distributional shifts between training and testing data using only unlabeled test data streams for continual model adaptation. However, most TTA methods assume benign test streams, while test samples could be unexpectedly diverse in the wild. For instance, an unseen object or noise could appear in autonomous driving. This leads to a new threat to existing TTA algorithms; we found that prior TTA algorithms suffer from those noisy test samples as they blindly adapt to incoming samples. To address this problem, we present Screening-out Test-Time Adaptation (SoTTA), a novel TTA algorithm that is robust to noisy samples. The key enabler of SoTTA is two-fold: (i) input-wise robustness via high-confidence uniform-class sampling that effectively filters out the impact of noisy samples and (ii) parameter-wise robustness via entropy-sharpness minimization that improves the robustness of model parameters against large gradients from noisy samples. Our evaluation with standard TTA benchmarks with various noisy scenarios shows that our method outperforms state-of-the-art TTA methods under the presence of noisy samples and achieves comparable accuracy to those methods without noisy samples. The source code is available at https://github.com/taeckyung/SoTTA.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a model using an unlabeled stream of test data to cope with distribution shifts. This paper examines what happens when that stream also contains noisy or unexpected samples. The authors find that existing methods can deteriorate because they adapt indiscriminately to incoming examples, including samples that should not drive their updates.

Screening-out Test-Time Adaptation, or SoTTA, addresses the problem at two levels. High-confidence uniform-class sampling reduces the influence of noisy inputs. SoTTA outperforms state-of-the-art methods when noisy samples are present and achieves comparable accuracy when they are absent. These results support treating the reliability of the adaptation stream as part of the learning problem, with input screening and parameter robustness working together to protect continual updates.
summary.tldr: SoTTA combines input screening and parameter robustness to improve test-time adaptation on streams containing noisy samples.

title: SoTTA: Robust Test-Time Adaptation on Noisy Data Streams

abstract: We present a comprehensive solution to learn and improve text-to-image models from human preference feedback.To begin with, we build ImageReward---the first general-purpose text-to-image human preference reward model---to effectively encode human preferences.Its training is based on our systematic annotation pipeline including rating and ranking, which collects 137k expert comparisons to date.In human evaluation, ImageReward outperforms existing scoring models and metrics, making it a promising automatic metric for evaluating text-to-image synthesis.On top of it, we propose Reward Feedback Learning (ReFL), a direct tuning algorithm to optimize diffusion models against a scorer.Both automatic and human evaluation support ReFL's advantages over compared methods.All code and datasets are provided at \url{https://github.com/THUDM/ImageReward}.

paragraphs: ImageReward addresses two connected tasks: evaluating generated images according to human preferences and using that feedback to improve image generation. The authors build a general-purpose reward model for text-to-image outputs, trained through a systematic annotation process involving ratings and rankings. The reported collection contains 137,000 expert comparisons.

The reward model learns a scoring signal from those judgments. In human evaluation, it performs better than the existing scoring models and metrics considered in the paper. This supports its use as a promising automatic evaluation measure for text-to-image synthesis: a learned score can reflect preference information gathered from people.

The authors then introduce Reward Feedback Learning, or ReFL, which directly tunes diffusion models against a scorer. Both automatic and human evaluations support its advantages over the compared methods. The work therefore connects preference measurement with a way to act on that measurement during model tuning. Its evidence supports the usefulness of the learned feedback and tuning procedure in the evaluated settings, rather than establishing a universal measure of image quality.
summary.tldr: ImageReward learns human preferences for generated images, and ReFL uses a scoring signal to improve diffusion models.

title: ImageReward: Learning and Evaluating Human Preferences for Text-to-Image Generation

abstract: This paper introduces Elastic Decision Transformer (EDT), a significant advancement over the existing Decision Transformer (DT) and its variants. Although DT purports to generate an optimal trajectory, empirical evidence suggests it struggles with trajectory stitching, a process involving the generation of an optimal or near-optimal trajectory from the best parts of a set of sub-optimal trajectories. The proposed EDT differentiates itself by facilitating trajectory stitching during action inference at test time, achieved by adjusting the history length maintained in DT. Further, the EDT optimizes the trajectory by retaining a longer history when the previous trajectory is optimal and a shorter one when it is sub-optimal, enabling it to "stitch" with a more optimal trajectory. Extensive experimentation demonstrates EDT's ability to bridge the performance gap between DT-based and Q Learning-based approaches. In particular, the EDT outperforms Q Learning-based methods in a multi-task regime on the D4RL locomotion benchmark and Atari games.

paragraphs: A collection of imperfect trajectories can contain useful segments that could form a better trajectory when combined. This process, called trajectory stitching, is a challenge for Decision Transformers according to the paper's empirical motivation. Elastic Decision Transformer addresses that challenge by changing how much past experience the model considers when selecting its next action.

The adjustment happens during action inference at test time. EDT keeps a longer history when the preceding trajectory is optimal and shortens the history when it is suboptimal. Reducing the influence of a poor preceding trajectory allows the model to connect with a better continuation. History length becomes an adaptive part of decision-making.

The reported experiments show EDT narrowing the performance gap between Decision Transformer methods and Q-learning methods. In the multi-task setting, it outperforms Q-learning methods on the D4RL locomotion benchmark and Atari games. These findings support adaptive history as a useful mechanism for trajectory stitching, with the strongest comparison in the abstract specifically tied to multi-task evaluation.
summary.tldr: Elastic Decision Transformer adjusts its history length at test time to combine useful trajectory segments and improve decision-making.

title: Elastic Decision Transformer

abstract: Novelty detection is a fundamental task of machine learning which aims to detect abnormal (*i.e.* out-of-distribution (OOD)) samples. Since diffusion models have recently emerged as the de facto standard generative framework with surprising generation results, novelty detection via diffusion models has also gained much attention. Recent methods have mainly utilized the reconstruction property of in-distribution samples. However, they often suffer from detecting OOD samples that share similar background information to the in-distribution data. Based on our observation that diffusion models can *project* any sample to an in-distribution sample with similar background information, we propose *Projection Regret (PR)*, an efficient novelty detection method that mitigates the bias of non-semantic information. To be specific, PR computes the perceptual distance between the test image and its diffusion-based projection to detect abnormality. Since the perceptual distance often fails to capture semantic changes when the background information is dominant, we cancel out the background bias by comparing it against recursive projections. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PR outperforms the prior art of generative-model-based novelty detection methods by a significant margin.

paragraphs: Novelty detection aims to identify inputs that fall outside the distribution a model knows. Diffusion-based detectors often use reconstruction behavior, but they can struggle when an abnormal image shares background information with familiar images. In that situation, background similarity can obscure a meaningful difference in what the image depicts.

Projection Regret builds on the observation that a diffusion model can project an image toward an in-distribution image with similar background information. The method measures the perceptual distance between the original image and that projection. Because background content can dominate even this distance, it compares the measurement against recursive projections to cancel background bias.

The key idea is to judge the first projection in relation to further projections rather than using its perceptual distance alone. This comparison is designed to reduce the influence of nonsemantic information on the abnormality score. Extensive experiments report a significant improvement over prior generative-model-based novelty detectors. The findings support the proposed comparison as an effective way to address background bias within the evaluated detection setting.
summary.tldr: Projection Regret compares recursive diffusion projections to reduce background bias and improve novelty detection.

title: Projection Regret: Reducing Background Bias for Novelty Detection via Diffusion Models

abstract: We consider the problem of \emph{blocked} collaborative bandits where there are multiple users, each with an associated multi-armed bandit problem. These users are grouped into \emph{latent} clusters such that the mean reward vectors of users within the same cluster are identical. Our goal is to design algorithms that maximize the cumulative reward accrued by all the users over time, under the \emph{constraint} that no arm of a user is pulled more than $\mathsf{B}$ times. This problem has been originally considered by \cite{Bresler:2014}, and designing regret-optimal algorithms for it has since remained an open problem.In this work, we propose an algorithm called B-LATTICE (Blocked Latent bAndiTs via maTrIx ComplEtion) that collaborates across users, while simultaneously satisfying the budget constraints, to maximize their cumulative rewards. Theoretically, under certain reasonable assumptions on the latent structure, with $\mathsf{M}$ users, $\mathsf{N}$ arms, $\mathsf{T}$ rounds per user, and $\mathsf{C}=O(1)$ latent clusters, B-LATTICE achieves a per-user regret of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\mathsf{T}(1 + \mathsf{N}\mathsf{M}^{-1})})$ under a budget constraint of $\mathsf{B}=\Theta(\log \mathsf{T})$. These are the first sub-linear regret bounds for this problem, and match the minimax regret bounds when $\mathsf{B}=\mathsf{T}$. Empirically, we demonstrate that our algorithm has superior performance over baselines even when $\mathsf{B}=1$. B-LATTICE is a phased algorithm where in each phase it clusters users into groups and collaborates across users within a group to quickly learn their reward models.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of \emph{blocked} collaborative bandits where there are multiple users, each with an associated multi-armed bandit problem. These users are grouped into \emph{latent} clusters such that the mean reward vectors of users within the same cluster are identical. Our goal is to design algorithms that maximize the cumulative reward accrued by all the users over time, under the \emph{constraint} that no arm of a user is pulled more than $\mathsf{B}$ times. This problem has been originally considered by \cite{Bresler:2014}, and designing regret-optimal algorithms for it has since remained an open problem.In this work, we propose an algorithm called B-LATTICE (Blocked Latent bAndiTs via maTrIx ComplEtion) that collaborates across users, while simultaneously satisfying the budget constraints, to maximize their cumulative rewards. Theoretically, under certain reasonable assumptions on the latent structure, with $\mathsf{M}$ users, $\mathsf{N}$ arms, $\mathsf{T}$ rounds per user, and $\mathsf{C}=O(1)$ latent clusters, B-LATTICE achieves a per-user regret of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\mathsf{T}(1 + \mathsf{N}\mathsf{M}^{-1})})$ under a budget constraint of $\mathsf{B}=\Theta(\log \mathsf{T})$. These are the first sub-linear regret bounds for this problem, and match the minimax regret bounds when $\mathsf{B}=\mathsf{T}$. Empirically, we demonstrate that our algorithm has superior performance over baselines even when $\mathsf{B}=1$. B-LATTICE is a phased algorithm where in each phase it clusters users into groups and collaborates across users within a group to quickly learn their reward models.

paragraphs: This paper studies recommendation-like learning where each user can try each option only a limited number of times. Users belong to unknown clusters, and users in the same cluster have identical mean rewards for the available options. The aim is to maximize total reward while respecting the separate usage budget for every user-option pair.

The proposed B-LATTICE algorithm learns in phases. Each phase groups users and shares information within those groups to learn their reward models more quickly. This collaboration matters because an option cannot simply be tried repeatedly by one user whenever more evidence is needed.

Under assumptions on the latent structure, a constant number of clusters, and budgets proportional to log T, the authors prove the first sublinear regret bounds for this problem. The per-user bound is approximately the square root of T times (1 + N/M), ignoring logarithmic factors. It matches the minimax bounds for budget T. Experiments also show better performance than baselines when the budget is one, a stricter setting than the stated theorem covers.
summary.tldr: B-LATTICE shares information across user clusters to learn rewarding choices while respecting strict per-user, per-option budgets.

title: Blocked Collaborative Bandits: Online Collaborative Filtering with Per-Item Budget Constraints

abstract: One of the most impactful findings in computational neuroscience over the past decade is that the object recognition accuracy of deep neural networks (DNNs) correlates with their ability to predict neural responses to natural images in the inferotemporal (IT) cortex. This discovery supported the long-held theory that object recognition is a core objective of the visual cortex, and suggested that more accurate DNNs would serve as better models of IT neuron responses to images. Since then, deep learning has undergone a revolution of scale: billion parameter-scale DNNs trained on billions of images are rivaling or outperforming humans at visual tasks including object recognition. Have today's DNNs become more accurate at predicting IT neuron responses to images as they have grown more accurate at object recognition?Surprisingly, across three independent experiments, we find that this is not the case. DNNs have become progressively worse models of IT as their accuracy has increased on ImageNet. To understand why DNNs experience this trade-off and evaluate if they are still an appropriate paradigm for modeling the visual system, we turn to recordings of IT that capture spatially resolved maps of neuronal activity elicited by natural images. These neuronal activity maps reveal that DNNs trained on ImageNet learn to rely on different visual features than those encoded by IT and that this problem worsens as their accuracy increases. We successfully resolved this issue with the neural harmonizer, a plug-and-play training routine for DNNs that aligns their learned representations with humans. Our results suggest that harmonized DNNs break the trade-off between ImageNet accuracy and neural prediction accuracy that assails current DNNs and offer a path to more accurate models of biological vision. Our work indicates that the standard approach for modeling IT with task-optimized DNNs needs revision, and other biological constraints, including human psychophysics data, are needed to accurately reverse-engineer the visual cortex.

title: Performance-optimized deep neural networks are evolving into worse models of inferotemporal visual cortex

abstract: Many modern machine learning applications - from online principal component analysis to covariance matrix identification and dictionary learning - can be formulated as minimization problems on Riemannian manifolds, typically solved with a Riemannian stochastic gradient method (or some variant thereof). However, in many cases of interest, the resulting minimization problem is _not_ geodesically convex, so the convergence of the chosen solver to a desirable solution - i.e., a local minimizer - is by no means guaranteed. In this paper, we study precisely this question, that is, whether stochastic Riemannian optimization algorithms are guaranteed to avoid saddle points with probability $1$. For generality, we study a family of retraction-based methods which, in addition to having a potentially much lower per-iteration cost relative to Riemannian gradient descent, include other widely used algorithms, such as natural policy gradient methods and mirror descent in ordinary convex spaces. In this general setting, we show that, under mild assumptions for the ambient manifold and the oracle providing gradient information, the policies under study avoid strict saddle points / submanifolds with probability $1$, from any initial condition. This result provides an important sanity check for the use of gradient methods on manifolds as it shows that, almost always, the end state of a stochastic Riemannian algorithm can only be a local minimizer.
