paragraphs: Learning an optimizer is useful only if the resulting update rule can handle problems beyond its training examples without excessive overhead. This paper addresses both transfer to new tasks and scaling to larger models. It introduces a learned gradient descent optimizer built around a hierarchical recurrent neural network.

The architecture keeps per-parameter overhead small and incorporates features reflecting known optimization structure. Training uses an ensemble of small, diverse optimization tasks designed to capture common properties of loss landscapes. The optimizer learns to outperform RMSProp and ADAM on problems in that training corpus, establishing its effectiveness within the setting used to teach it.

The more consequential tests examine transfer. Despite receiving no neural networks in meta-training, the optimizer performs comparably or better on small convolutional networks. It also trains Inception V3 and ResNet V2 on ImageNet for thousands of steps. These results demonstrate transfer across substantial changes in task type and scale, with the large-model claim specifically covering the reported optimization runs.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical recurrent optimizer trained on small tasks transfers to neural-network training at much larger scales with reduced overhead.

title: Learned Optimizers that Scale and Generalize

abstract: The number of parameters in a deep neural network is usually very large, which helps with its learning capacity but also hinders its scalability and practicality due to memory/time inefficiency and overfitting. To resolve this issue, we propose a sparsity regularization method that exploits both positive and negative correlations among the features to enforce the network to be sparse, and at the same time remove any redundancies among the features to fully utilize the capacity of the network. Specifically, we propose to use an exclusive sparsity regularization based on (1,2)-norm, which promotes competition for features between different weights, thus enforcing them to fit to disjoint sets of features. We further combine the exclusive sparsity with the group sparsity based on (2,1)-norm, to promote both sharing and competition for features in training of a deep neural network. We validate our method on multiple public datasets, and the results show that our method can obtain more compact and efficient networks while also improving the performance over the base networks with full weights, as opposed to existing sparsity regularizations that often obtain efficiency at the expense of prediction accuracy.

To resolve this issue, we propose a sparsity regularization method that exploits both positive and negative correlations among the features to enforce the network to be sparse, and at the same time remove any redundancies among the features to fully utilize the capacity of the network. Specifically, we propose to use an exclusive sparsity regularization based on (1,2)-norm, which promotes competition for features between different weights, thus enforcing them to fit to disjoint sets of features. We further combine the exclusive sparsity with the group sparsity based on (2,1)-norm, to promote both sharing and competition for features in training of a deep neural network. We validate our method on multiple public datasets, and the results show that our method can obtain more compact and efficient networks while also improving the performance over the base networks with full weights, as opposed to existing sparsity regularizations that often obtain efficiency at the expense of prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: Large neural networks have substantial learning capacity, but their many parameters also increase memory use, computation, and the risk of overfitting. This paper proposes a regularization approach that makes networks sparse while reducing redundancy among the features used by their weights. It draws on both positive and negative feature correlations.

The method combines two complementary penalties. Exclusive sparsity, expressed through a (1,2)-norm, encourages different weights to compete for features and use disjoint feature sets. Group sparsity, based on a (2,1)-norm, promotes feature sharing. Combining them allows training to encourage shared structure and specialization within the same network, rather than relying on a single sparsity preference.

Across multiple public datasets, the authors report more compact and efficient networks that also improve on the predictive performance of their fully weighted counterparts. These findings show that the tested compression benefits did not require an accuracy sacrifice. The contribution is therefore about organizing the remaining capacity as well as reducing parameter use: the penalties encourage weights to use features less redundantly.
summary.tldr: Combining feature-sharing and feature-competition penalties produces more compact networks with improved predictive performance in the reported experiments.

title: Combined Group and Exclusive Sparsity for Deep Neural Networks

abstract: We provide initial seedings to the Quick Shift clustering algorithm, which approximate the locally high-density regions of the data. Such seedings act as more stable and expressive cluster-cores than the singleton modes found by Quick Shift. We establish statistical consistency guarantees for this modification. We then show strong clustering performance on real datasets as well as promising applications to image segmentation.
originalAbstract: We provide initial seedings to the Quick Shift clustering algorithm, which approximate the locally high-density regions of the data. Such seedings act as more stable and expressive cluster-cores than the singleton modes found by Quick Shift. We establish statistical consistency guarantees for this modification. We then show strong clustering performance on real datasets as well as promising applications to image segmentation.

paragraphs: Quickshift++ changes how the Quick Shift clustering algorithm is initialized. Its seeds approximate regions where the data are locally dense. This gives the clustering procedure starting structures that describe a region of concentrated observations, rather than representing each cluster core through a single mode point found by Quick Shift.

The authors describe these regional seeds as more stable and expressive cluster cores. The distinction concerns what the initialization captures: a singleton mode identifies one location, while a core represents a locally high-density region. That richer starting representation is the central modification studied in the paper, linking the choice of seeds to the structure the clustering algorithm is meant to recover.

The paper establishes statistical consistency guarantees for the modification and reports strong clustering performance on real datasets. It also presents promising applications to image segmentation. The theory supports the statistical basis of the initialization, while the experiments show its usefulness in practical clustering settings. Together, these contributions make seed construction an explicit part of the clustering method's design.
summary.tldr: Quickshift++ initializes clustering with locally dense regions, providing richer cluster cores, consistency guarantees, and strong reported clustering results.

title: Quickshift++: Provably Good Initializations for Sample-Based Mean Shift

abstract: We consider active learning with logged data, where labeled examples are drawn conditioned on a predetermined logging policy, and the goal is to learn a classifier on the entire population, not just conditioned on the logging policy. Prior work addresses this problem either when only logged data is available, or purely in a controlled random experimentation setting where the logged data is ignored. In this work, we combine both approaches to provide an algorithm that uses logged data to bootstrap and inform experimentation, thus achieving the best of both worlds. Our work is inspired by a connection between controlled random experimentation and active learning, and modifies existing disagreement-based active learning algorithms to exploit logged data.
originalAbstract: We consider active learning with logged data, where labeled examples are drawn conditioned on a predetermined logging policy, and the goal is to learn a classifier on the entire population, not just conditioned on the logging policy. Prior work addresses this problem either when only logged data is available, or purely in a controlled random experimentation setting where the logged data is ignored. In this work, we combine both approaches to provide an algorithm that uses logged data to bootstrap and inform experimentation, thus achieving the best of both worlds. Our work is inspired by a connection between controlled random experimentation and active learning, and modifies existing disagreement-based active learning algorithms to exploit logged data.

paragraphs: The paper considers learning a classifier when existing labeled examples were collected according to a predetermined logging policy. That policy influences which examples receive labels, so the available records reflect a selected portion of the population. The intended classifier, however, must work across the whole population. This makes the way labels were collected central to the learning problem.

The authors combine existing logged data with new, controlled experimentation. The historical examples provide a starting point and help inform subsequent experiments. This joins two approaches that earlier work treated separately: learning from the records already available and collecting new information through controlled experiments while ignoring those records.

The algorithm builds on a connection between controlled experimentation and active learning, where the learner helps determine which examples to label. Specifically, it adapts disagreement-based active learning to use logged data. The contribution is a way to coordinate historical evidence and further information gathering around the same population-level classification objective.
summary.tldr: The paper adapts active learning to use logged labels as both a starting point and a guide for new experiments.

title: Active Learning with Logged Data

abstract: Machine learning is increasingly targeting areas where input data cannot be accurately described by a single vector, but can be modeled instead using the more flexible concept of random vectors, namely probability measures or more simply point clouds of varying cardinality. Using deep architectures on measures poses, however, many challenging issues. Indeed, deep architectures are originally designed to handle fixed-length vectors, or, using recursive mechanisms, ordered sequences thereof. In sharp contrast, measures describe a varying number of weighted observations with no particular order. We propose in this work a deep framework designed to handle crucial aspects of measures, namely permutation invariances, variations in weights and cardinality. Architectures derived from this pipeline can (i) map measures to measures - using the concept of push-forward operators; (ii) bridge the gap between measures and Euclidean spaces - through integration steps. This allows to design discriminative networks (to classify or reduce the dimensionality of input measures), generative architectures (to synthesize measures) and recurrent pipelines (to predict measure dynamics). We provide a theoretical analysis of these building blocks, review our architectures’ approximation abilities and robustness w.r.t. perturbation, and try them on various discriminative and generative tasks.

paragraphs: Some inputs are better represented as probability measures or point clouds than as a single fixed-length vector. Such inputs contain unordered observations, potentially with different weights and varying numbers of points. This paper develops a deep learning framework that explicitly accommodates those properties rather than requiring an ordered sequence or fixed-size vector representation.

Its building blocks include push-forward operators, which map measures to measures, and integration steps, which connect measures with ordinary Euclidean representations. These operations allow networks to transform an input distribution while also connecting distribution-valued data to familiar vector-valued computations. The design addresses permutation invariance as well as changes in weights and cardinality.

The framework supports discriminative models for classification or dimensionality reduction, generative models that synthesize measures, and recurrent pipelines for predicting measure dynamics. The paper analyzes the building blocks theoretically, discusses approximation capabilities and robustness to perturbations, and evaluates architectures on discriminative and generative tasks. Its central contribution is a shared architectural foundation for several kinds of learning with distribution-valued inputs.
summary.tldr: A deep learning framework processes probability measures and variable-size point clouds through measure transformations and integration.

title: Stochastic Deep Networks

abstract: Existing techniques for certifying the robustness of models for discrete data either work only for a small class of models or are general at the expense of efficiency or tightness. Moreover, they do not account for sparsity in the input which, as our findings show, is often essential for obtaining non-trivial guarantees. We propose a model-agnostic certificate based on the randomized smoothing framework which subsumes earlier work and is tight, efficient, and sparsity-aware. Its computational complexity does not depend on the number of discrete categories or the dimension of the input (e.g. the graph size), making it highly scalable. We show the effectiveness of our approach on a wide variety of models, datasets, and tasks – specifically highlighting its use for Graph Neural Networks. So far, obtaining provable guarantees for GNNs has been difficult due to the discrete and non-i.i.d. nature of graph data. Our method can certify any GNN and handles perturbations to both the graph structure and the node attributes.

So far, obtaining provable guarantees for GNNs has been difficult due to the discrete and non-i.i.d. nature of graph data. paragraphs: Robustness certification asks for a mathematical guarantee that a model's prediction withstands specified changes to its input. For discrete data, existing approaches faced tradeoffs between the models they supported, computational efficiency, and the tightness of their guarantees. This paper identifies input sparsity as another important consideration: the authors find that accounting for it is often essential for obtaining meaningful certificates.

The proposed certificate uses randomized smoothing and is designed to work independently of the model architecture. It incorporates sparsity, subsumes earlier work, and is described as both tight and efficient. Its computational complexity does not depend on the input dimension or number of discrete categories. This makes the certification procedure scalable even when the discrete representation is large.

The evaluation covers multiple models, datasets, and tasks, with particular attention to graph neural networks. Graphs are difficult to certify because their data are discrete and observations are not independent and identically distributed. The method can certify any GNN architecture and handle changes to both connections and node attributes, extending its applicability across two distinct sources of graph perturbations.
summary.tldr: A sparsity-aware randomized smoothing certificate provides scalable robustness guarantees for discrete inputs, including graph structure and node attributes.

title: Efficient Robustness Certificates for Discrete Data: Sparsity-Aware Randomized Smoothing for Graphs, Images and More

abstract: Training on datasets with long-tailed distributions has been challenging for major recognition tasks such as classification and detection. To deal with this challenge, image resampling is typically introduced as a simple but effective approach. However, we observe that long-tailed detection differs from classification since multiple classes may be present in one image. As a result, image resampling alone is not enough to yield a sufficiently balanced distribution at the object-level. We address object-level resampling by introducing an object-centric sampling strategy based on a dynamic, episodic memory bank. Our proposed strategy has two benefits: 1) convenient object-level resampling without significant extra computation, and 2) implicit feature-level augmentation from model updates. We show that image-level and object-level resamplings are both important, and thus unify them with a joint resampling strategy. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the rare categories of LVIS, with 1.89% and 3.13% relative improvements over Forest R-CNN on detection and instance segmentation.

To deal with this challenge, image resampling is typically introduced as a simple but effective approach. However, we observe that long-tailed detection differs from classification since multiple classes may be present in one image. As a result, image resampling alone is not enough to yield a sufficiently balanced distribution at the object-level. We address object-level resampling by introducing an object-centric sampling strategy based on a dynamic, episodic memory bank. Our proposed strategy has two benefits: 1) convenient object-level resampling without significant extra computation, and 2) implicit feature-level augmentation from model updates. We show that image-level and object-level resamplings are both important, and thus unify them with a joint resampling strategy. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the rare categories of LVIS, with 1.89% and 3.13% relative improvements over Forest R-CNN on detection and instance segmentation.

paragraphs: Object detection datasets can contain many examples of common categories and few examples of rare ones. Resampling images can help, but an image may contain several categories at once. Increasing how often a rare-category image is selected can therefore also increase exposure to common objects, leaving the object-level training distribution insufficiently balanced.

The paper introduces object-centered sampling through a dynamic episodic memory bank. This makes it possible to resample objects without significant additional computation. Updates to the model also provide an implicit form of feature-level augmentation. The authors combine this mechanism with image resampling, arguing that the two operate at complementary levels and both contribute to effective training.

The joint strategy achieves state-of-the-art performance on rare LVIS categories in the reported evaluation. Relative improvements over Forest R-CNN are 1.89% for detection and 3.13% for instance segmentation. The results support addressing imbalance at the object level as well as the image level, particularly when multiple categories share the same training images.
summary.tldr: Combining image resampling with memory-based object resampling improves detection and segmentation of rare categories.

title: Image-Level or Object-Level? A Tale of Two Resampling Strategies for Long-Tailed Detection

abstract: Most of the current self-supervised representation learning (SSL) methods are based on the contrastive loss and the instance-discrimination task, where augmented versions of the same image instance ("positives") are contrasted with instances extracted from other images ("negatives"). For the learning to be effective, many negatives should be compared with a positive pair, which is computationally demanding. In this paper, we propose a different direction and a new loss function for SSL, which is based on the whitening of the latent-space features. The whitening operation has a "scattering" effect on the batch samples, avoiding degenerate solutions where all the sample representations collapse to a single point. Our solution does not require asymmetric networks and it is conceptually simple. Moreover, since negatives are not needed, we can extract multiple positive pairs from the same image instance. The source code of the method and of all the experiments is available at: https://github.com/htdt/self-supervised.

For the learning to be effective, many negatives should be compared with a positive pair, which is computationally demanding. In this paper, we propose a different direction and a new loss function for SSL, which is based on the whitening of the latent-space features. The whitening operation has a "scattering" effect on the batch samples, avoiding degenerate solutions where all the sample representations collapse to a single point. Our solution does not require asymmetric networks and it is conceptually simple. Moreover, since negatives are not needed, we can extract multiple positive pairs from the same image instance. The source code of the method and of all the experiments is available at: https://github.com/htdt/self-supervised.

paragraphs: Many self-supervised image-learning methods compare augmented views of the same image with examples from other images. The matching views are positives, while the other examples serve as negatives. Using many negatives can be computationally demanding. This paper proposes a different loss built around whitening the learned features.

The key role of whitening is to spread the representations of samples within a batch. This counters a degenerate solution in which every input receives the same representation, collapsing all samples to one point. Preventing that collapse is essential because agreement between views is uninformative if the network represents every image identically. The proposed objective uses the structure of the feature batch to address this issue.

The approach does not require negatives or asymmetric networks. Without negative examples, it can also draw multiple positive pairs from one image. The contribution is thus an alternative design for self-supervised representation learning: whitening supplies an anti-collapse mechanism while allowing learning to be organized around multiple views of the same instance.
summary.tldr: A whitening-based self-supervised loss prevents representation collapse without negative examples or asymmetric networks.

title: Whitening for Self-Supervised Representation Learning

abstract: We propose a novel approach to disentangle the generative factors of variation underlying a given set of observations. Our method builds upon the idea that the (unknown) low-dimensional manifold underlying the data space can be explicitly modeled as a product of submanifolds. This definition of disentanglement gives rise to a novel weakly-supervised algorithm for recovering the unknown explanatory factors behind the data. At training time, our algorithm only requires pairs of non i.i.d. data samples whose elements share at least one, possibly multidimensional, generative factor of variation. We require no knowledge on the nature of these transformations, and do not make any limiting assumption on the properties of each subspace. Our approach is easy to implement, and can be successfully applied to different kinds of data (from images to 3D surfaces) undergoing arbitrary transformations. In addition to standard synthetic benchmarks, we showcase our method in challenging real-world applications, where we compare favorably with the state of the art.
originalAbstract: We propose a novel approach to disentangle the generative factors of variation underlying a given set of observations. Our method builds upon the idea that the (unknown) low-dimensional manifold underlying the data space can be explicitly modeled as a product of submanifolds. This definition of disentanglement gives rise to a novel weakly-supervised algorithm for recovering the unknown explanatory factors behind the data. At training time, our algorithm only requires pairs of non i.i.d. data samples whose elements share at least one, possibly multidimensional, generative factor of variation. We require no knowledge on the nature of these transformations, and do not make any limiting assumption on the properties of each subspace. Our approach is easy to implement, and can be successfully applied to different kinds of data (from images to 3D surfaces) undergoing arbitrary transformations. In addition to standard synthetic benchmarks, we showcase our method in challenging real-world applications, where we compare favorably with the state of the art.

paragraphs: Disentangled representation learning seeks to separate the underlying factors responsible for variation in observations. This paper gives that goal a geometric formulation: the unknown low-dimensional manifold underlying the data is modeled as a product of smaller manifolds. The separate components provide a way to represent distinct explanatory factors.

The resulting algorithm uses weak supervision through pairs of dependent samples. Each pair must share at least one generative factor, which may itself have multiple dimensions. The method does not require knowing the nature of the transformations and does not impose restrictive properties on each subspace. The shared-factor pairing is therefore the key supplied structure used to learn the decomposition.

The authors describe the approach as easy to implement and applicable to different data types, including images and three-dimensional surfaces undergoing arbitrary transformations. Evaluations cover synthetic benchmarks and challenging real-world applications, with favorable comparisons to the state of the art. These results support using product-manifold structure as a practical organizing principle for recovering distinct sources of variation.
summary.tldr: The method learns disentangled factors through a product-manifold model using paired observations that share at least one generative factor.

title: Learning disentangled representations via product manifold projection

abstract: Retrosynthetic planning is a fundamental problem in chemistry for finding a pathway of reactions to synthesize a target molecule. Recently, search algorithms have shown promising results for solving this problem by using deep neural networks (DNNs) to expand their candidate solutions, i.e., adding new reactions to reaction pathways. However, the existing works on this line are suboptimal; the retrosynthetic planning problem requires the reaction pathways to be (a) represented by real-world reactions and (b) executable using “building block” molecules, yet the DNNs expand reaction pathways without fully incorporating such requirements. Motivated by this, we propose an end-to-end framework for directly training the DNNs towards generating reaction pathways with the desirable properties. Our main idea is based on a self-improving procedure that trains the model to imitate successful trajectories found by itself. We also propose a novel reaction augmentation scheme based on a forward reaction model. Our experiments demonstrate that our scheme significantly improves the success rate of solving the retrosynthetic problem from 86.84% to 96.32% while maintaining the performance of DNN for predicting valid reactions.

The paper proposes an end-to-end framework that trains the neural model toward generating routes with these properties. title: Self-Improved Retrosynthetic Planning

abstract: This paper proposes Omnidirectional Representations from Transformers (OMNINET). In OmniNet, instead of maintaining a strictly horizon-tal receptive field, each token is allowed to attend to all tokens in the entire network. This process can also be interpreted as a form of extreme or intensive attention mechanism that has the receptive field of the entire width and depth of the network. To this end, the omnidirectional attention is learned via a meta-learner, which is essentially another self-attention based model. In order to mitigate the computationally expensive costs of full receptive field attention, we leverage efficient self-attention models such as kernel-based, low-rank attention and/or Big Bird as the meta-learner. Extensive experiments are conducted on autoregressive language modeling(LM1B, C4), Machine Translation, Long Range Arena (LRA), and Image Recognition.The experiments show that OmniNet achieves considerable improvements across these tasks, including achieving state-of-the-art performance on LM1B,WMT’14 En-De/En-Fr, and Long Range Arena.Moreover, using omnidirectional representation in Vision Transformers leads to significant improvements on image recognition tasks on both few-shot learning and fine-tuning setups.

paragraphs: OmniNet expands what a Transformer token can attend to. Instead of restricting attention to a horizontal collection of token representations, it allows access across both the width and depth of the network. This gives attention a receptive field spanning representations throughout the network, bringing information from multiple layers into the attention process.

A separate self-attention model acts as a meta-learner that learns this omnidirectional attention. Because attending across the full network can be computationally expensive, the authors use efficient attention mechanisms for that component. The options include kernel-based attention, low-rank attention, and Big Bird, addressing the cost introduced by the broader receptive field.

Experiments cover autoregressive language modeling, translation, Long Range Arena, and image recognition. The paper reports considerable improvements, including state-of-the-art performance on LM1B, WMT’14 English–German and English–French, and Long Range Arena. Applying the same representation idea to Vision Transformers also significantly improves image recognition in both few-shot learning and fine-tuning. These findings support the usefulness of attention that can combine information across network depth.
summary.tldr: OmniNet learns attention across network width and depth, reporting improvements across language, translation, long-range reasoning, and vision tasks.

title: OmniNet: Omnidirectional Representations from Transformers

abstract: Efficient evaluation of a network architecture drawn from a large search space remains a key challenge in Neural Architecture Search (NAS). Vanilla NAS evaluates each architecture by training from scratch, which gives the true performance but is extremely time-consuming. Recently, one-shot NAS substantially reduces the computation cost by training only one supernetwork, a.k.a. supernet, to approximate the performance of every architecture in the search space via weight-sharing. However, the performance estimation can be very inaccurate due to the co-adaption among operations. In this paper, we propose few-shot NAS that uses multiple supernetworks, called sub-supernet, each covering different regions of the search space to alleviate the undesired co-adaption. Compared to one-shot NAS, few-shot NAS improves the accuracy of architecture evaluation with a small increase of evaluation cost. With only up to 7 sub-supernets, few-shot NAS establishes new SoTAs: on ImageNet, it finds models that reach 80.5% top-1 accuracy at 600 MB FLOPS and 77.5% top-1 accuracy at 238 MFLOPS; on CIFAR10, it reaches 98.72% top-1 accuracy without using extra data or transfer learning. In Auto-GAN, few-shot NAS outperforms the previously published results by up to 20%. Extensive experiments show that few-shot NAS significantly improves various one-shot methods, including 4 gradient-based and 6 search-based methods on 3 different tasks in NasBench-201 and NasBench1-shot-1.

Few-shot NAS divides the search space among several smaller supernetworks. Each covers a different region, reducing the unwanted co-adaptation caused by placing every candidate in one shared network. summary.tldr: Few-shot NAS improves architecture evaluation by distributing weight sharing across several supernetworks, with a small increase in evaluation cost.

title: Few-Shot Neural Architecture Search

abstract: A few-shot generative model should be able to generate data from a novel distribution by only observing a limited set of examples. In few-shot learning the model is trained on data from many sets from distributions sharing some underlying properties such as sets of characters from different alphabets or objects from different categories. We extend current latent variable models for sets to a fully hierarchical approach with an attention-based point to set-level aggregation and call our method SCHA-VAE for Set-Context-Hierarchical-Aggregation Variational Autoencoder. We explore likelihood-based model comparison, iterative data sampling, and adaptation-free out-of-distribution generalization. Our results show that the hierarchical formulation better captures the intrinsic variability within the sets in the small data regime. This work generalizes deep latent variable approaches to few-shot learning, taking a step toward large-scale few-shot generation with a formulation that readily works with current state-of-the-art deep generative models.

paragraphs: Few-shot generation asks a model to produce data from a new distribution after seeing only a small set of examples. Training draws on many sets whose distributions share underlying properties, such as characters from different alphabets or objects from different categories. The challenge is to use those few observations to capture the variation within a new set.

SCHA-VAE extends latent-variable models for sets into a fully hierarchical formulation. It uses attention to aggregate information from individual points into set-level context. This provides a hierarchical way to combine example-specific information with information describing the set as a whole, forming the model’s basis for few-shot generation.

The paper explores likelihood-based comparisons, iterative sampling, and out-of-distribution generalization without adaptation. Its results show that the hierarchical formulation better captures variation within sets when data are scarce. The authors position the method as a step toward large-scale few-shot generation, with a formulation compatible with current deep generative models, rather than claiming that this broader goal has already been completed.
summary.tldr: SCHA-VAE uses hierarchical latent variables and attention-based set aggregation to better capture variability for few-shot generation.

title: SCHA-VAE: Hierarchical Context Aggregation for Few-Shot Generation

abstract: Leading graph contrastive learning (GCL) methods perform graph augmentations in two fashions: (1) randomly corrupting the anchor graph, which could cause the loss of semantic information, or (2) using domain knowledge to maintain salient features, which undermines the generalization to other domains. Taking an invariance look at GCL, we argue that a high-performing augmentation should preserve the salient semantics of anchor graphs regarding instance-discrimination. To this end, we relate GCL with invariant rationale discovery, and propose a new framework, Rationale-aware Graph Contrastive Learning (RGCL). Specifically, without supervision signals, RGCL uses a rationale generator to reveal salient features about graph instance-discrimination as the rationale, and then creates rationale-aware views for contrastive learning. This rationale-aware pre-training scheme endows the backbone model with the powerful representation ability, further facilitating the fine-tuning on downstream tasks. On MNIST-Superpixel and MUTAG datasets, visual inspections on the discovered rationales showcase that the rationale generator successfully captures the salient features (\ie distinguishing semantic nodes in graphs). On biochemical molecule and social network benchmark datasets, the state-of-the-art performance of RGCL demonstrates the effectiveness of rationale-aware views for contrastive learning. Our codes are available at https://github.com/lsh0520/RGCL.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning trains representations using multiple views of a graph. Random changes can remove meaningful information, while manually preserving features using domain knowledge can restrict transfer to other domains. This paper proposes learning which parts of a graph should survive augmentation because they help distinguish that graph from others.

Rationale-aware Graph Contrastive Learning, or RGCL, uses a rationale generator without supervision signals to identify these salient features. It then creates graph views informed by the discovered rationales. The underlying idea is that useful augmentations should preserve the semantics relevant to instance discrimination. Pre-training on such views is intended to produce representations that support later fine-tuning.

Visual inspections on MNIST-Superpixel and MUTAG show that the generator identifies distinguishing semantic nodes. On biochemical molecule and social network benchmarks, RGCL achieves state-of-the-art performance. These findings provide two kinds of support: inspection connects the learned rationales to salient graph content, while downstream results support the effectiveness of using those rationales to construct contrastive views.
summary.tldr: RGCL learns salient graph features without supervision and uses them to construct contrastive views that preserve distinguishing information.

title: Let Invariant Rationale Discovery Inspire Graph Contrastive Learning

abstract: In temporal-difference reinforcement learning algorithms, variance in value estimation can cause instability and overestimation of the maximal target value. Many algorithms have been proposed to reduce overestimation, including several recent ensemble methods, however none have shown success in sample-efficient learning through addressing estimation variance as the root cause of overestimation. In this paper, we propose MeanQ, a simple ensemble method that estimates target values as ensemble means. Despite its simplicity, MeanQ shows remarkable sample efficiency in experiments on the Atari Learning Environment benchmark. Importantly, we find that an ensemble of size 5 sufficiently reduces estimation variance to obviate the lagging target network, eliminating it as a source of bias and further gaining sample efficiency. We justify intuitively and empirically the design choices in MeanQ, including the necessity of independent experience sampling. On a set of 26 benchmark Atari environments, MeanQ outperforms all tested baselines, including the best available baseline, SUNRISE, at 100K interaction steps in 16/26 environments, and by 68% on average. MeanQ also outperforms Rainbow DQN at 500K steps in 21/26 environments, and by 49% on average, and achieves average human-level performance using 200K ($\pm$100K) interaction steps. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/indylab/MeanQ.

MeanQ addresses this source of overestimation by averaging target-value estimates across an ensemble of deep networks. Its emphasis is on reducing estimation variance to improve sample efficiency.

The authors find that five ensemble members reduce variance enough in their experiments to remove the lagging target network. This also removes that network as a source of bias and further improves sample efficiency. The paper supports its design choices through intuition and experiments, including the importance of independently sampling experience for ensemble members.

summary.tldr: MeanQ averages ensemble value estimates to reduce variance and improve Atari sample efficiency, with five members sufficient to remove the lagging target network in experiments.

title: Reducing Variance in Temporal-Difference Value Estimation via Ensemble of Deep Networks

abstract: Deep generative models have achieved tremendous success in designing novel drug molecules in recent years. A new thread of works have shown potential in advancing the specificity and success rate of in silico drug design by considering the structure of protein pockets. This setting posts fundamental computational challenges in sampling new chemical compounds that could satisfy multiple geometrical constraints imposed by pockets. Previous sampling algorithms either sample in the graph space or only consider the 3D coordinates of atoms while ignoring other detailed chemical structures such as bond types and functional groups. To address the challenge, we develop an E(3)-equivariant generative network composed of two modules: 1) a new graph neural network capturing both spatial and bonding relationships between atoms of the binding pockets and 2) a new efficient algorithm which samples new drug candidates conditioned on the pocket representations from a tractable distribution without relying on MCMC. Experimental results demonstrate that molecules sampled from Pocket2Mol achieve significantly better binding affinity and other drug properties such as drug-likeness and synthetic accessibility.

paragraphs: Designing molecules for a protein pocket requires satisfying three-dimensional geometric constraints alongside chemical structure. Earlier generators could focus on molecular graphs or atom coordinates without fully integrating bonding details. Pocket2Mol develops a pocket-conditioned generator that treats spatial and chemical relationships together.

Its E(3)-equivariant network contains a graph neural component that captures spatial and bonding relationships in the pocket representation. A second component samples candidate molecules from a tractable distribution conditioned on that representation. This sampling procedure avoids reliance on Markov chain Monte Carlo, addressing a computational obstacle in generating geometrically suitable compounds.

The reported experiments produce molecules with better binding affinity and other assessed properties, including drug-likeness and synthetic accessibility. These are results of the paper’s molecular-design evaluation; they do not establish clinical effectiveness or completed laboratory synthesis. The contribution is an efficient generation method that incorporates both the pocket’s geometry and the detailed chemical structure needed for candidate design.
summary.tldr: Pocket2Mol jointly models pocket geometry and chemical structure to sample improved molecular candidates without MCMC.

title: Pocket2Mol: Efficient Molecular Sampling Based on 3D Protein Pockets

abstract: Large pretrained Transformer language models have been shown to exhibit zero-shot generalization, i.e. they can perform a wide variety of tasks that they were not explicitly trained on. However, the architectures and pretraining objectives used across state-of-the-art models differ significantly, and there has been limited systematic comparison of these factors. In this work, we present a large-scale evaluation of modeling choices and their impact on zero-shot generalization. In particular, we focus on text-to-text models and experiment with three model architectures (causal/non-causal decoder-only and encoder-decoder), trained with two different pretraining objectives (autoregressive and masked language modeling), and evaluated with and without multitask prompted finetuning. We train models with over 5 billion parameters for more than 168 billion tokens, thereby increasing the likelihood that our conclusions will transfer to even larger scales. Our experiments show that causal decoder-only models trained on an autoregressive language modeling objective exhibit the strongest zero-shot generalization after purely self-supervised pretraining. However, models with non-causal visibility on their input trained with a masked language modeling objective followed by multitask finetuning perform the best among our experiments. We therefore consider the adaptation of pretrained models across architectures and objectives. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/bigscience- workshop/architecture-objective.

This paper systematically compares those choices for text-to-text models. It examines causal and non-causal decoder-only architectures alongside encoder-decoder models, using autoregressive and masked language-modeling objectives.

The evaluation also distinguishes models used after self-supervised pretraining from those receiving multitask prompted finetuning. The authors train models exceeding five billion parameters for more than 168 billion tokens. These findings motivate considering adaptations across architectures and objectives, because the preferred configuration changes with whether multitask finetuning is included.
summary.tldr: The best tested language-model configuration for zero-shot generalization changes depending on whether multitask prompted finetuning follows pretraining.

title: What Language Model Architecture and Pretraining Objective Works Best for Zero-Shot Generalization?

abstract: Unsupervised/self-supervised graph representation learning is critical for downstream node- and graph-level classification tasks. Global structure of graphs helps discriminating representations and existing methods mainly utilize the global structure by imposing additional supervisions. However, their global semantics are usually invariant for all nodes/graphs and they fail to explicitly embed the global semantics to enrich the representations. In this paper, we propose Omni-Granular Ego-Semantic Propagation for Self-Supervised Graph Representation Learning (OEPG). Specifically, we introduce instance-adaptive global-aware ego-semantic descriptors, leveraging the first- and second-order feature differences between each node/graph and hierarchical global clusters of the entire graph dataset. The descriptors can be explicitly integrated into local graph convolution as new neighbor nodes. Besides, we design an omni-granular normalization on the whole scales and hierarchies of the ego-semantic to assign attentional weight to each descriptor from an omni-granular perspective. Specialized pretext tasks and cross-iteration momentum update are further developed for local-global mutual adaptation. In downstream tasks, OEPG consistently achieves the best performance with a 2%~6% accuracy gain on multiple datasets cross scales and domains. Notably, OEPG also generalizes to quantity- and topology-imbalance scenarios.

paragraphs: Global graph structure can improve representations, but the authors argue that existing self-supervised methods often use global information that is identical across instances and does not explicitly enrich their features. OEPG addresses this by giving each node or graph its own description of how it relates to the wider dataset.

These descriptors use first- and second-order feature differences between an instance and hierarchical global clusters. They enter local graph convolution as additional neighbor nodes, making global relationships available within local computation. A normalization mechanism across scales and hierarchy levels assigns attention weights to the descriptors, allowing their contributions to reflect the broader collection of available global information.

The method also uses specialized pretext tasks and momentum updates across iterations so local representations and global information adapt together. On downstream tasks, the authors report consistently best performance with accuracy gains of 2%–6% across multiple datasets, scales, and domains. They also report generalization to quantity and topology imbalance. The central design is explicit, instance-adaptive integration of global context.
summary.tldr: OEPG injects instance-specific relationships to hierarchical global clusters into local graph learning, improving downstream performance across the evaluated settings.

title: Omni-Granular Ego-Semantic Propagation for Self-Supervised Graph Representation Learning

abstract: Model stitching—where the internal representations of two neural networks are aligned linearly—helped demonstrate that the representations of different neural networks for the same task are surprisingly similar in a functional sense. At the same time, the representations of adversarially robust networks are considered to be different from non-robust representations. For example, robust image classifiers are invertible, while non-robust networks are not. Here, we investigate the functional similarity of robust and non-robust representations for image classification with the help of model stitching. We find that robust and non-robust networks indeed have different representations. However, these representations are compatible regarding accuracy. From the point of view of robust accuracy, compatibility decreases quickly after the first few layers but the representations become compatible again in the last layers, in the sense that the properties of the front model can be recovered. Moreover, this is true even in the case of cross-task stitching. Our results suggest that stitching in the initial, preprocessing layers and the final, abstract layers test different kinds of compatibilities. In particular, the final layers are easy to match, because their representations depend mostly on the same abstract task specification, in our case, the classification of the input into $n$ classes.

For example, robust image classifiers are invertible, while non-robust networks are not. title: On the Functional Similarity of Robust and Non-Robust Neural Representations

abstract: A treatment policy defines when and what treatments are applied to affect some outcome of interest. Data-driven decision-making requires the ability to predict what happens if a policy is changed . Existing methods that predict how the outcome evolves under different scenarios assume that the tentative sequences of future treatments are fixed in advance, while in practice the treatments are determined stochastically by a policy and may depend, for example, on the efficiency of previous treatments. Therefore, the current methods are not applicable if the treatment policy is unknown or a counterfactual analysis is needed. To handle these limitations, we model the treatments and outcomes jointly in continuous time, by combining Gaussian processes and point processes. Our model enables the estimation of a treatment policy from observational sequences of treatments and outcomes, and it can predict the interventional and counterfactual progression of the outcome after an intervention on the treatment policy (in contrast with the causal effect of a single treatment). We show with real-world and semi-synthetic data on blood glucose progression that our method can answer causal queries more accurately than existing alternatives.

This paper addresses causal questions about those policy changes, including cases where the original policy must first be estimated from observed treatment and outcome histories.

The authors jointly model treatments and outcomes in continuous time by combining Gaussian processes with point processes. Joint modeling allows the treatment process and the evolving outcome to be considered together. The model can estimate a treatment policy from observational sequences and predict outcome progression after an intervention changes that policy.

Evaluations using real-world and semi-synthetic blood glucose data show more accurate answers to causal queries than the alternatives considered. The central contribution is a framework that represents the policy generating treatments as part of the causal prediction problem.
summary.tldr: A continuous-time joint model of treatments and outcomes estimates treatment policies and predicts causal effects of changing them.

title: Causal Modeling of Policy Interventions From Treatment-Outcome Sequences

abstract: Denoising diffusion models (DDMs) have led to staggering performance leaps in image generation, editing and restoration. However, existing DDMs use very large datasets for training. Here, we introduce a framework for training a DDM on a single image. Our method, which we coin SinDDM, learns the internal statistics of the training image by using a multi-scale diffusion process. To drive the reverse diffusion process, we use a fully-convolutional light-weight denoiser, which is conditioned on both the noise level and the scale. This architecture allows generating samples of arbitrary dimensions, in a coarse-to-fine manner. As we illustrate, SinDDM generates diverse high-quality samples, and is applicable in a wide array of tasks, including style transfer and harmonization. Furthermore, it can be easily guided by external supervision. Particularly, we demonstrate text-guided generation from a single image using a pre-trained CLIP model.

paragraphs: SinDDM explores training a denoising diffusion model on just one image. Instead of drawing its training statistics from a large image collection, it learns the internal statistics of that single example. A multiscale diffusion process lets the model work with the image at different levels of detail.

The reverse diffusion process uses a lightweight, fully convolutional denoiser conditioned on both noise level and scale. Generation proceeds from coarse structure toward finer detail. The architecture permits output samples with arbitrary dimensions, making the learned image statistics usable beyond the original image's dimensions.

They also show that external supervision can guide the model, demonstrating text-guided generation with a pretrained CLIP model. This distinguishes learning from one image from the separate use of a pretrained guidance model. The contribution is a diffusion framework that learns from minimal image-specific training data while supporting several forms of generation and editing.
summary.tldr: SinDDM learns a multiscale diffusion model from one image to generate varied outputs and support editing and externally guided generation.

title: SinDDM: A Single Image Denoising Diffusion Model

abstract: In domain generalization (DG), the target domain is unknown when the model is being trained, and the trained model should successfully work on an arbitrary (and possibly unseen) target domain during inference. This is a difficult problem, and despite active studies in recent years, it remains a great challenge. In this paper, we take a simple yet effective approach to tackle this issue. We propose test-time style shifting, which shifts the style of the test sample (that has a large style gap with the source domains) to the nearest source domain that the model is already familiar with, before making the prediction. This strategy enables the model to handle any target domains with arbitrary style statistics, without additional model update at test-time. Additionally, we propose style balancing, which provides a great platform for maximizing the advantage of test-time style shifting by handling the DG-specific imbalance issues. The proposed ideas are easy to implement and successfully work in conjunction with various other DG schemes. Experimental results on different datasets show the effectiveness of our methods.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks a model to work in a target domain that was unknown during training. A major difficulty is that test examples may have styles far from those seen in the source domains. This paper addresses that mismatch by changing the style of an incoming example before the model makes its prediction.

The proposed test-time style shifting moves a sample with a large style gap toward the nearest source domain familiar to the model. It requires no model update at test time. The authors also introduce style balancing to address imbalance issues specific to domain generalization, creating better conditions for style shifting to help.

The methods are described as easy to implement and compatible with various other domain-generalization approaches. Experiments on different datasets demonstrate their effectiveness. The core idea is to handle unfamiliar style statistics through a transformation of the test input, using known source styles as reference points. Style balancing complements this by addressing the training-side imbalance that affects how much benefit the shift can provide.
summary.tldr: Shifting unfamiliar test styles toward known source domains improves domain generalization without updating the model at test time.

title: Test-Time Style Shifting: Handling Arbitrary Styles in Domain Generalization

abstract: There exist complex patterns behind the decision-making processes of different individuals across different environments. For instance, in a social recommender system, various user behaviors are driven by highly entangled latent factors from two environments, i.e., consuming environment where users consume items and social environment where users connect with each other. Uncovering the disentanglement of these latent factors for users can benefit in enhanced explainability and controllability for recommendation. However, in literature there has been no work on social recommendation capable of disentangling user representations across consuming and social environments. To solve this problem, we study co-disentangled representation learning across different environments via proposing the curriculum co-disentangled representation learning (CurCoDis) model to disentangle the hidden factors for users across both consuming and social environments. To co-disentangle joint representations for user-item consumption and user-user social graph simultaneously, we partition the social graph into equal-size sub-graphs with minimum number of edges being cut, and design a curriculum weighing strategy for subgraph training through measuring the complexity of subgraphs via Descartes’ rule of signs. We further develop the prototype-routing optimization mechanism, which achieves co-disentanglement of user representations across consuming and social environments. Extensive experiments for social recommendation demonstrate that our proposed CurCoDis model can significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods on several real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Social recommendation draws on two kinds of behavior: the items people consume and the people they connect with. Hidden influences on these behaviors can become tangled together in a user representation. This paper proposes CurCoDis to separate those influences jointly across the consumption and social environments, with the motivation of making recommendations more explainable and controllable.

The method learns from user-item interactions and the user-user social graph together. It divides the social graph into equally sized subgraphs while minimizing the number of connections cut between them. A curriculum weighting strategy then uses subgraph complexity, measured through Descartes’ rule of signs, to guide how those subgraphs contribute during training.

CurCoDis also introduces a prototype-routing optimization mechanism to achieve joint disentanglement across the two environments. Experiments on several real-world recommendation datasets show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The reported result supports learning the two sources of user behavior together while explicitly separating their hidden factors; explainability and controllability provide the motivation for that representation design.
summary.tldr: CurCoDis jointly separates hidden factors in consumption and social behavior to improve social recommendation.

title: Curriculum Co-disentangled Representation Learning across Multiple Environments for Social Recommendation

abstract: Competitions for shareable and limited resources have long been studied with strategic agents. In reality, agents often have to learn and maximize the rewards of the resources at the same time. To design an individualized competing policy, we model the competition between agents in a novel multi-player multi-armed bandit (MPMAB) setting where players are selfish and aim to maximize their own rewards. In addition, when several players pull the same arm, we assume that these players averagely share the arms’ rewards by expectation. Under this setting, we first analyze the Nash equilibrium when arms’ rewards are known. Subsequently, we propose a novel Selfish MPMAB with Averaging Allocation (SMAA) approach based on the equilibrium. We theoretically demonstrate that SMAA could achieve a good regret guarantee for each player when all players follow the algorithm. Additionally, we establish that no single selfish player can significantly increase their rewards through deviation, nor can they detrimentally affect other players’ rewards without incurring substantial losses for themselves. We finally validate the effectiveness of the method in extensive synthetic experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies agents that compete for limited resources while learning how rewarding those resources are. Each agent acts selfishly to maximize its own reward. The model allows several players to choose the same resource, with the specific assumption that its reward is shared equally among them in expectation.

The authors first analyze Nash equilibrium when resource rewards are already known: a configuration where unilateral changes do not improve a player’s outcome. They then use that equilibrium analysis to design Selfish MPMAB with Averaging Allocation, or SMAA, for the learning setting. This connects the question of how to explore unknown resources with the question of how strategic players can coexist.

The theoretical results give each player a regret guarantee when all players follow SMAA. They also establish qualified protections against deviation: a single player cannot substantially improve its reward by deviating, or substantially harm others without suffering considerable losses itself. Synthetic experiments support the method’s effectiveness. These findings concern both learning performance and incentives under the stated reward-sharing model.
summary.tldr: SMAA combines learning and equilibrium reasoning for selfish players competing over resources whose rewards are shared.

title: Competing for Shareable Arms in Multi-Player Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: As the field of Graph Neural Networks (GNN) continues to grow, it experiences a corresponding increase in the need for large, real-world datasets to train and test new GNN models on challenging, realistic problems. Unfortunately, such graph datasets are often generated from online, highly privacy-restricted ecosystems, which makes research and development on these datasets hard, if not impossible. This greatly reduces the amount of benchmark graphs available to researchers, causing the field to rely only on a handful of publicly-available datasets. To address this problem, we introduce a novel graph generative model, Computation Graph Transformer (CGT) that learns and reproduces the distribution of real-world graphs in a privacy-controlled way. More specifically, CGT (1) generates effective benchmark graphs on which GNNs show similar task performance as on the source graphs, (2) scales to process large-scale graphs, (3) incorporates off-the-shelf privacy modules to guarantee end-user privacy of the generated graph. Extensive experiments across a vast body of graph generative models show that only our model can successfully generate privacy-controlled, synthetic substitutes of large-scale real-world graphs that can be effectively used to benchmark GNN models.

paragraphs: Graph-neural-network research needs challenging datasets, but many large real-world graphs come from systems with strong privacy restrictions. This limits access and encourages repeated reliance on a small collection of public benchmarks. The paper proposes generating synthetic substitutes that retain useful characteristics for evaluating graph models.

The Computation Graph Transformer, or CGT, learns and reproduces real-world graph distributions with privacy control. Its objectives include processing large graphs and producing benchmarks on which graph neural networks perform similarly to how they perform on the source data. It incorporates existing privacy modules to provide end-user privacy guarantees for the generated graphs.

The authors compare CGT with a broad collection of graph-generative models. Within those experiments, they report that only CGT successfully combines large-scale generation, privacy control, and effective substitution for real-world benchmarking. The important outcome is not simply generating plausible graphs: it is preserving their usefulness as tests of graph-neural-network performance while addressing the privacy constraints that restrict access to the originals.
summary.tldr: CGT generates privacy-controlled synthetic graphs that preserve useful graph-neural-network benchmarking behavior at large scale.

title: Graph Generative Model for Benchmarking Graph Neural Networks

abstract: This paper explores the connections between tempering (for Sequential Monte Carlo; SMC) and entropic mirror descent to sample from a target probability distribution whose unnormalized density is known. We establish that tempering SMC corresponds to entropic mirror descent applied to the reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and obtain convergence rates for the tempering iterates. Our result motivates the tempering iterates from an optimization point of view, showing that tempering can be seen as a descent scheme of the KL divergence with respect to the Fisher-Rao geometry, in contrast to Langevin dynamics that perform descent of the KL with respect to the Wasserstein-2 geometry. We exploit the connection between tempering and mirror descent iterates to justify common practices in SMC and derive adaptive tempering rules that improve over other alternative benchmarks in the literature.

paragraphs: The paper studies sampling when a target probability distribution is known only through its unnormalized density. It connects tempering, used in Sequential Monte Carlo, with entropic mirror descent, an optimization method. This gives a mathematical explanation for how a sampling procedure can also make progress on an optimization objective.

The authors establish that tempering corresponds to entropic mirror descent on the reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence, a measure of discrepancy between distributions. They also obtain convergence rates for the tempering iterates. From this perspective, tempering reduces that discrepancy according to Fisher–Rao geometry. Langevin dynamics provide a contrasting route: they descend a KL objective using Wasserstein-2 geometry.

The connection has practical consequences beyond reinterpreting an existing method. The authors use it to justify common Sequential Monte Carlo practices and derive adaptive tempering rules that improve on alternative benchmarks. The contribution is therefore both explanatory and constructive: an optimization viewpoint helps explain familiar sampling choices and supplies a basis for designing better ones.
summary.tldr: Tempering can be understood as entropic mirror descent, yielding convergence results and improved adaptive sampling rules.

title: A connection between Tempering and Entropic Mirror Descent

abstract: Tokenization is an understudied and often neglected component of modern LLMs. Most published works use a single tokenizer for all experiments, often borrowed from another model, without performing ablations or analysis to optimize tokenization. Moreover, the tokenizer is generally kept unchanged when fine-tuning a base model. In this paper, we show that the size, pre-tokenization regular expression, and training data of a tokenizer can significantly impact the model’s generation speed, effective context size, memory usage, and downstream performance. We train specialized Byte-Pair Encoding code tokenizers, and conduct extensive ablations on the impact of tokenizer design on the performance of LLMs for code generation tasks such as HumanEval and MBPP, and provide recommendations for tokenizer hyper-parameters selection and switching the tokenizer in a pre-trained LLM. We perform our experiments on models trained from scratch and from pre-trained models, verifying their applicability to a wide range of use-cases. We find that when fine-tuning on more than 50 billion tokens, we can specialize the tokenizer of a pre-trained LLM to obtain large gains in generation speed and effective context size.

paragraphs: A tokenizer determines how text is divided into the units a language model processes. This paper argues that treating it as a fixed, inherited component can overlook consequential design choices. The authors investigate how vocabulary size, the regular expression used for pre-tokenization, and tokenizer training data affect model behavior and efficiency.

They train specialized Byte-Pair Encoding tokenizers for code and conduct ablations on code generation tasks, including HumanEval and MBPP. The experiments cover both models trained from scratch and adaptation of pretrained models. The reported effects span generation speed, effective context size, memory use, and downstream performance, showing that tokenizer design affects several aspects of the system together.

The paper provides recommendations for selecting tokenizer hyperparameters and replacing a pretrained model’s tokenizer. A highlighted finding is that specialization can yield large gains in generation speed and effective context size when fine-tuning uses more than 50 billion tokens. That training scale qualifies the stated result and makes the amount of adaptation data relevant to the decision.
summary.tldr: Tokenizer design materially affects code language models, with substantial speed and context gains reported after specialization using more than 50 billion fine-tuning tokens.

title: Getting the most out of your tokenizer for pre-training and domain adaptation

abstract: For binary classification in $d$ dimensions, it is known that with a sample size of $n$, an excess adversarial risk of $O(d/n)$ is achievable under strong parametric assumptions about the underlying data distribution (e.g., assuming a Gaussian mixture model). In the case of well-separated distributions, this rate can be further refined to $O(1/n)$. Our work studies the non-parametric setting, where very little is known. With only mild regularity conditions on the conditional distribution of the features, we examine adversarial attacks with respect to arbitrary norms and introduce a straightforward yet effective estimator with provable consistency w.r.t adversarial risk. Our estimator is given by minimizing a series of smoothed versions of the robust 0/1 loss, with a smoothing bandwidth that adapts to both $n$ and $d$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our estimator can achieve the minimax excess adversarial risk of $\widetilde O(\sqrt{d/n})$ for linear classifiers, at the cost of solving possibly rougher optimization problems.

paragraphs: Adversarially robust classification asks whether predictions remain correct when inputs are deliberately perturbed. Strong statistical guarantees are known under restrictive distributional models, but much less is established without those models. This paper studies binary linear classification in a non-parametric setting, assuming only mild regularity of the feature distribution conditional on the class.

The authors introduce an estimator that minimizes a sequence of smoothed versions of the robust 0/1 loss. Its smoothing bandwidth changes with both the number of observations and the number of dimensions. Their analysis accommodates attacks measured using arbitrary norms and proves consistency with respect to adversarial risk under the stated conditions.

The estimator can also attain the minimax excess adversarial risk rate of roughly the square root of dimension divided by sample size, up to logarithmic factors. Achieving that rate may require solving rougher optimization problems. The result therefore connects statistical robustness under weaker distributional assumptions with a concrete optimization tradeoff, rather than transferring the faster rates available under strong parametric assumptions.
summary.tldr: A progressively smoothed estimator achieves consistent adversarially robust linear classification under mild distributional conditions, with an optimal rate available at an optimization cost.

title: Consistent Adversarially Robust Linear Classification: Non-Parametric Setting

abstract: Dataset Distillation seeks to summarize a large dataset by generating a reduced set of synthetic samples. While there has been much success at distilling small datasets such as CIFAR-10 on smaller neural architectures, Dataset Distillation methods fail to scale to larger high-resolution datasets and architectures. In this work, we introduce Dataset Distillation with Domain Shift (D3S), a scalable distillation algorithm, made by reframing the dataset distillation problem as a domain shift one. In doing so, we derive a universal bound on the distillation loss, and provide a method for efficiently approximately optimizing it. We achieve state-of-the-art results on Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-1k, and ImageNet-21K over a variety of recently proposed baselines, including high cross-architecture generalization. Additionally, our ablation studies provide lessons on the importance of validation-time hyperparameters on distillation performance, motivating the need for standardization.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation compresses the training information in a large dataset into a smaller collection of synthetic examples. The paper addresses the difficulty of extending successful small-dataset methods to larger, higher-resolution datasets and larger neural architectures. Its proposed algorithm, D3S, approaches that scaling problem by treating distillation as a domain-shift problem.

This reframing supplies a mathematical target: the authors derive a universal bound on distillation loss and develop an efficient method for approximately optimizing it. The distinction between the bound and its approximate optimization matters. The approach provides a principled objective together with a practical way to pursue it at scales that earlier distillation methods struggled to handle.

D3S reports state-of-the-art results on Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-1k, and ImageNet-21K against a variety of recent baselines, including strong transfer across architectures. Ablation studies also show that validation-time hyperparameters materially affect distillation performance. That finding motivates standardized evaluation choices, because apparent differences between distillation methods can depend on how the resulting synthetic datasets are assessed.
summary.tldr: D3S reframes dataset distillation as domain shift to scale synthetic-data compression and improve transfer across neural architectures.

title: Large Scale Dataset Distillation with Domain Shift

abstract: Recent advances in powerful pre-trained diffusion models encourage the development of methods to improve the sampling performance under well-trained diffusion models. This paper introduces Diffusion Rejection Sampling (DiffRS), which uses a rejection sampling scheme that aligns the sampling transition kernels with the true ones at each timestep. The proposed method can be viewed as a mechanism that evaluates the quality of samples at each intermediate timestep and refines them with varying effort depending on the sample. Theoretical analysis shows that DiffRS can achieve a tighter bound on sampling error compared to pre-trained models. Empirical results demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of DiffRS on the benchmark datasets and the effectiveness of DiffRS for fast diffusion samplers and large-scale text-to-image diffusion models. Our code is available at https://github.com/aailabkaist/DiffRS.

paragraphs: Diffusion Rejection Sampling addresses how to improve generation from an already trained diffusion model. Its focus is the sampling process: the sequence of intermediate transitions through which the model produces a sample. Errors in these transitions motivate a mechanism that checks and refines samples along the way.

The method, called DiffRS, applies rejection sampling to align the model’s transition kernels with the true kernels at each timestep. A transition kernel describes how the sampling process moves from one intermediate state to the next. Viewed operationally, DiffRS evaluates intermediate sample quality and varies the refinement effort according to the sample, rather than assigning identical effort to every generated result.

The theoretical analysis shows that DiffRS can obtain a tighter sampling-error bound than the pretrained models. Experiments report state-of-the-art benchmark performance and demonstrate effectiveness with fast diffusion samplers and large text-to-image models. These results support intermediate rejection and refinement as a way to improve sampling from powerful existing diffusion models.
summary.tldr: DiffRS refines intermediate diffusion samples through rejection sampling, with improved error bounds and strong reported benchmark performance.

title: Diffusion Rejection Sampling

abstract: In Federated Continual Learning (FCL), the challenge lies in effectively facilitating knowledge transfer and enhancing the performance across various tasks on different clients. Current FCL methods predominantly focus on avoiding interference between tasks, thereby overlooking the potential for positive knowledge transfer across tasks learned by different clients at separate time intervals. To address this issue, we introduce a Prompt-based knowledge transfer FCL algorithm, called Powder, designed to effectively foster the transfer of knowledge encapsulated in prompts between various sequentially learned tasks and clients. Furthermore, we have devised a unique approach for prompt generation and aggregation, intending to alleviate privacy protection concerns and communication overhead, while still promoting knowledge transfer. Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method in terms of reduction in communication costs, and enhancement of knowledge transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/piaohongming/Powder.
