paragraphs: Federated continual learning combines two sources of change: different clients hold different data, and each client learns tasks over time. Existing methods primarily try to keep tasks from interfering with one another. This paper emphasizes another opportunity: knowledge learned by one client on an earlier task may help a different client with another task.

The proposed algorithm, Powder, uses prompts to carry this knowledge between sequential tasks and across clients. It introduces a prompt generation and aggregation approach designed to support that transfer while reducing communication overhead and addressing privacy concerns. Prompts therefore serve as the representation through which the method organizes shared task knowledge.

The reported experiments show improved knowledge transfer and reduced communication costs. These findings support making positive transfer an explicit goal alongside managing interference in federated continual learning. The privacy component is described as a design intention to alleviate concerns; the abstract's stated experimental findings specifically concern communication savings and improved transfer.
summary.tldr: Powder transfers knowledge through prompts across clients and sequential tasks, improving transfer and reducing communication costs in the reported experiments.

title: Federated Continual Learning via Prompt-based Dual Knowledge Transfer

abstract: Semi-supervised learning has made remarkable strides by effectively utilizing a limited amount of labeled data while capitalizing on the abundant information present in unlabeled data. However, current algorithms often prioritize aligning image predictions with specific classes generated through self-training techniques, thereby neglecting the inherent relationships that exist within these classes. In this paper, we present a new approach called OTMatch, which leverages semantic relationships among classes by employing an optimal transport loss function to match distributions. We conduct experiments on many standard vision and language datasets. The empirical results show improvements in our method above baseline, this demonstrates the effectiveness and superiority of our approach in harnessing semantic relationships to enhance learning performance in a semi-supervised setting.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines a small amount of labeled data with a larger pool of unlabeled examples. Many approaches use self-training to generate class targets and then encourage predictions to match them. The paper identifies a weakness in that emphasis: matching predictions to individual classes can overlook meaningful relationships among the classes themselves.

OTMatch incorporates those semantic relationships through an optimal-transport loss for matching distributions. This makes relationships between classes part of the learning objective, rather than relying only on alignment with a generated class target. The proposed change therefore concerns how information from unlabeled examples guides training and how class structure enters that guidance.

The authors evaluate OTMatch on standard vision and language datasets and report improvements over baseline methods. Those results support the usefulness of semantic class relationships in the tested semi-supervised settings. The broader significance is that unlabeled-data learning can benefit from a richer notion of agreement between distributions, one that incorporates relationships among possible outcomes alongside the predictions assigned to individual examples.
summary.tldr: OTMatch uses optimal transport to incorporate semantic relationships among classes, improving semi-supervised learning on evaluated vision and language datasets.

title: OTMatch: Improving Semi-Supervised Learning with Optimal Transport

abstract: Due to the high cost of training DNN models, how to protect the intellectual property of DNN models, especially when the models are deployed to users’ devices, is becoming an important topic. One practical solution is to use Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) and researchers have proposed various model obfuscation solutions to make full use of the high-security guarantee of TEEs and the high performance of collocated GPUs. In this paper, we first identify a common vulnerability, namely the fragility of randomness, that is shared by existing TEE-based model obfuscation solutions. This vulnerability benefits model-stealing attacks and allows the adversary to recover about 97% of the secret model. To improve the security of TEE-shielded DNN models, we further propose a new model obfuscation approach GroupCover, which uses sufficient randomization and mutual covering obfuscation to protect model weights. Experimental results demonstrate that GroupCover can achieve a comparable security level as the upper-bound (black-box protection), which is remarkably over 3x compared with existing solutions. Besides, GroupCover introduces 19% overhead and negligible accuracy loss compared to model unprotected scheme.

paragraphs: Deploying a neural network on a user's device raises the problem of protecting its valuable model weights. Existing approaches combine trusted execution environments with nearby GPUs, using obfuscation to balance protection and inference performance. This paper identifies a shared weakness in such schemes that it calls fragility of randomness.

The authors show that this vulnerability can help a model-stealing adversary recover about 97% of a secret model. GroupCover responds with sufficient randomization and mutual covering obfuscation to protect the weights. Its focus is the strength of the obfuscation surrounding computation, addressing a weakness that remains relevant even when a trusted execution environment is involved.

Experiments report protection comparable to the paper's black-box protection upper bound, with a security improvement of more than three times over existing solutions. Relative to unprotected inference, GroupCover introduces 19% overhead and negligible accuracy loss. These reported results show the security and efficiency tradeoff achieved in the evaluation, combining stronger weight protection with a measured increase in inference cost.
summary.tldr: GroupCover strengthens TEE-based model protection through improved randomization and obfuscation, with reported 19% overhead and negligible accuracy loss.

title: GroupCover: A Secure, Efficient and Scalable Inference Framework for On-device Model Protection based on TEEs

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) present a promising pathway for advancing the domain of formal theorem proving. In this paper, we aim to improve the performance of LLMs in formal theorem proving by thoroughly examining the structure and organization of demonstrative in-context examples. We introduce a subgoal-based demonstration learning framework, specifically designed to enhance the efficiency of proof search in LLMs. First, drawing upon the insights of subgoal learning from reinforcement learning and robotics, we propose the construction of distinct subgoals for each demonstration example and refine these subgoals in accordance with the pertinent theories of subgoal learning. Second, we build upon recent advances in diffusion models to predict the optimal organization, simultaneously addressing two intricate issues that persist within the domain of demonstration organization: subset selection and order determination. Our integration of subgoal-based learning has notably increased proof accuracy from 38.9% to 44.1% on the miniF2F benchmark. Furthermore, the adoption of diffusion models for demonstration organization can lead to an additional enhancement in accuracy to 45.5%, or a $5\times$ improvement in sampling efficiency compared to previously established methods.

paragraphs: This paper improves language-model theorem proving by changing how demonstration examples are structured and presented. Demonstrations provide examples within the model's context, so their usefulness depends on both their content and their organization. The researchers focus on making intermediate proof goals explicit and choosing a helpful collection and ordering of examples.

The framework constructs distinct subgoals for each demonstration and refines them using ideas from subgoal learning in reinforcement learning and robotics. It then uses diffusion models to predict an organization of demonstrations, addressing subset selection and ordering together. These are complementary interventions: one changes the structure of each example, while the other changes which examples the prover sees and in what sequence.

On miniF2F, subgoal-based demonstrations raise proof accuracy from 38.9% to 44.1%. Adding diffusion-based organization can increase accuracy to 45.5%, or provide a fivefold improvement in sampling efficiency compared with established methods. The stated alternatives show that better demonstration organization can benefit either proof success or the sampling effort required.
summary.tldr: Explicit subgoals and diffusion-based demonstration organization improve theorem-proving accuracy or sampling efficiency on miniF2F.

title: Subgoal-based Demonstration Learning for Formal Theorem Proving

abstract: As deep learning models are increasingly deployed in high-risk applications, robust defenses against adversarial attacks and reliable performance guarantees become paramount. Moreover, accuracy alone does not provide sufficient assurance or reliable uncertainty estimates for these models. This study advances adversarial training by leveraging principles from Conformal Prediction. Specifically, we develop an adversarial attack method, termed OPSA (OPtimal Size Attack), designed to reduce the efficiency of conformal prediction at any significance level by maximizing model uncertainty without requiring coverage guarantees. Correspondingly, we introduce OPSA-AT (Adversarial Training), a defense strategy that integrates OPSA within a novel conformal training paradigm. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our OPSA attack method induces greater uncertainty compared to baseline approaches for various defenses. Conversely, our OPSA-AT defensive model significantly enhances robustness not only against OPSA but also other adversarial attacks, and maintains reliable prediction. Our findings highlight the effectiveness of this integrated approach for developing trustworthy and resilient deep learning models for safety-critical domains. Our code is available at https://github.com/bjbbbb/Enhancing-Adversarial-Robustness-with-Conformal-Prediction.

paragraphs: Accuracy does not fully describe how a model behaves under adversarial attack, especially when reliable uncertainty estimates matter. This paper connects adversarial training with conformal prediction, examining both how an attacker can undermine prediction efficiency and how a defender can train against that pressure. Uncertainty becomes a central target of the analysis.

The proposed attack, OPSA, aims to maximize model uncertainty and thereby reduce conformal prediction efficiency at any significance level. Its construction does not require coverage guarantees. The corresponding defense, OPSA-AT, incorporates this attack into a new conformal training framework, making the uncertainty-focused attack part of the model's training process.

Models trained with OPSA-AT show improved robustness against OPSA and other adversarial attacks while maintaining reliable predictions in the evaluations. The findings support combining uncertainty-aware evaluation with adversarial training, extending the focus beyond whether an attacked model simply returns the correct class.
summary.tldr: OPSA attacks conformal prediction efficiency by increasing uncertainty, while OPSA-AT uses that attack to improve empirical adversarial robustness.

title: Enhancing Adversarial Robustness with Conformal Prediction: A Framework for Guaranteed Model Reliability

abstract: Next to scaling considerations, architectural design choices profoundly shape the solution space of transformers. In this work, we analyze the solutions simple transformer blocks implement when tackling the histogram task: counting items in sequences. Despite its simplicity, this task reveals a complex interplay between predictive performance, vocabulary and embedding sizes, token-mixing mechanisms, and feed-forward layer capacity. We identify two theoretical counting strategies transformers adopt, relation-based and inventory-based counting, each defining distinct learning regimes for the task. These strategies dictate how functionality is distributed between attention and feed-forward layers. We further show that adding softmax and beginning-of-sequence tokens allow for more robustness when embedding dimensions are comparatively small. Empirical introspection of trained models closely confirms both the learning regimes of the various architectures and the formation of these strategies during training. We demonstrate how a basic task that requires only aggregation and selection is significantly impacted by minor design changes.

paragraphs: Counting occurrences in a sequence seems simple, yet it exposes important choices in transformer design. This paper studies small transformer blocks on the histogram task to understand how vocabulary size, embedding size, token mixing, and feed-forward capacity shape the solutions a model can learn. The focus is on how architectural components share the work.

The authors identify two theoretical strategies, called relation-based and inventory-based counting. These define distinct learning regimes and distribute functionality differently between attention and feed-forward layers. Their analysis makes counting a way to examine how the same task can be implemented through different internal arrangements, depending on the available architecture.

The paper also finds that softmax and beginning-of-sequence tokens improve robustness when embedding dimensions are relatively small. Inspection of trained models closely supports the predicted regimes and the emergence of the two strategies during learning. The findings show that even a task built from aggregation and selection can respond strongly to small design changes. They connect observed performance to specific architectural choices and the counting strategies those choices support.
summary.tldr: Small transformers learn distinct counting strategies whose success depends on how attention, embeddings, and feed-forward capacity work together.

title: Counting in Small Transformers: The Delicate Interplay between Attention and Feed-Forward Layers

abstract: This paper focuses on the estimation of distributional treatment effects in randomized experiments that use covariate-adaptive randomization (CAR). These include designs such as Efron’s biased-coin design and stratified block randomization, where participants are first grouped into strata based on baseline covariates and assigned treatments within each stratum to ensure balance across groups. In practice, datasets often contain additional covariates beyond the strata indicators. We propose a flexible distribution regression framework that leverages off-the-shelf machine learning methods to incorporate these additional covariates, enhancing the precision of distributional treatment effect estimates. We establish the asymptotic distribution of the proposed estimator and introduce a valid inference procedure. Furthermore, we derive the semiparametric efficiency bound for distributional treatment effects under CAR and demonstrate that our regression-adjusted estimator attains this bound. Simulation studies and analyses of real-world datasets highlight the practical advantages of our method.

paragraphs: Randomized experiments often group participants by baseline characteristics and balance treatment assignment within those groups. This paper studies distributional treatment effects under such covariate-adaptive randomization. The available data may contain useful characteristics beyond those used to define the groups, raising the question of how to incorporate that information to obtain more precise estimates.

The authors propose a flexible distribution regression framework that uses standard machine learning methods to adjust for these additional covariates. They establish the estimator’s asymptotic distribution and provide a valid inference procedure. These results connect flexible prediction tools with statistical inference that accounts for the experiment’s treatment-assignment design.

The paper also derives the semiparametric efficiency bound for distributional treatment effects under this randomization setting and shows that its adjusted estimator attains that bound. This is an asymptotic efficiency result, describing the estimator’s precision in the relevant large-sample framework. Simulations and real-data analyses demonstrate practical advantages, supporting the use of additional covariates alongside the original balancing strata.
summary.tldr: Machine-learning-based regression adjustment improves distributional treatment-effect estimation and attains the asymptotic efficiency bound under covariate-adaptive randomization.

title: On Efficient Estimation of Distributional Treatment Effects under Covariate-Adaptive Randomization

abstract: Recent developments in prompt learning of large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have significantly improved performance in target-specific tasks. However, these prompting methods often struggle to tackle the target-unspecific or generalizable tasks effectively. It may be attributed to the fact that overfitting training causes the model to forget its general knowledge. The general knowledge has a strong promotion on target-unspecific tasks. To alleviate this issue, we propose a novel Features Matrix (FM) approach designed to enhance these models on target-unspecific tasks. Our method extracts and leverages general knowledge, shaping a Features Matrix (FM). Specifically, the FM captures the semantics of diverse inputs from a deep and fine perspective, preserving essential general knowledge, which mitigates the risk of overfitting. Representative evaluations demonstrate that: 1) the FM is compatible with existing frameworks as a generic and flexible module, and 2) the FM significantly showcases its effectiveness in enhancing target-unspecific tasks (base-to-novel generalization, domain generalization, and cross-dataset generalization), achieving state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Prompt learning can adapt a large vision-language model to a particular target, yet that adaptation may transfer poorly to other tasks or settings. The authors suggest that overfitting during training may cause the model to forget general knowledge. Their Features Matrix approach aims to preserve and use that knowledge when broader generalization matters.

The Features Matrix extracts semantic information from diverse inputs at a deep and fine-grained level. It is designed to retain useful general knowledge and reduce the risk of overfitting during adaptation. The authors present it as a generic module that can fit within existing frameworks, making preservation of general information part of the adaptation process.

Evaluations examine generalization from base to novel categories, across domains, and across datasets. The paper reports compatibility with existing frameworks and state-of-the-art performance on the evaluated generalization tasks. These findings support the usefulness of the Features Matrix in those settings. The explanation that forgetting causes prompting difficulties remains a proposed motivation, rather than an established universal account of why transfer fails.
summary.tldr: A Features Matrix preserves general semantic knowledge to improve vision-language model generalization beyond the targets used for adaptation.

title: Enhancing Target-unspecific Tasks through a Features Matrix

abstract: Transformer models have achieved remarkable empirical successes, largely due to their in-context learning capabilities. Inspired by this, we explore training an autoregressive transformer for in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL). In this setting, we initially train a transformer on an offline dataset consisting of trajectories collected from various RL tasks, and then fix and use this transformer to create an action policy for new RL tasks. Notably, we consider the setting where the offline dataset contains trajectories sampled from suboptimal behavioral policies. In this case, standard autoregressive training corresponds to imitation learning and results in suboptimal performance. To address this, we propose the Decision Importance Transformer (DIT) framework, which emulates the actor-critic algorithm in an in-context manner. In particular, we first train a transformer-based value function that estimates the advantage functions of the behavior policies that collected the suboptimal trajectories. Then we train a transformer-based policy via a weighted maximum likelihood estimation loss, where the weights are constructed based on the trained value function to steer the suboptimal policies to the optimal ones. We conduct extensive experiments to test the performance of DIT on both bandit and Markov Decision Process problems. Our results show that DIT achieves superior performance, particularly when the offline dataset contains suboptimal historical data.

paragraphs: The paper studies a transformer trained on recorded interactions from multiple reinforcement learning tasks and then used, with fixed parameters, to produce actions for new tasks. The challenge is that historical data may come from policies that make poor decisions. Ordinary autoregressive training then imitates those policies, carrying their shortcomings into the learned behavior.

The Decision Importance Transformer addresses this by reproducing an actor-critic approach through in-context learning. First, a transformer-based value function estimates advantages for the policies that generated the data. These estimates characterize which decisions were relatively beneficial. A second transformer learns the policy through weighted maximum likelihood, with the value estimates determining how strongly different training decisions influence learning.

The weighting is designed to steer learning from suboptimal behavior toward optimal policies. Experiments on bandit problems and Markov decision processes report superior performance, especially when historical trajectories are suboptimal. The findings support using estimated decision quality to learn more effectively from imperfect experience, while preserving the setup in which the trained transformer stays fixed on new tasks.
summary.tldr: Decision Importance Transformer uses advantage-weighted training to improve in-context reinforcement learning from suboptimal historical trajectories.

title: In-Context Reinforcement Learning From Suboptimal Historical Data

abstract: With the increasing size of frontier LLMs, post-training quantization has become the standard for memory-efficient deployment. Recent work has shown that basic rounding-based quantization schemes pose security risks, as they can be exploited to inject malicious behaviors into quantized models that remain hidden in full precision. However, existing attacks cannot be applied to more complex quantization methods, such as the GGUF family used in the popular ollama and llama.cpp frameworks. In this work, we address this gap by introducing the first attack on GGUF. Our key insight is that the quantization error – the difference between the full-precision weights and their (de-)quantized version – provides sufficient flexibility to construct malicious quantized models that appear benign in full precision. Leveraging this, we develop an attack that trains the target malicious LLM while constraining its weights based on quantization errors. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our attack on three popular LLMs across nine GGUF quantization data types on three diverse attack scenarios: insecure code generation ($\Delta$=$88.7%$), targeted content injection ($\Delta$=$85.0%$), and benign instruction refusal ($\Delta$=$30.1%$). Our attack highlights that (1) the most widely used post-training quantization method is susceptible to adversarial interferences, and (2) the complexity of quantization schemes alone is insufficient as a defense.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces the numerical precision of model weights to make large language models easier to deploy. This paper studies a security risk in which a model appears benign at full precision but exhibits malicious behavior after quantization. Earlier attacks addressed simpler rounding schemes; this work extends the threat to the more complex GGUF family.

The authors exploit quantization error, the difference between original weights and their quantized-and-restored values. Their attack trains a malicious target model while constraining its weights according to those errors. The central finding is that the discrepancy introduced by quantization provides enough flexibility for different behavior to emerge in the deployed, lower-precision model.

The attack is evaluated on three language models, nine GGUF data types, and scenarios involving insecure code generation, targeted content injection, and refusal of benign instructions. The reported deltas are 88.7%, 85.0%, and 30.1%, respectively. These experiments show susceptibility in the tested configurations and support the conclusion that quantization complexity alone is insufficient protection against this form of manipulation.
summary.tldr: The paper demonstrates attacks that hide malicious behavior at full precision and reveal it after GGUF quantization.

title: Mind the Gap: A Practical Attack on GGUF Quantization

abstract: On-device LLMs have gained increasing attention for their ability to enhance privacy and provide a personalized user experience. To facilitate private learning with scarce data, Federated Learning has become a standard approach. However, it faces challenges such as computational resource heterogeneity and data heterogeneity among end users. We propose CoMiGS ($\textbf{Co}$llaborative learning with a $\textbf{Mi}$xture of $\textbf{G}$eneralists and $\textbf{S}$pecialists), the first approach to address both challenges. A key innovation of our method is the bi-level optimization formulation of the Mixture-of-Experts learning objective, where the router is optimized using a separate validation set to ensure alignment with the target distribution. We solve our objective with alternating minimization, for which we provide a theoretical analysis. Our method shares generalist experts across users while localizing a varying number of specialist experts, thereby adapting to users’ computational resources and preserving privacy. Through extensive experiments, we show CoMiGS effectively balances general and personalized knowledge for each token generation. We demonstrate that CoMiGS remains robust against overfitting—due to the generalists’ regularizing effect—while adapting to local data through specialist expertise. We open source our codebase for collaborative LLMs.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning for on-device language models must accommodate users with different data and devices with different computational resources. CoMiGS addresses these challenges through a mixture of shared generalist experts and local specialist experts, combining broadly useful knowledge with information specific to each user.

title: On-Device Collaborative Language Modeling via a Mixture of Generalists and Specialists

abstract: Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection is essential for the trustworthiness of AI systems. Methods using prior information (i.e., subspace-based methods) have shown effective performance by extracting information geometry to detect OOD data with a more appropriate distance metric. However, these methods fail to address the geometry distorted by ill-distributed samples, due to the limitation of statically extracting information geometry from the training distribution. In this paper, we argue that the influence of ill-distributed samples can be corrected by dynamically adjusting the prior geometry in response to new data. Based on this insight, we propose a novel approach that dynamically updates the prior covariance matrix using real-time input features, refining its information. Specifically, we reduce the covariance along the direction of real-time input features and constrain adjustments to the residual space, thus preserving essential data characteristics and avoiding effects on unintended directions in the principal space. We evaluate our method on two pre-trained models for the CIFAR dataset and five pre-trained models for ImageNet-1k, including the self-supervised DINO model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances OOD detection across various models. The code is released at https://github.com/workerbcd/ooddcc.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the data a model is expected to handle. Some methods use the geometry of training features to define a suitable distance measure. This paper argues that an uneven distribution of samples can distort that geometry, and that a fixed estimate cannot correct the distortion when new inputs arrive.

The proposed method adjusts the prior covariance matrix using the features of the current input. It reduces covariance along the input-feature direction while restricting the adjustment to the residual space. This restriction is intended to retain essential data characteristics and prevent unintended changes to directions in the principal space.

The method is evaluated with two pretrained models for CIFAR and five for ImageNet-1k, including the self-supervised DINO model. The authors report significant improvements in out-of-distribution detection across the evaluated models. The contribution is an input-responsive correction to the geometry used for detection, showing that information extracted from training data can be refined dynamically when assessing a new sample.
summary.tldr: Dynamic covariance calibration uses each incoming input to refine feature geometry and improve out-of-distribution detection.

title: Improving Out-of-Distribution Detection via Dynamic Covariance Calibration

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) activates only a subset of experts during inference, allowing the model to maintain low inference FLOPs and latency even as the parameter count scales up. However, since MoE dynamically selects the experts, all the experts need to be loaded into VRAM. Their large parameter size still limits deployment, and offloading, which load experts into VRAM only when needed, significantly increase inference latency. To address this, we propose Mixture of Lookup Experts (MoLE), a new MoE architecture that is efficient in both communication and VRAM usage. In MoLE, the experts are Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) during training, taking the output of the embedding layer as input. Before inference, these experts can be re-parameterized as lookup tables (LUTs) that retrieves expert outputs based on input ids, and offloaded to storage devices. Therefore, we do not need to perform expert computations during inference. Instead, we directly retrieve the expert’s computation results based on input ids and load them into VRAM, and thus the resulting communication overhead is negligible. Experiments show that, with the same FLOPs and VRAM usage, MoLE achieves inference speeds comparable to dense models and significantly faster than MoE with experts offloading, while maintaining performance on par with MoE. Code: https://github.com/JieShibo/MoLE.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts models activate only some experts for each input, reducing computation while retaining many parameters. However, keeping all experts in GPU memory is costly, and loading them from elsewhere on demand adds latency. Mixture of Lookup Experts, or MoLE, changes the expert architecture so inference can retrieve previously computed outputs instead of loading and executing whole experts.

During training, MoLE’s experts are feed-forward networks whose inputs come from the embedding layer. Before inference, these networks can be re-parameterized as lookup tables indexed by input IDs and stored off the GPU. Inference retrieves the corresponding expert results and transfers them into GPU memory, eliminating expert computation and making the reported communication overhead negligible.

At the same FLOPs and GPU-memory usage, experiments show inference speeds comparable to dense models and substantially faster than expert-offloaded MoE models, while maintaining performance on par with MoE. The architectural choice is central to that result: expert outputs become retrievable by input ID, allowing storage to hold results that inference would otherwise need to compute.
summary.tldr: MoLE converts trained experts into lookup tables, enabling fast retrieval of expert outputs with low GPU-memory and communication costs.

title: Mixture of Lookup Experts

abstract: A major challenge in estimating treatment effects in observational studies is the reliance on untestable conditions such as the assumption of no unmeasured confounding. In this work, we propose an algorithm that can falsify the assumption of no unmeasured confounding in a setting with observational data from multiple heterogeneous sources, which we refer to as environments. Our proposed falsification strategy leverages a key observation that unmeasured confounding can cause observed causal mechanisms to appear dependent. Building on this observation, we develop a novel two-stage procedure that detects these dependencies with high statistical power while controlling false positives. The algorithm does not require access to randomized data and, in contrast to other falsification approaches, functions even under transportability violations when the environment has a direct effect on the outcome of interest. To showcase the practical relevance of our approach, we show that our method is able to efficiently detect confounding on both simulated and semi-synthetic data.

paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects from observational data often relies on assuming that no relevant confounder went unmeasured. This paper develops a way to challenge that assumption when observations come from multiple heterogeneous environments. Its aim is falsification: detecting evidence against the assumption, rather than establishing that hidden confounding is absent.

The method builds on the observation that unmeasured confounding can make observed causal mechanisms appear dependent. The authors turn this into a two-stage procedure designed to detect such dependencies with high statistical power while controlling false positives. The approach uses differences across environments and does not require randomized experimental data.

A notable feature is that the procedure can still operate when environments directly affect the outcome, a violation of transportability that obstructs some other falsification approaches. Evaluations on simulated and semi-synthetic data demonstrate efficient confounding detection. The contribution is a statistical check on a consequential causal assumption in a multi-environment setting, including cases where outcome behavior cannot simply be treated as unchanged across sources.
summary.tldr: A two-stage test uses dependencies across heterogeneous environments to detect evidence of hidden confounding without randomized data.

title: Falsification of Unconfoundedness by Testing Independence of Causal Mechanisms

abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) has gained considerable attention due to its capacity to accommodate new classes during learning. Replay-based methods demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in CIL but suffer from high memory consumption to save a set of old exemplars for revisiting. To address this challenge, many memory-efficient replay methods have been developed by exploiting image compression techniques. However, the gains are often bittersweet when pixel-level compression methods are used. Here, we present a simple yet efficient approach that employs tensor decomposition to address these limitations. This method fully exploits the low intrinsic dimensionality and pixel correlation of images to achieve high compression efficiency while preserving sufficient discriminative information, significantly enhancing performance. We also introduce a hybrid exemplar selection strategy to improve the representativeness and diversity of stored exemplars. Extensive experiments across datasets with varying resolutions consistently demonstrate that our approach substantially boosts the performance of baseline methods, showcasing strong generalization and robustness.

paragraphs: Class-incremental learning adds new classes over time while trying to retain knowledge of earlier ones. Replay methods support this by storing old examples and revisiting them, but those examples consume memory. Compressing the stored images can help, although the paper argues that existing pixel-level compression approaches offer an imperfect trade-off.

The proposed method uses tensor decomposition to exploit correlations among image pixels and the images' low intrinsic dimensionality. This produces compact representations while preserving enough discriminative information to support learning. The authors also introduce a hybrid exemplar-selection strategy intended to improve both how representative the stored examples are and how much diversity they cover.

Experiments across datasets with different image resolutions report substantial improvements to baseline methods, along with strong generalization and robustness. The approach combines two decisions that jointly determine the value of a replay memory: which examples to retain and how to represent them compactly. Its reported benefit comes from preserving useful learning information within compressed examples while improving the composition of the stored collection.
summary.tldr: Tensor decomposition and hybrid exemplar selection make replay memory more efficient for learning new classes while retaining earlier knowledge.

title: Tensor Decomposition Based Memory-Efficient Incremental Learning

abstract: Recent advancements in data-driven weather forecasting models have delivered deterministic models that outperform the leading operational forecast systems based on traditional, physics-based models. However, these data-driven models are typically trained with a mean squared error loss function, which causes smoothing of fine scales through a “double penalty” effect. We develop a simple, parameter-free modification to this loss function that avoids this problem by separating the loss attributable to decorrelation from the loss attributable to spectral amplitude errors. Fine-tuning the GraphCast model with this new loss function results in sharp deterministic weather forecasts, an increase of the model’s effective resolution from 1,250km to 160km, improvements to ensemble spread, and improvements to predictions of tropical cyclone strength and surface wind extremes.

paragraphs: Data-driven weather models can perform strongly overall while producing forecasts that smooth away fine-scale structure. This paper links that smoothing to the mean squared error objective commonly used in training. Its double-penalty effect makes the loss function itself an obstacle to preserving detailed weather patterns, even when the forecasting model is otherwise capable.

The authors develop a simple modification that separates errors caused by decorrelation from errors in spectral amplitude. This distinguishes two sources of mismatch that the usual objective combines. The proposed loss introduces no additional parameters, giving the authors a direct way to change the training signal without adding a new set of loss parameters to tune.

Fine-tuning GraphCast with this objective produces sharper deterministic forecasts and increases its effective resolution from 1,250 kilometers to 160 kilometers. The reported benefits also include improved ensemble spread and better predictions of tropical cyclone strength and extreme surface winds. These results show that changing the objective can materially improve the detail and weather phenomena represented in this forecasting model.
summary.tldr: A parameter-free loss modification gives GraphCast sharper forecasts and improves its effective resolution and predictions of weather extremes.

title: Fixing the Double Penalty in Data-Driven Weather Forecasting Through a Modified Spherical Harmonic Loss Function

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) embed sensitive, human-generated data, prompting the need for unlearning methods. Although certified unlearning offers strong privacy guarantees, its restrictive assumptions make it unsuitable for LLMs, giving rise to various heuristic approaches typically assessed through empirical evaluations. These standard evaluations randomly select data for removal, apply unlearning techniques, and use membership inference attacks (MIAs) to compare unlearned models against models retrained without the removed data. However, to ensure robust privacy protections for every data point, it is essential to account for scenarios in which certain data subsets face elevated risks. Prior research suggests that outliers, particularly including data tied to minority groups, often exhibit higher memorization propensity which indicates they may be more difficult to unlearn. Building on these insights, we introduce a complementary, minority-aware evaluation framework to highlight blind spots in existing frameworks. We substantiate our findings with carefully designed experiments, using canaries with personally identifiable information (PII) to represent these minority subsets and demonstrate that they suffer at least 20% higher privacy leakage across various unlearning methods, MIAs, datasets, and LLM scales. Our proposed minority-aware evaluation framework marks an essential step toward more equitable and comprehensive assessments of LLM unlearning efficacy.

paragraphs: Language-model unlearning aims to remove the influence of sensitive training data. Standard evaluations often choose removal examples randomly and use membership inference attacks to compare the unlearned model with one retrained without those examples. This paper argues that such evaluations can miss subsets facing unusually high privacy risk.

The motivation is that outlying examples, including data associated with minority groups, may be memorized more strongly and therefore be harder to unlearn. The authors introduce a complementary evaluation framework that explicitly examines minority subsets. Their experiments use canaries containing personally identifiable information to represent those subsets and probe the privacy left after unlearning.

Across the tested unlearning methods, membership attacks, datasets, and language-model scales, these minority-representing canaries show at least 20% higher privacy leakage. The result identifies a blind spot in randomly sampled evaluations: performance averaged over removal data can obscure elevated leakage for particular subsets. The proposed framework broadens how unlearning is assessed, emphasizing that evidence of privacy protection should account for differences in risk across the data being removed.
summary.tldr: Minority-aware unlearning evaluations reveal at least 20% higher privacy leakage for minority-representing canaries in the reported experiments.

title: Underestimated Privacy Risks for Minority Populations in Large Language Model Unlearning

abstract: In real-world crowdsourcing scenarios, most workers often annotate a few instances only, which results in a significantly sparse crowdsourced label matrix and subsequently harms the performance of label integration algorithms. Recent work called worker similarity-based label completion (WSLC) has been proven to be an effective algorithm to addressing this issue. However, WSLC considers solely the correlation of the labels annotated by different workers on per individual instance while totally ignoring the correlation of the labels annotated by different workers among similar instances. To fill this gap, we propose a novel label distribution propagation-based label completion (LDPLC) algorithm. At first, we use worker similarity weighted majority voting to initialize a label distribution for each missing label. Then, we design a label distribution propagation algorithm to enable each missing label of each instance to iteratively absorb its neighbors’ label distributions. Finally, we complete each missing label based on its converged label distribution. Experimental results on both real-world and simulated crowdsourced datasets show that LDPLC significantly outperforms WSLC in enhancing the performance of label integration algorithms. Our codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/jiangliangxiao/LDPLC.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced annotation often produces a sparse matrix because each worker labels only a few examples. Missing entries can weaken algorithms that combine worker responses into final labels. Earlier worker-similarity completion considers relationships among workers' labels on the same example, but overlooks information linking labels across similar examples.

LDPLC fills missing entries through label distributions. It first uses majority voting weighted by worker similarity to initialize a distribution for each missing label. It then repeatedly propagates neighboring label distributions, allowing each missing entry to absorb information associated with nearby examples. Once the distributions converge, the method uses them to assign the missing labels.

This process combines two sources of evidence: similarities between workers and relationships among examples. Keeping a distribution during propagation allows multiple label possibilities to participate before completion produces a label. Experiments on real and simulated crowdsourced datasets show that LDPLC significantly outperforms the earlier worker-similarity method in improving label integration. The reported benefit concerns the quality of the downstream integration process, which is the reason for completing the sparse annotations.
summary.tldr: LDPLC completes missing crowdsourced labels by combining worker similarity with label-distribution propagation across neighboring examples.

title: Label Distribution Propagation-based Label Completion for Crowdsourcing

abstract: The advancements in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have enabled various multimodal tasks to be addressed under a zero-shot paradigm. This paradigm sidesteps the cost of model fine-tuning, emerging as a dominant trend in practical application. Nevertheless, Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA), a pivotal challenge in the quest for general artificial intelligence, fails to accommodate this convenience. The zero-shot paradigm exhibits undesirable performance on MSA, casting doubt on whether MLLMs can perceive sentiments as competent as supervised models. By extending the zero-shot paradigm to In-Context Learning (ICL) and conducting an in-depth study on configuring demonstrations, we validate that MLLMs indeed possess such capability. Specifically, three key factors that cover demonstrations’ retrieval, presentation, and distribution are comprehensively investigated and optimized. A sentimental predictive bias inherent in MLLMs is also discovered and later effectively counteracted. By complementing each other, the devised strategies for three factors result in average accuracy improvements of 15.9% on six MSA datasets against the zero-shot paradigm and 11.2% against the random ICL baseline.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can handle many tasks without task-specific training, but their zero-shot sentiment analysis performs poorly. This raises a practical question: do the models lack sentiment perception, or does the way they are asked fail to bring it out? The paper investigates this through demonstrations supplied in the input.

The study examines three aspects of in-context learning: how demonstrations are retrieved, how they are presented, and how they are distributed. It optimizes these factors and also identifies an inherent bias in the models’ sentiment predictions. The proposed strategies counteract that bias and complement one another, showing that the composition of the example context matters beyond simply including examples.

Across six multimodal sentiment datasets, the combined strategies deliver reported average accuracy improvements of 15.9% over zero-shot use and 11.2% over random demonstration selection. These findings support the authors’ conclusion that the tested models possess sentiment perception capabilities that weak prompting can obscure. They also make demonstration configuration a substantive part of the method, rather than a minor presentation choice.
summary.tldr: Carefully configuring in-context examples substantially improves multimodal sentiment analysis over zero-shot use and random demonstrations.

title: An Empirical Study on Configuring In-Context Learning Demonstrations for Unleashing MLLMs’ Sentimental Perception Capability

abstract: Domain Incremental Learning (DIL) aims to learn from non-stationary data streams across domains while retaining and utilizing past knowledge. Although prompt-based methods effectively store multi-domain knowledge in prompt parameters and obtain advanced performance through cross-domain prompt fusion, we reveal an intrinsic limitation: component-wise misalignment between domain-specific prompts leads to conflicting knowledge integration and degraded predictions. This arises from the random positioning of knowledge components within prompts, where irrelevant component fusion introduces interference. To address this, we propose Componential Prompt-Knowledge Alignment (KA-Prompt), a novel prompt-based DIL method that introduces component-aware prompt-knowledge alignment during training, significantly improving both the learning and inference capacity of the model. KA-Prompt operates in two phases: (1) Initial Componential Structure Configuring, where a set of old prompts containing knowledge relevant to the new domain are mined via greedy search, which is then exploited to initialize new prompts to achieve reusable knowledge transfer and establish intrinsic alignment between new and old prompts. (2) Online Alignment Preservation, which dynamically identifies the target old prompts and applies adaptive componential consistency constraints as new prompts evolve. Extensive experiments on DIL benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our KA-Prompt. Our source code is available at https://github.com/zhoujiahuan1991/ICML2025-KA-Prompt.

paragraphs: Domain incremental learning requires a model to learn from changing domains while retaining useful earlier knowledge. Prompt-based methods store domain knowledge in learned prompts and combine those prompts across domains. The paper identifies a problem inside this combination: corresponding prompt components can hold unrelated knowledge, so mixing them introduces interference and harms predictions.

KA-Prompt addresses this problem through two stages. First, a greedy search finds older prompts containing knowledge relevant to the incoming domain. These prompts initialize the new prompts, transferring useful information while establishing component alignment. Second, as training changes the new prompts, the method dynamically identifies relevant old prompts and applies adaptive consistency constraints to preserve that alignment.

The contribution is to treat the internal arrangement of prompt knowledge as something that needs coordination throughout learning. Relevant knowledge must be positioned compatibly for later fusion to work well. Experiments on domain incremental learning benchmarks support the method's effectiveness, with the abstract reporting improvements in both learning and inference capacity.
summary.tldr: KA-Prompt aligns knowledge components across domain-specific prompts so that combining them causes less interference.

title: Componential Prompt-Knowledge Alignment for Domain Incremental Learning

abstract: Most existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) compression schemes focus on producing compact 3DGS representation via implicit data embedding. They have long encoding and decoding times and highly customized data format, making it difficult for widespread deployment. This paper presents a new 3DGS compression framework called HybridGS, which takes advantage of both compact generation and standardized point cloud data encoding. HybridGS first generates compact and explicit 3DGS data. A dual-channel sparse representation is introduced to supervise the primitive position and feature bit depth. It then utilizes a canonical point cloud encoder to carry out further data compression and form standard output bitstreams. A simple and effective rate control scheme is proposed to pivot the interpretable data compression scheme. HybridGS does not include any modules aimed at improving 3DGS quality during generation. But experiment results show that it still provides comparable reconstruction performance against state-of-the-art methods, with evidently faster encoding and decoding speed. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Qi-Yangsjtu/HybridGS .

But experiment results show that it still provides comparable reconstruction performance against state-of-the-art methods, with evidently faster encoding and decoding speed. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Qi-Yangsjtu/HybridGS .

paragraphs: Compressing a 3D Gaussian Splatting representation must balance data size, reconstruction quality, and the time required to encode and decode it. The paper identifies deployment difficulties in approaches that embed data implicitly: they can be slow and rely on highly customized formats. HybridGS combines compact explicit representations with standardized point cloud encoding.

The framework first generates compact 3DGS data. A dual-channel sparse representation supervises the positions of the primitives and the bit depth used for their features. A conventional point cloud encoder then compresses this explicit data into standard output bitstreams. A rate control scheme provides a way to manage compression within this interpretable representation.

HybridGS includes no generation modules specifically intended to improve 3DGS quality. Even so, experiments show reconstruction performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, alongside clearly faster encoding and decoding. The result supports the practical value of coordinating compact representation generation with an established data encoder. Here, maintaining reconstruction quality while simplifying and accelerating data handling is the central reported benefit.
summary.tldr: HybridGS combines compact explicit Gaussian representations with standard point cloud encoding for faster compression and decompression at comparable reconstruction quality.

title: HybridGS: High-Efficiency Gaussian Splatting Data Compression using Dual-Channel Sparse Representation and Point Cloud Encoder

abstract: When training deep neural networks with gradient descent, sharpness often increases—a phenomenon known as progressive sharpening—before saturating at the edge of stability. Although commonly observed in practice, the underlying mechanisms behind progressive sharpening remain poorly understood. In this work, we study this phenomenon using a minimalist model: a deep linear network with a single neuron per layer. We show that this simple model effectively captures the sharpness dynamics observed in recent empirical studies, offering a simple testbed to better understand neural network training. Moreover, we theoretically analyze how dataset properties, network depth, stochasticity of optimizers, and step size affect the degree of progressive sharpening in the minimalist model. We then empirically demonstrate how these theoretical insights extend to practical scenarios. This study offers a deeper understanding of sharpness dynamics in neural network training, highlighting the interplay between depth, training data, and optimizers.

paragraphs: During neural-network training, the loss landscape around the current parameters often becomes sharper before leveling off near the edge of stability. This progressive sharpening is widely observed, yet its mechanisms remain difficult to explain. The paper studies it using a deliberately minimal network with multiple linear layers and just one neuron in each layer.

Despite its simplicity, this model reproduces sharpness dynamics seen in recent empirical studies. That makes it a manageable setting for theoretical analysis. The authors examine how properties of the dataset, network depth, optimizer randomness, and step size influence the extent of progressive sharpening within this minimal model.

They then present empirical evidence that insights from the analysis extend to practical training scenarios. The theoretical results concern the simplified model, while the broader relevance is supported experimentally. The contribution is a tractable testbed for understanding how data, architecture, and optimization interact during training, helping explain a pattern that would otherwise be difficult to isolate in a full-scale neural network.
summary.tldr: A minimal deep linear network explains how data, depth, optimizer randomness, and step size shape progressive sharpening during training.

title: Understanding Sharpness Dynamics in NN Training with a Minimalist Example: The Effects of Dataset Difficulty, Depth, Stochasticity, and More

abstract: Scaling test-time computation, or affording a generator large language model (LLM) extra compute during inference, typically employs the help of external non-generative evaluators (i.e., reward models). Concurrently, LLM-judges, models trained to generate evaluations and critiques (explanations) in natural language, are becoming increasingly popular in automatic evaluation. Despite judge empirical successes, their effectiveness as evaluators in test-time scaling settings is largely unknown. In this paper, we introduce the Judge Evaluation for Test-Time Scaling (JETTS) benchmark, which evaluates judge performance in three domains (math reasoning, code generation, and instruction following) under three task settings: response reranking, step-level beam search, and critique-based response refinement. We evaluate 10 different judge models (7B-70B parameters) for 8 different base generator models (6.7B-72B parameters). Our benchmark shows that while judges are competitive with outcome reward models in reranking, they are consistently worse than process reward models in beam search procedures. Furthermore, though unique to LLM-judges, their natural language critiques are currently ineffective in guiding the generator towards better responses.

paragraphs: Giving a language model more computation while answering often requires another model to evaluate its candidate responses or reasoning steps. JETTS asks whether language models that generate judgments and critiques are effective evaluators for this purpose. Their success in automatic evaluation does not by itself establish that they help generators improve during inference.

The benchmark covers mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following. It tests three uses of judges: reranking complete responses, selecting intermediate steps through beam search, and guiding revisions with critiques. The evaluation includes 10 judge models with 7–70 billion parameters and eight generator models with 6.7–72 billion parameters.

The results differ across these settings. Judges are competitive with outcome reward models when reranking responses, but consistently trail process reward models in step-level beam search. Their natural-language critiques are also ineffective at improving generator responses in the reported evaluation. The findings show why evaluator selection should account for its role in the inference procedure, rather than treating judging ability as a single transferable capability.
summary.tldr: JETTS finds that LLM judges can rerank responses competitively but struggle with step-level search and critique-guided improvement.

title: Evaluating Judges as Evaluators: The JETTS Benchmark of LLM-as-Judges as Test-Time Scaling Evaluators

abstract: We study the transit stop placement (TrSP) problem in general metric spaces, where agents travel between source–destination pairs and may either walk directly or utilize a shuttle service via selected transit stops. We investigate fairness in TrSP through the lens of justified representation (JR) and the core, and uncover a structural correspondence with fair clustering. Specifically, we show that a constant-factor approximation to proportional fairness in clustering can be used to guarantee a constant-factor bi-parameterized approximation to core. We establish a lower bound of $1.366$ on the approximability of JR, and moreover show that no clustering algorithm can approximate JR within a factor better than $3$. Going beyond clustering, we propose the Expanding Cost Algorithm, which achieves a tight $2.414$-approximation for JR, but does not give any bounded core guarantee. In light of this, we introduce a parameterized algorithm that interpolates between these approaches, and enables a tunable trade-off between JR and core. Finally, we complement our results with an experimental analysis using small-market public carpooling data.

paragraphs: The paper studies where to place transit stops when travelers can either walk directly or use a shuttle between selected stops. It considers general metric spaces and evaluates fairness through two formal notions: justified representation, or JR, and the core. The central question is how stop placement can satisfy these different fairness requirements.

The authors establish a connection to fair clustering. A constant-factor approximation to proportional fairness in clustering yields a constant-factor, bi-parameterized approximation to the core. However, clustering also has limits: no clustering algorithm can approximate JR by a factor better than 3. A separate lower bound of 1.366 applies to the approximability of JR.

The contribution is a set of explicit fairness trade-offs rather than one placement rule that optimizes both criteria.
summary.tldr: The paper develops transit-stop algorithms with explicit trade-offs between justified representation and core fairness guarantees.

title: Fair Transit Stop Placement: A Clustering Perspective and Beyond

abstract: Traditional text-based person retrieval approaches typically rely on single-shot textual queries, which are generally incomplete or vague in real-world scenarios. Recently, chat-based person retrieval methods enable iterative query refinement via question-answering interactions between the system and users. However, these methods fall short of direct user interaction with retrieved candidates during conversation, making it challenging to effectively refine the retrieval results. To address these limitations, we propose multimodal interactive person retrieval (MInterPR), a new retrieval paradigm that allows users to iteratively refine retrieved candidates by providing feedback on visual differences from the target person. To support this task, we establish MInterPEDES, a multimodal conversational dataset constructed by augmenting existing question-answering dialogues with synthesized visual feedbacks. Furthermore, to tackle the challenge of accurate and efficient semantics understanding in multimodal dialogues, we propose a multimodal conversational memory-enhanced framework MNEMO, which incorporates an atomic turn encoding (ATE) module to model each dialogue turn independently, and a dialogue memory aggregation (DMA) module to capture the fine-grained information and cross-turn dependencies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MNEMO achieves substantial improvements in both retrieval accuracy and generalization ability, highlighting its promising potential in real-world scenarios. The code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/Flame-Chasers/MNEMO.

paragraphs: Finding a person from a written description is difficult when the initial query is vague or incomplete. Conversational search can refine the description through questions, but existing approaches offer limited interaction with the actual retrieved candidates. This paper introduces a task in which users refine results by commenting on visual differences between candidates and the target person.

To support this interaction, the authors build MInterPEDES by adding synthesized visual feedback to existing question-and-answer dialogues. They also propose MNEMO, a framework for understanding the resulting multimodal conversations. Its atomic turn encoding module represents each dialogue turn independently, while a dialogue memory aggregation module combines fine-grained details and dependencies across turns.

This division lets the framework represent individual pieces of feedback while retaining how the conversation develops over time. Experiments show substantial improvements in retrieval accuracy and generalization. The findings support the usefulness of combining candidate-specific visual feedback with conversational memory, and suggest potential for practical person retrieval when a user’s first description is insufficient.
summary.tldr: MNEMO improves interactive person retrieval by combining feedback on candidate images with memory across conversation turns.

title: Interactive Person Retrieval via Multi-Turn Multimodal Conversation

abstract: LLMs excel at reasoning, but validating their steps remains challenging. Formal verification offers a solution through mechanically checkable proofs. Interactive theorem provers (ITPs) dominate mathematical reasoning but require detailed low-level proof steps, while auto-active verifiers offer automation but focus on software verification. Recent work has begun bridging this divide by evaluating LLMs for software verification in ITPs, but the complementary direction—LLMs for mathematical theorem proving in auto-active verifiers—remains unexplored. We present miniF2F-Dafny, the first translation of the widely-used mathematical benchmark miniF2F to an auto-active verifier: Dafny. We find that Dafny’s automation alone solves 39-44% of problems with empty proofs, whereas many require substantial proof guidance in ITPs. We evaluate 8 off-the-shelf LLMs on proof generation, with the best model (Claude Opus 4.6) achieving 62.7% cumulative pass@4 on the full test set, improving over the 38.9% empty-proof baseline by 23.8 percentage points. These results show that auto-active verification offers a complementary empirical setting for AI-assisted mathematical reasoning, where LLMs provide high-level guidance while SMT automation handles low-level details. Our benchmark and evaluation infrastructure are publicly available on GitHub.

paragraphs: A language model’s mathematical argument becomes more trustworthy when a formal verifier can check it. Interactive theorem provers often require detailed proof steps, whereas auto-active verifiers automate more low-level reasoning but have primarily been used for software. This paper brings mathematical theorem proving into the latter setting by translating the miniF2F benchmark into Dafny.

The resulting miniF2F-Dafny benchmark separates what the verifier can establish automatically from what language-model guidance contributes. Dafny alone solves 39–44% of problems with empty proofs. summary.tldr: miniF2F-Dafny shows that automated verification can solve many benchmark theorems unaided, with LLM guidance improving the best reported result to 62.7% pass@4.

title: miniF2F-Dafny: LLM-Guided Mathematical Theorem Proving via Auto-Active Verification

abstract: Flow-matching has emerged as a leading framework for high-fidelity text-to-image generation. However, its alignment with human preferences through RL is often hindered by substantial computational overhead. In this paper, we introduce Flow-TTRL, the first test-time reinforcement learning framework that achieves alignment on the fly. Our approach reinterprets intermediate latent representations as an implicit policy and utilizes SDE-based rollouts to explore high-reward trajectories within the learned vector field. Specifically, we propose a two-stage optimization strategy: Proximal Reward Difference Prediction (PRDP) ensures structural stability in high-noise regimes through pairwise reward regression, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) refines fine-grained aesthetic details by maximizing relative advantages within sampled candidate groups. Experimental results show that Flow-TTRL significantly boosts aesthetic quality, text-image alignment, and human preference across diverse backbones. On the GenEval benchmark, Flow-TTRL elevates the accuracy of SD 3.5-Medium from 63% to 87% and Flux.1 Dev from 66% to 83%. Furthermore, our framework achieves an average gain of 15% to 20% across T2I-CompBench metrics, delivering performance comparable to state-of-the-art RL-based fine-tuning methods without the need for additional fine-tuning. Our code is available at https://github.com/TheShy-Dream/Flow-TTRL.

Conventional reinforcement-learning alignment for flow-matching models can require substantial computation. This framework instead treats intermediate latent representations as an implicit policy and explores candidate trajectories through stochastic differential equation rollouts within the learned vector field.

The optimization has two stages with different roles. Proximal Reward Difference Prediction uses pairwise reward regression to maintain structural stability when noise is high. The findings show that preference-guided optimization at generation time can deliver substantial benefits.
summary.tldr: Flow-TTRL improves flow-matching image generation through reinforcement learning on intermediate latents at test time, without additional fine-tuning.

title: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning for Flow Matching

abstract: An artificial intelligence must have a model of its environment that is causal, supporting reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals, and also combinatorial, supporting generalization to unseen combinations of objects. In this work, we formally study when and how such a model can be learned. We develop relational structural causal models, extending structural causal models (Pearl 2009) to settings where objects and their relations vary. First, we show how answers to not only causal but also observational queries about unseen combinations of objects can not be identified without further assumptions. To enable such identification—including in the presence of unobserved confounding—we define relational causal graphs and derive symbolic identification criteria. Finally, we propose relational neural causal models, a provably correct approach that outperforms non-relational baselines on simulated traffic scenes with varying cars, signals, and pedestrians.

paragraphs: Reasoning about an environment can require both causal understanding and the ability to handle unfamiliar combinations of objects. This paper develops relational structural causal models for settings where the objects and relationships themselves vary. The framework extends causal modeling to support questions about interventions and counterfactuals in these changing configurations.

The authors first establish an identification obstacle: without additional assumptions, even observational queries about unseen object combinations cannot necessarily be determined, and causal queries face the same problem. They introduce relational causal graphs and symbolic identification criteria to specify when such questions can be answered, including settings with unobserved confounding.

The paper then proposes relational neural causal models as a provably correct approach within the developed framework. On simulated traffic scenes with varying cars, signals, and pedestrians, these models outperform non-relational baselines. The theoretical and empirical contributions address complementary parts of the problem: identifying when the evidence supports an answer and constructing a model that can exploit relational structure to answer across changing object combinations.
summary.tldr: Relational causal models establish conditions for answering queries about unseen object combinations and outperform non-relational baselines in simulated traffic scenes.

title: Relational Structural Causal Models

abstract: Pearl’s Causal Hierarchy (PCH) is a central framework for reasoning about probabilistic, interventional, and counterfactual statements, yet the satisfiability problem for PCH formulas is computationally intractable in almost all classical settings. We revisit this challenge through the lens of parameterized complexity and identify the first gateways to tractability. Our results include fixed-parameter and XP-algorithms for satisfiability in key probabilistic and counterfactual fragments, using parameters such as primal treewidth and the number of variables, together with matching hardness results that map the limits of tractability. Technically, we depart from the dynamic programming paradigm typically employed for treewidth-based algorithms and instead exploit structural characterizations of well-formed causal models, providing a new algorithmic toolkit for causal reasoning.

Our results include fixed-parameter and XP-algorithms for satisfiability in key probabilistic and counterfactual fragments, using parameters such as primal treewidth and the number of variables, together with matching hardness results that map the limits of tractability. Technically, we depart from the dynamic programming paradigm typically employed for treewidth-based algorithms and instead exploit structural characterizations of well-formed causal models, providing a new algorithmic toolkit for causal reasoning.

paragraphs: Pearl’s Causal Hierarchy distinguishes statements about observations, interventions, and counterfactuals. Satisfiability asks whether a collection of such statements can hold together in a causal model. This is computationally intractable in almost all classical settings considered by the paper, motivating a closer look at which structural features make particular cases manageable.

The authors use parameterized complexity to separate overall problem size from parameters such as the number of variables and primal treewidth, a measure of structural interconnectedness. They obtain fixed-parameter and XP algorithms for selected probabilistic and counterfactual fragments. These are distinct forms of parameter-dependent tractability, rather than a claim that general causal satisfiability has become easy.

Matching hardness results delineate where those algorithmic improvements stop applying. Technically, the methods exploit structural descriptions of well-formed causal models instead of the dynamic programming commonly used for treewidth-based algorithms. The contribution is both a map of tractable cases and a different algorithmic toolkit for checking whether causal statements are mutually compatible.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies parameter-dependent tractable cases for causal satisfiability and proves hardness results marking their limits.

title: Gateways to Tractability for Satisfiability in Pearl’s Causal Hierarchy

abstract: Standard machine learning pipelines often admit many near-optimal models. These "Rashomon sets" pose a range of challenges and opportunities for uncertainty-aware, robust decision making. They allow users to incorporate domain knowledge and preferences that would otherwise be difficult to specify directly in an objective, and they quantify diversity among valid models for a given training dataset and objective function. However, computation of Rashomon sets, even for simple, interpretable model classes such as sparse decision trees, continues to require immense memory and runtime resources. We present PRAXIS, an algorithm to approximate this Rashomon set with orders of magnitude improvement in runtime and memory usage. We validate that PRAXIS regularly recovers almost all of the full Rashomon set. PRAXIS allows researchers and practitioners to scalably model the Rashomon set for real-world datasets.

paragraphs: A training dataset and objective can support many models with nearly equally good performance. This collection is called a Rashomon set. Examining it can reveal diversity among acceptable models and let users choose according to domain knowledge or preferences that are difficult to express directly in the training objective.

Computing these collections is expensive even for sparse decision trees, an interpretable model class. PRAXIS is an algorithm designed to approximate the decision-tree Rashomon set while sharply reducing memory use and runtime. Its purpose is to make exploring multiple valid models computationally practical, so that model choice can consider more than the score of a single fitted tree.

The authors report orders-of-magnitude resource improvements and find that PRAXIS regularly recovers almost all of the full set in their validation. That is an empirical recovery result for an approximation method. It supports broader use of Rashomon-set analysis on real-world datasets, where the cost of constructing the collection has otherwise constrained its usefulness.
summary.tldr: PRAXIS efficiently approximates collections of near-optimal decision trees, regularly recovering almost all of the full set in validation.

title: From Rashomon Theory to PRAXIS: Efficient Decision Tree Rashomon Sets

abstract: Beyond conditional average treatment effects, treatments may impact the entire outcome distribution in covariate-dependent ways, for example, by altering the variance or tail risks for specific subpopulations. We propose a novel estimand to capture such conditional distributional treatment effects, and develop a doubly robust estimator that is minimax optimal in the local asymptotic sense. Using this, we develop a test for the global homogeneity of conditional potential outcome distributions that accommodates discrepancies beyond the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), has provably valid type 1 error, and is consistent against fixed alternatives—the first test, to our knowledge, with such guarantees in this setting. We then provide a test that aggregates evidence across a grid of kernel-bandwidth choices. Furthermore, we derive exact closed-form expressions for two natural discrepancies (including the MMD), and provide a computationally efficient, permutation-free algorithm for our test.
