paragraphs: A treatment can change more than an average outcome. Its effects on variability or extreme outcomes may also differ between subpopulations. This paper introduces a statistical target for describing those conditional distributional effects, allowing treatment comparisons to account for changes across an outcome distribution rather than focusing only on its mean.

The authors develop a doubly robust estimator and establish minimax optimality in a local asymptotic sense. They then use it to construct a global test of homogeneity for conditional potential outcome distributions. The test accommodates distributional discrepancies beyond maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD. Its theoretical guarantees include valid type 1 error control and consistency against fixed alternatives, addressing both false positives and eventual detection of persistent differences.

The paper also tackles practical choices and computation. One test combines evidence across a grid of kernel bandwidths, rather than depending on a single choice. Exact closed-form expressions are derived for two discrepancies, including MMD, and the testing algorithm avoids permutations. These contributions connect a richer causal target with statistically justified and computationally efficient inference.
summary.tldr: The paper develops estimation and testing tools for treatment effects on entire outcome distributions across subpopulations.

title: Conditional Distributional Treatment Effects: Doubly Robust Estimation and Testing

abstract: It is a fundamental challenge to ascertain whether the causal effect of a treatment on an outcome is identifiable in the presence of latent confounders, which serves as the logical prerequisite for recovering the causal effect in a partially observed system. While prior literature demonstrates that the causal effect is identifiable when there exist auxiliary variables subject to stringent structural constraints, this paper investigates identifiability of the causal effect without such variables. This means that we ground identifiability solely in the joint distribution of the treatment-outcome pair, which constitutes the irreducible statistical basis for causal effect identification. Focusing on linear structural causal models (SCMs), we provide a nuanced and complete characterization of identifiability of the causal effect contingent on the distributional properties of exogenous noises. Specifically, we formulate a set of mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive conditions regarding the Gaussianity of exogenous noises, ascertain under which conditions the causal effect is identifiable and under which it is not, while also quantifying the cardinality of the feasible solution set for the unidentifiable cases. Finally, we empirically validate our theoretical findings.
originalAbstract: It is a fundamental challenge to ascertain whether the causal effect of a treatment on an outcome is identifiable in the presence of latent confounders, which serves as the logical prerequisite for recovering the causal effect in a partially observed system. While prior literature demonstrates that the causal effect is identifiable when there exist auxiliary variables subject to stringent structural constraints, this paper investigates identifiability of the causal effect without such variables. This means that we ground identifiability solely in the joint distribution of the treatment-outcome pair, which constitutes the irreducible statistical basis for causal effect identification. Focusing on linear structural causal models (SCMs), we provide a nuanced and complete characterization of identifiability of the causal effect contingent on the distributional properties of exogenous noises. Specifically, we formulate a set of mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive conditions regarding the Gaussianity of exogenous noises, ascertain under which conditions the causal effect is identifiable and under which it is not, while also quantifying the cardinality of the feasible solution set for the unidentifiable cases. Finally, we empirically validate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Before estimating a treatment’s causal effect, one must establish whether the available observations determine that effect at all. Hidden confounders complicate this question because they can influence both treatment and outcome. This paper asks what can be identified using only the joint distribution of those two observed variables, without additional variables that satisfy special structural requirements.

The analysis focuses on linear structural causal models. Within that setting, the authors organize the possibilities according to whether the external noise terms are Gaussian. Their conditions are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, providing a complete classification within the studied framework. The classification distinguishes situations with an identifiable causal effect from those in which multiple effects remain compatible with the observations.

For the unidentifiable cases, the paper also determines how many feasible solutions remain. That describes the extent of ambiguity, rather than stopping at a yes-or-no verdict. Empirical results validate the theoretical findings. The central message is conditional: noise distributions can determine identifiability in these linear models even without auxiliary observations.
summary.tldr: For linear causal models with hidden confounders, the paper characterizes when treatment–outcome observations alone identify a causal effect.

title: Causal Effect Identifiability in the Presence of Latent Confounders Without Auxiliary Variables

abstract: Actor-critic (AC) methods are a cornerstone of reinforcement learning (RL) but offer limited interpretability. Current explainable RL methods seldom use state attributions to assist training. Rather, they treat all state features equally, thereby neglecting the heterogeneous impacts of individual state dimensions on the reward. We propose RKHS-SHAP-based Advanced Actor-Critic (RSA2C), an attribution-aware, kernelized, two-timescale AC algorithm, including Actor, Value Critic, and Advantage Critic. The Actor is instantiated in a vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) with a Mahalanobis-weighted operator-valued kernel, while the Value Critic and Advantage Critic reside in scalar RKHSs. These RKHS-enhanced components use sparsified dictionaries: the Value Critic maintains its own dictionary, while the Actor and Advantage Critic share one. State attributions, computed from the Value Critic via RKHS-SHAP (kernel mean embedding for on-manifold and conditional mean embedding for off-manifold expectations), are converted into Mahalanobis-gated weights that modulate Actor gradients and Advantage Critic targets. We derive a global, non-asymptotic convergence bound under state perturbations, showing stability through the perturbation-error term and efficiency through the convergence-error term. Empirical results on three continuous-control environments show that RSA2C achieves efficiency, stability, and interpretability. Our code is available at https://github.com/Na-Li66/RSA2C.

summary.tldr: RSA2C uses SHAP-derived state-feature importance to guide kernel actor–critic learning, with convergence analysis and continuous-control evaluations.

title: SHAP-Guided Kernel Actor-Critic for Explainable Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show remarkable semantic understanding but often struggle with structural understanding when processing graph topologies in a serialized format. Existing solutions rely on training external graph-based adapters or fine-tuning, which incur high costs and lost generalizability. In this work, we investigate the internal mechanisms of LLMs and present a critical finding: LLMs spontaneously reconstruct the graph’s topology internally, evidenced by a distinct "sawtooth" pattern in their attention maps that structurally aligns with the "token-level adjacency matrix". However, this intrinsic structural understanding is diluted by the attention sink. We theoretically formalize this dilution as a representation bottleneck, stemming from a fundamental conflict: the model’s anisotropic bias, essential for language tasks, suppresses the topology-aware local aggregation required for graph reasoning. To address this, we propose a training-free solution, named StructuraL Attention SHarpening (SLASH), which amplifies this internal structural understanding via a plug-and-play attention redistribution. Experiments on pure graph tasks and molecular prediction validate that SLASH delivers significant and consistent performance gains across diverse LLMs.

paragraphs: SLASH examines why language models struggle with graph structure when graphs are presented as serialized text. The authors find evidence that models already reconstruct topology internally: their attention maps exhibit a sawtooth pattern aligned with a token-level representation of graph adjacency. This suggests that useful structural information exists inside the model.

The paper argues that an attention sink dilutes this information. Its theoretical account describes a representation bottleneck: the model's directional bias, useful for language processing, suppresses the local aggregation needed to reason over graph connections. The problem therefore involves how existing structural signals influence computation, as well as whether the model can represent those signals.

Structural Attention Sharpening redistributes attention to amplify the internal topology-aware behavior. It is training-free and designed as a plug-in intervention, avoiding the need to train an external graph adapter or fine-tune the model. Experiments on graph tasks and molecular prediction report significant, consistent improvements across diverse language models. These findings support attention redistribution as a way to make existing structural representations more useful for prediction.
summary.tldr: SLASH redistributes attention without training to strengthen graph-structure signals already present inside language models.

title: SLASH the Sink: Sharpening Structural Attention Inside LLMs

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for reachability specifications is fundamental in sequential decision-making, yet theoretical guarantees remain less explored. A recent work achieves asymptotic convergence to optimal policies. However, this approach provides limited insight into convergence dynamics. In this work, we present an alternative approach that provides deeper theoretical insights into convergence. Our approach builds on PAC learning with assumptions. PAC learning guarantees near-optimal policies with high confidence in finite time but requires knowing internal MDP parameters like minimum transition probability. We argue that while these parameters are unknown in RL, they can be iteratively refined and estimated with increasing accuracy. By iteratively satisfying PAC conditions, we show that exact optimality can be achieved in the limit. Empirical evaluations on standard benchmarks validate our theoretical insights into convergence dynamics.

paragraphs: Reachability problems ask an agent to learn behavior that optimizes the chance of reaching a specified target. This paper studies how reinforcement learning can approach an exactly optimal policy and what explains its convergence along the way. Its starting point is probably approximately correct learning, which provides finite-time, high-confidence guarantees of near-optimal behavior under assumptions.

Those guarantees ordinarily require information about the underlying Markov decision process, such as the smallest transition probability. In reinforcement learning, such internal parameters are unknown. The authors propose refining their estimates iteratively, with increasing accuracy, so that the conditions needed for the approximate-learning guarantees can be progressively satisfied.

By repeatedly satisfying these conditions, the method achieves exact optimality in the limit. The distinction matters: finite-time guarantees concern near-optimal policies with high confidence, while exact optimality is an asymptotic result. Evaluations on standard benchmarks support the theoretical account of convergence dynamics. The contribution is an alternative route from assumption-dependent approximate guarantees to limiting optimality, together with greater insight into how the learning process converges.
summary.tldr: Iteratively refining unknown environment parameters connects finite-time approximate reachability guarantees to exact optimality in the limit.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Reachability: Guaranteeing Asymptotic Optimality

abstract: Accurately predicting the future trajectories of traffic participants is critical for safe, efficient, and human-friendly autonomous driving. Existing learning-based trajectory prediction methods are predominantly time-domain and insufficiently exploit latent frequency information, which limits their capability to capture low-frequency long-term dependencies and high-frequency short-term dynamics. To address this, we propose TF-FACE, a time-frequency learning framework via frequency-domain adaptive and controllable enhancement. TF-FACE introduces a fusion encoder with learnable gated frequency-domain attention that adaptively manipulates band-specific features for trajectory prediction. Building on the fused representation, we design a dual-stage decoder and a band-specific time–frequency dual-consistency loss to enable controllable decoupling and coupling across long- and short-term temporal scales, global and local scales, and then generate final multimodal predictions. Experiments on Argoverse 1 demonstrate that TF-FACE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, while maintaining real-time inference for autonomous driving. Additional experiments are conducted on Argoverse 2, further validating TF-FACE’s performance and generalizability.

paragraphs: TF-FACE predicts future trajectories of traffic participants by combining time-domain and frequency-domain information. The paper argues that predominantly time-domain methods underuse frequency structure, which can help distinguish slower, long-term patterns from faster, short-term dynamics. Capturing both is relevant to predicting movement across multiple temporal scales.

A fusion encoder uses learnable gated attention in the frequency domain to adaptively modify features from different frequency bands. A dual-stage decoder then works with the fused representation. Its band-specific time–frequency consistency loss supports controlled separation and recombination of long- and short-term information, as well as global and local structure, before producing multiple possible future trajectories.

This design makes the treatment of different motion scales an explicit part of both representation learning and prediction. On Argoverse 1, the method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while maintaining real-time inference. Additional Argoverse 2 experiments support its performance and generalizability. The findings suggest that adaptive frequency processing can improve trajectory prediction without sacrificing the reported real-time operating capability.
summary.tldr: TF-FACE adaptively combines temporal and frequency features to improve multimodal traffic trajectory prediction with real-time inference.

title: TF-FACE: Time-Frequency Fusion Learning via Frequency-Domain Adaptive and Controllable Enhancement for Trajectory Prediction

abstract: Medical diagnosis tasks often rely on heterogeneous information from multiple sources, such as medical images and clinical text. Multimodal fusion is therefore essential for improving classification performance and robustness. However, most existing methods assume a fixed and known modality set, making them less effective when the number or composition of modalities changes. To address this limitation, we propose a modality-agnostic medical multimodal fusion framework that can naturally accommodate an arbitrary number of input modalities. At the coarse-grained modality level, we represent each modality’s estimation of latent semantics as an uncertainty-aware probability distribution, and impose symmetric consistency constraints to achieve global cross-modal semantic alignment. At the fine-grained token level, we further design a token-level consistency constraint based on linear reconstruction. This constraint enables structured mutual verification of local semantics across modalities. Finally, for multimodal fusion, we adopt a multi-view consistency strategy to obtain a unified representation for diagnosis prediction. In particular, each modality is sequentially treated as a conditional view to suppress noise in the remaining modalities and extract shared semantics. Extensive experiments on five public and self-constructed multimodal medical datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed approach. Code is available at https://github.com/gjhgjbkg/SMMF.

paragraphs: Medical classification can draw on sources such as images and clinical text, but many fusion methods assume a fixed set of input modalities. This paper proposes a framework designed to accommodate an arbitrary number of modalities. Its central idea is to make the sources agree about shared meaning at both broad and detailed levels.

At the modality level, each source represents its estimate of latent semantics as a probability distribution that accounts for uncertainty. Symmetric consistency constraints align those estimates across sources. At the token level, a linear reconstruction constraint enables local pieces of information from different modalities to verify one another in a structured way.

For the final prediction, the framework treats each modality in turn as a conditional view, using it to suppress noise in the others and extract shared semantics. These views contribute to a unified representation for diagnosis prediction. Experiments on five public and self-constructed medical datasets demonstrate effectiveness and scalability, supporting consistency modeling as a way to combine changing collections of medical inputs.
summary.tldr: A modality-agnostic fusion framework aligns uncertain global meanings and local details to combine varying numbers of medical data sources.

title: Scalable Medical Multimodal Fusion via Symmetric Consistency Modeling

abstract: Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have advanced cross-modal reasoning by extending Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting to visual tasks. However, existing methods still rely heavily on explicit textual reasoning steps, leading to information loss, unstable perception–reasoning interaction, and high computational cost. Inspired by human cognition, we argue that effective visual reasoning emerges from a dynamic interplay between perception and latent thought, rather than a purely linear verbalization process. Motivated by this insight, we propose Latent-Driven Progressive Visual Reasoning (LDPVR), a framework that formulates multimodal reasoning as a Markov Chain of Recursive State Simplification, where explicit textual states are progressively refined under the guidance of latent transitions. Central to LDPVR is Interleaved Latent Grounding, which leverages latent semantic intent to actively retrieve fine-grained visual evidence and drive robust state evolution, enabling the model to iteratively reduce uncertainty before committing to simplified textual states. To optimize this process, we introduce a three-stage curriculum combining supervised fine-tuning, latent-text distillation, and reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Experiments on six multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that LDPVR improves reasoning accuracy while maintaining low inference latency.

paragraphs: Visual reasoning systems often express intermediate steps in text, which can lose visual information and make the interaction between perception and reasoning unstable or expensive. LDPVR approaches reasoning as a repeated exchange between latent thought and visual evidence. Explicit textual states become progressively simpler as latent transitions guide their refinement.

The framework models this process as a Markov chain of recursive state simplification. Its Interleaved Latent Grounding component uses latent semantic intent to retrieve detailed visual evidence. This allows the system to reduce uncertainty before settling on a simplified textual state, connecting each refinement to information from the image.

Training follows three stages: supervised fine-tuning, distillation between latent and textual representations, and reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization. Across six multimodal reasoning benchmarks, the authors report improved reasoning accuracy while maintaining low inference latency. The findings support an iterative relationship between visual grounding and internal reasoning, with concise textual states emerging through refinement rather than carrying the entire reasoning process.
summary.tldr: LDPVR alternates latent reasoning with targeted visual grounding to simplify textual states, improving accuracy while maintaining low inference latency.

title: Thinking in Latent Space: Progressive Multimodal Simplification for Visual Reasoning

abstract: Recent large language models (LLMs) have shown rapid progress on reading-based question answering (QA), where the evidence is explicitly provided or trivially retrievable. In contrast, real-world questions are often not paired with accurate evidence documents. The useful evidence resides in a massive collection of data lakes, necessitating searching as a prerequisite for answering. However, there is a lack of a comprehensive benchmark that requires searching and reasoning over a large collection of data lakes. To this end, we introduce LakeQA, a comprehensive benchmark for search-centric question answering over data lakes that jointly emphasizes searching and reasoning capabilities. LakeQA is built on a heterogeneous collection of 9.5 TB text resources from Wikipedia and open-source government data, spanning structured and unstructured data. To ensure the quality of LakeQA’s tasks, each sample is annotated by at least one Ph.D level expert. Each task requires long-horizon multi-hop reasoning with implicit intermediate steps: agents need to discover the correct document(s) and then compose evidence across sources to produce the answer. Intensive experiment results on seven frontier LLMs have demonstrated that LakeQA is challenging. For instance, GPT-5.2 only obtains an exact matching score of 14.73% on LakeQA. Overall LakeQA provides a realistic testbed for developing LLM agents that can both find and analyze data in modern data lakes.

paragraphs: LakeQA tests question answering when finding the right evidence is itself a substantial part of the problem. Many reading-based evaluations provide relevant material or make it easy to retrieve. This benchmark instead places useful information inside a large, heterogeneous data collection, requiring agents to search before they can assemble an answer.

Each task is annotated by at least one Ph.D.-level expert. This result reflects performance on a task that combines evidence discovery and reasoning. LakeQA provides a way to evaluate the complete process of locating and analyzing information in a large data lake.
summary.tldr: LakeQA evaluates agents on finding and combining evidence across a 9.5 TB data lake, exposing substantial challenges for tested frontier models.

title: LakeQA: An Exploratory QA Benchmark over a Million-Scale Data Lake

abstract: Recent progress in vision-language models (VLMs) has driven significant advances in video understanding. However, existing methods often act as naive empiricists, mapping video input directly to output without any mechanism to introspect or challenge inherent bias. In this work, we challenge this paradigm by reframing video reasoning as a Bayesian cognitive process. We propose Video-BCI (Bayesian Cognitive Integration of Self-Prior Hypotheses), a novel framework that first samples a set of Self-Prior Hypotheses to represent the model’s intuitive yet potentially biased cognitive state, and then guides the VLMs to perform a critical integration of these priors. This process encourages the model to challenge erroneous majority consensus in cases of high information divergence and to distill superior reasoning chains from its own prior space. The integration is driven by a composite Cognitive Utility Function comprising two intrinsic learning signals: Dialectical Uncertainty Signal (DUS) and Process Tracing Signal (PTS). The DUS incentivizes correct, non-majority judgments by quantifying both the conflict (entropy) among priors and their consensus-challenging strength. The PTS guides the model to trace and learn from reasoning paths within its own priors that lead to better answers, enabling self-driven procedural knowledge distillation. Extensive experiments on six mainstream benchmarks show that Video-BCI achieves new state-of-the-art (SOTA) results across the board. For example, it surpasses the previous best on the MMVU benchmark by 3.8%.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can answer a video question using an initial interpretation that reflects its own biases. Video-BCI makes those interpretations explicit by first sampling several self-prior hypotheses. It then guides the model to critically integrate them, treating video reasoning as a Bayesian cognitive process that can challenge its initial consensus.

A composite utility function supplies two learning signals. The Dialectical Uncertainty Signal considers disagreement among hypotheses and rewards correct judgments that challenge the majority. The Process Tracing Signal directs learning toward reasoning paths within the model’s own hypotheses that produce better answers. Together, they encourage scrutiny of conflicting interpretations and extraction of useful reasoning procedures from the model’s existing proposals.

Across six mainstream video-understanding benchmarks, Video-BCI achieves reported state-of-the-art results, including a 3.8% improvement over the previous best on MMVU. The findings support using multiple internal hypotheses as material for critical reasoning. The mechanism goes beyond counting agreement by considering when a majority interpretation is wrong and which reasoning paths lead toward better answers.
summary.tldr: Video-BCI improves video reasoning by critically combining the model’s own hypotheses and learning from reasoning paths that yield better answers.

title: Video-BCI: Bayesian Cognitive Integration of Self-Prior Hypotheses for Video Understanding

abstract: Unlike diffusion-based models that operate in continuous latent spaces, autoregressive unified multimodal models produce images by sequentially predicting discretized visual tokens. These tokens are derived from a codebook that maps embeddings to quantized visual patterns. The language-like architecture enables unified multimodal models to effectively capture text conditional information for generation, making them promising for text-to-image tasks. This also raises an interesting question: how safe are the images generated in such an autoregressive way? In this work, we propose iterative self-improving codebooks for safe autoregressive generation. We leverage the understanding and judgment capabilities of the unified multimodal model itself to identify unsafe generated images without human annotation. Subsequently, the inherent representations in the codebook are fixed to eliminate harmful mappings. Our method comprises two steps: first, we use the unified model to identify unsafe generations and construct corresponding harmful and safe image-text pairs. These pairs are used to construct the Harmful Space and guide updates to the codebook, thereby eliminating harmful outputs. Second, we perform adaptive fine-tuning on the codebook within the harmless space using safe image-text pairs to ensure the quality of generated images. These two steps are repeated until no further improvement is observed, producing a safety-enhanced model codebook. Without additional external feedback, the safety of models is improved iteratively.

paragraphs: Autoregressive multimodal models generate images as sequences of discrete visual tokens. A codebook connects these tokens to quantized visual patterns, making it a direct point of intervention for image safety. This paper proposes repeatedly updating that codebook using the model's own ability to understand and judge its generated images.

The first step identifies unsafe generations without human annotation and constructs corresponding harmful and safe image-text pairs. These pairs define a harmful representation space and guide codebook changes aimed at removing harmful mappings. The second step adaptively fine-tunes the codebook within the harmless space using safe pairs, with the goal of preserving the quality of generated images.

The two steps repeat until further improvement is no longer observed. The authors report iterative safety improvement without additional external feedback. The approach matters because it connects the model's judgment capability to the visual representations used for generation, while including a separate quality-preservation step. Its stopping rule is based on observed improvement in this iterative process.
summary.tldr: A multimodal model uses its own safety judgments to iteratively revise its visual codebook while fine-tuning safe representations to preserve image quality.

title: Safe Autoregressive Image Generation with Iterative Self-Improving Codebooks

abstract: Large language models are beginning to introduce a new paradigm for compilation: instead of only assisting at the source level, they can operate directly on intermediate representations (IRs), the compiler’s internal code representation, Early studies suggest that LLM-guided optimization can sometimes rival traditional compiler optimizations on selected programs, but evidence remains fragmented. Yet the community still lacks a rigorous IR-level benchmark that tests whether a model not only understands IR but can rewrite it under compiler-grade semantic constraints with meaningful performance impact. We present CIRBench, a benchmark of 800 curated IR instances spanning four compiler-oriented tracks: Analysis infers IR properties, Repair fixes invalid IR, Refactor applies a single semantics-preserving compiler optimization, and Transform performs performance-oriented rewrites, together mirroring core optimization responsibilities in modern compilers. CIRBench combines verifier, equivalence checking, and end-to-end performance measurement into a unified, layered correctness-aware evaluation of LLMs on IR. On six mainstream LLMs, CIRBench shows that current models fail on many IR analysis and rewriting instances and on median underperform the compiler baseline, but we also observe a maximum speedup of $4.96\times$ over -O3. These findings highlight both the opportunities and the remaining challenges of using LLMs inside optimizing compilers.

paragraphs: CIRBench asks whether language models can reliably work on LLVM intermediate representation, the internal code format used during compilation. Producing plausible code is insufficient here: a rewrite must satisfy compiler constraints, preserve program meaning when required, and deliver useful performance. The benchmark brings these requirements into a single evaluation.

Its 800 curated instances cover four responsibilities. Analysis tests understanding of IR properties; Repair tests correction of invalid IR; Refactor asks for one semantics-preserving optimization; and Transform targets performance-oriented rewrites. Evaluation combines a verifier, equivalence checking, and end-to-end performance measurement, so structural validity, behavioral correctness, and speed can all inform the result.

Across six mainstream language models, the results show frequent failures in both analysis and rewriting, with median performance below the compiler baseline. There are also individual successes, including a maximum speedup of 4.96 times over -O3. The combination matters: the best observed result demonstrates an opportunity for model-guided optimization, while the median and failure results show that such gains are not yet dependable across the benchmark.
summary.tldr: CIRBench finds occasional large compiler-optimization gains from LLMs, alongside frequent failures and median performance below the compiler baseline.

title: CIRBench: Evaluating Large Language Models as LLVM IR Optimizers

abstract: Inferring cellular trajectories from destructive snapshots is complicated by the challenges of stochasticity and non-conservative mass dynamics such as cell proliferation and apoptosis. Existing unbalanced Optimal Transport (OT) methods treat mass as a continuous fluid, performing inference at the population level. However, this macroscopic view often fails to capture the discrete, jump-like nature of birth-death events at single-cell resolution, which is essential for understanding lineage branching and fate decisions. We present Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridge (USB), a simulation-free framework for learning underlying dynamics that effectively integrates both stochastic and unbalanced effects which also models the discrete, jump-like birth–death dynamics at single-cell resolution. Theoretically, USB provides a tractable solution to the Branching Schrödinger Bridge (BSB) problem, offering a rigorous microscopic interpretation where individual cells undergo both Brownian motion and discrete birth-death jumps. Technically, the method implements an efficient solver by introducing a simulation-free training objective that effectively scales to high-dimensional omics data. Empirically, we demonstrate on both simulated and real-world datasets that USB not only achieves trajectory reconstruction performance better than or comparable to deterministic baselines but also uniquely enables realistic discrete simulation of birth-death dynamics at single-cell resolution.

paragraphs: Reconstructing how cells change over time is difficult when measurements destroy the cells being observed. Researchers must connect separate snapshots while accounting for random changes, cell division, and cell death. Existing unbalanced optimal transport methods represent changing cell populations as continuous mass, which can obscure the individual birth and death events that produce branching lineages.

Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridge, or USB, instead gives the dynamics an individual-cell interpretation. Cells undergo both Brownian motion and discrete birth–death jumps. The framework provides a tractable solution to the Branching Schrödinger Bridge problem, connecting population-level observations with a microscopic account of how cells move, multiply, and disappear. Its training objective avoids simulation and is designed to scale to high-dimensional omics measurements.

On simulated and real datasets, USB reconstructs trajectories better than or comparably to deterministic baselines. The additional contribution is its ability to simulate discrete birth–death events at single-cell resolution. Simulation-free training therefore supports a model that can subsequently generate branching cellular dynamics, rather than only describe population movement.
summary.tldr: USB learns cellular trajectories from snapshots while explicitly modeling random movement and discrete cell birth and death.

title: Beyond Continuity: Simulation-free Reconstruction of Discrete Branching Dynamics from Single-cell Snapshots

abstract: Graph learning has been increasingly deployed in critical and sensitive domains, raising pressing demands for trustworthiness-robustness, fairness, and beyond. However, these properties are often undermined by various perturbations, which induce distributional uncertainty and compromise the trustworthiness of graph learning. To address this, we propose DICT, a novel framework that models distributional uncertainty to achieve trustworthy graph learning. Specifically, DICT formulates a unified optimization objective that captures perturbation-induced distributional shifts in graph topology, node features, and labels, and minimizes the worst-case risk over the uncertainty set. However, directly optimizing this objective in its primal form leads to an infinite-dimensional problem. To make this problem tractable, we integrate strong duality and local Lipschitz continuity of the loss, reformulating the objective as a finite-dimensional min-max problem. We focus on robustness and fairness as primary instantiations of DICT because they are not only critical in real-world applications, but also provide transferable modeling principles for broader trustworthiness objectives. By formulating fairness in the form of an uncertainty set, DICT pioneers unified robustness and fairness within a single optimization framework. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and backbones demonstrate that DICT consistently improves both robustness and fairness, validating the effectiveness and adaptability of the DICT framework.

paragraphs: Graph-learning systems can lose robustness or fairness when their connections, node features, or labels change. DICT treats such perturbations as uncertainty about the data distribution. It seeks a model that minimizes the worst-case risk over a specified set of possible distributions, bringing several sources of graph uncertainty into one optimization objective.

Directly solving that objective would require an infinite-dimensional optimization problem. The authors use strong duality and local Lipschitz continuity of the loss to reformulate it as a finite-dimensional min–max problem. This step makes the framework tractable while retaining its focus on adverse shifts represented by the uncertainty set.

The paper develops robustness and fairness as its main applications, expressing fairness requirements through an uncertainty set so both objectives fit the same framework. Experiments across diverse benchmarks and model backbones show consistent improvements in robustness and fairness. The results support uncertainty modeling as a shared approach to these two properties, with the formulation also intended to provide modeling principles for broader trustworthiness objectives.
summary.tldr: DICT unifies graph robustness and fairness through tractable worst-case optimization over distributional uncertainty.

title: Uncertainty-Constrained Trustworthiness for Graph Learning
Active Perception and Reinforcement Learning
Complexity and Cooperation in Q-Learning

abstract: We consider the task of driving a remote control car at high speeds through unstructured outdoor environments. We present an approach in which supervised learning is first used to estimate depths from single monocular images. The learning algorithm can be trained either on real camera images labeled with ground-truth distances to the closest obstacles, or on a training set consisting of synthetic graphics images. The resulting algorithm is able to learn monocular vision cues that accurately estimate the relative depths of obstacles in a scene. Reinforcement learning/policy search is then applied within a simulator that renders synthetic scenes. This learns a control policy that selects a steering direction as a function of the vision system’s output. We present results evaluating the predictive ability of the algorithm both on held out test data, and in actual autonomous driving experiments.

The resulting algorithm is able to learn monocular vision cues that accurately estimate the relative depths of obstacles in a scene. paragraphs: This paper addresses steering a remote-control car at high speed through unstructured outdoor environments. Its approach connects two learned components: a vision system that estimates obstacle depth from a single image and a control policy that uses the vision system’s output to choose a steering direction.

The vision component is trained through supervised learning. Training examples can be real camera images labeled with measured distances to the nearest obstacles, or synthetic images generated with graphics. The resulting algorithm learns visual cues that estimate the relative depths of obstacles in a scene. This supplies depth information from individual monocular images for the steering component.

The control policy is learned using reinforcement learning or policy search inside a simulator that renders synthetic scenes. It learns how to turn the vision system’s output into steering decisions. The authors evaluate predictive ability on held-out data and report actual autonomous driving experiments. These evaluations connect the depth-estimation component with the broader driving task, while the overall method shows how supervised perception and simulated policy learning can be combined.
summary.tldr: A car learns to steer around obstacles by combining depth estimates from single images with a control policy trained in simulation.

title: High speed obstacle avoidance using monocular vision and reinforcement learning

abstract: Cost curves have recently been introduced as an alternative or complement to ROC curves in order to visualize binary classifiers performance. Of importance to both cost and ROC curves is the computation of confidence intervals along with the curves themselves so that the reliability of a classifier's performance can be assessed. Computing confidence intervals for the difference in performance between two classifiers allows to determine whether one classifier performs significantly better than another. A simple procedure to obtain confidence intervals for costs or the difference between two costs, under various operating conditions, is to perform bootstrap resampling of the testset. In this paper, we derive exact bootstrap distributions of these values and use these distributions to obtain confidence intervals, under various operating conditions. Performances of these confidence intervals are measured in terms of coverage accuracies. Simulations show excellent results.

paragraphs: Cost curves visualize binary classifier performance under different operating conditions. A curve alone does not convey how reliable its estimated costs are. This paper addresses that uncertainty by constructing confidence intervals for both a classifier's cost and the difference in cost between two classifiers.

Bootstrap resampling of a test set provides one route to such intervals. The authors derive the exact bootstrap distributions of the relevant quantities at individual operating conditions and use them to calculate confidence intervals. The resulting intervals for cost differences support assessing whether one classifier performs significantly better than another under the condition being considered.

The evaluation measures coverage accuracy: how well the confidence intervals achieve their intended coverage in simulations. The authors report excellent simulation results. The contribution is a precise account of the bootstrap distribution underlying pointwise cost comparisons. Exactness here refers to that bootstrap distribution; the empirical coverage evaluation separately assesses the behavior of the resulting intervals. This connects performance visualization with a more explicit treatment of statistical reliability.
summary.tldr: Exact pointwise bootstrap distributions provide confidence intervals for classifier costs and cost differences, with strong simulated coverage.

title: Pointwise exact bootstrap distributions of cost curves

abstract: For two-class classification, it is common to classify by setting a threshold on class probability estimates, where the threshold is determined by {ROC} curve analysis. An analog for multi-class classification is learning a new class partitioning of the multiclass probability simplex to minimize empirical misclassification costs. We analyze the interplay between systematic errors in the class probability estimates and cost matrices for multi-class classification. We explore the effect on the class partitioning of five different transformations of the cost matrix. Experiments on benchmark datasets with naive Bayes and quadratic discriminant analysis show the effectiveness of learning a new partition matrix compared to previously proposed methods.

paragraphs: In binary classification, a threshold on estimated class probabilities can determine the predicted class, with the threshold chosen through ROC analysis. This paper considers the multiclass counterpart: learning how to divide the space of class-probability estimates into decision regions. The objective is to minimize empirical misclassification costs.

The authors analyze how systematic errors in probability estimates interact with the cost matrix. This matters because the decision depends both on the estimated probabilities and on how costly different mistakes are. They also examine how five transformations of the cost matrix affect the resulting partition of the multiclass probability space.

Experiments on benchmark datasets use probability estimates from naive Bayes and quadratic discriminant analysis. The results show the effectiveness of learning a new partition matrix compared with previously proposed methods. The approach makes the decision stage itself an object of learning, addressing how imperfect probability estimates should be converted into cost-sensitive multiclass predictions in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Learning a new partition of multiclass probability estimates provides an effective way to make cost-sensitive predictions despite systematic estimation errors.

title: Cost-sensitive multi-class classification from probability estimates

abstract: In recent years, total variation (TV) and Euler's elastica (EE) have been successfully applied to image processing tasks such as denoising and inpainting. This paper investigates how to extend TV and EE to the supervised learning settings on high dimensional data. The supervised learning problem can be formulated as an energy functional minimization under Tikhonov regularization scheme, where the energy is composed of a squared loss and a total variation smoothing (or Euler's elastica smoothing). Its solution via variational principles leads to an Euler-Lagrange PDE. However, the PDE is always high-dimensional and cannot be directly solved by common methods. Instead, radial basis functions are utilized to approximate the target function, reducing the problem to finding the linear coefficients of basis functions. We apply the proposed methods to supervised learning tasks (including binary classification, multi-class classification, and regression) on benchmark data sets. Extensive experiments have demonstrated promising results of the proposed methods.

paragraphs: Total variation and Euler's elastica have been useful for image-processing tasks such as denoising and filling missing regions. This paper investigates how to bring these forms of smoothing into supervised learning on high-dimensional data. It frames learning as minimizing an energy that combines squared prediction loss with one of the two smoothing terms.

The formulation follows a Tikhonov regularization scheme, balancing agreement with training targets against the chosen smoothing requirement. Applying variational principles leads to an Euler–Lagrange partial differential equation. However, the equation is high-dimensional and cannot be directly handled by common solution methods, creating a computational obstacle to using the formulation.

The authors address that obstacle by approximating the target function with radial basis functions. This turns the task into finding the basis functions' linear coefficients. They evaluate the resulting methods on binary classification, multiclass classification, and regression benchmarks, reporting promising experimental results. The contribution is both an extension of these smoothing ideas to supervised learning and a workable approximation for the resulting high-dimensional problem.
summary.tldr: Radial basis approximations make total-variation and Euler's-elastica regularization usable for high-dimensional supervised learning.

title: Total Variation and Euler's Elastica for Supervised Learning

abstract: Low-rank matrix decomposition has gained great popularity recently in scaling up kernel methods to large amount of data. However, some limitations could prevent them from working effectively in certain domains. For example, many existing approaches are intrinsically unsupervised, which does not incorporate side information (e.g., class labels) to produce task specific decomposition; also, they typically work “transductively” and the factorization does not generalize to new samples, causing lot of inconvenience for updated environment. To solve these problems, in this paper we propose an “inductive”-flavored method for low-rank kernel decomposition with priors or side information. We achieve this by generalizing the Nystróm method in a novel way. On the one hand, our approach employs a highly flexible, nonparametric structure that allows us to generalize the low-rank factors to arbitrarily new samples; on the other hand, it has linear time and space complexities, which can be orders of magnitudes faster than existing approaches and renders great efficiency in learning a low-rank kernel decomposition. Empirical results demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of the proposed method.

paragraphs: This paper tackles two obstacles to using low-rank kernel decompositions in changing, task-specific settings. Many existing methods do not use side information such as class labels, and their factors are tied to the samples already present. The authors seek a decomposition that can reflect the learning task and also produce factors for newly arriving samples.

Their approach generalizes the Nyström method using a flexible nonparametric structure. Priors or side information can influence the decomposition, while the learned construction generalizes the low-rank factors to arbitrary new samples. These capabilities connect the approximation to supervised information and give it an inductive character, addressing the inconvenience of a factorization restricted to the original data.

The method has linear time and space complexities. The abstract states that it can be orders of magnitude faster than existing approaches, rather than claiming that speedup in every situation. Empirical results support its efficacy and efficiency. The contribution combines task-aware decomposition, extension to new samples, and computational scalability within one low-rank kernel method.
summary.tldr: A generalized Nyström method incorporates side information and extends low-rank kernel factors to new samples with linear time and space complexity.

title: Improved Nystrom Low-rank Decomposition with Priors
